entries.commentary: Judah took the daughter of Shuah and had Er, Onan, and Shelah; and Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord slew him.

Onan was told to go in unto his brother's wife and raise up seed to his brother, and he refused, spilling it on the ground, and the Lord slew him also. The sin was refusing to raise up seed to his brother, not the act itself; do not build a doctrine on the wrong point. What happened here later became law: the husband's brother raises up the name of the dead, and he that refuses has his shoe loosed and his face spat in, and his house carries the reproach.

Judah promised Tamar to Shelah and did not perform it. When she saw Shelah was grown and she was not given to him, she put off her widow's garments, covered herself with a vail, and sat where Judah would pass. Judah thought her to be an harlot because of the attire; the scriptures show a harlot was always known by her dress, as the woman with the attire of an harlot and subtil of heart. She took his signet, bracelets, and staff as a pledge, and conceived by him.

When Judah heard Tamar was with child by whoredom he said, Bring her forth, and let her be burnt. A woman promised in the covenant that plays the harlot and brings an heir by another disobeys the law of the Most High, and her reproach is not blotted out; that is why the judgment was so heavy. Then she produced the signet, bracelets, and staff, and Judah acknowledged them: She hath been more righteous than I, because that I gave her not to Shelah my son. And he knew her again no more.

Twins were in her womb: the midwife bound a scarlet thread on the hand of the first, but his brother broke forth first and was called Pharez, and after him came Zarah with the scarlet thread. Judah's line went down into Egypt in the end, and Judah died there with his brethren; and Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation.

If there be a controversy between men, the judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked; the wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine, for the labourer is worthy of his reward. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

If brethren dwell together and one of them die and have no child, the wife of the dead was not to marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother took her to wife, and the firstborn she bare succeeded in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife. It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt: he met thee by the way and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not. At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

Boaz went up to the gate, called the kinsman of whom he had spoken to turn aside and sit down, and took ten men of the elders of the city to sit with them. What he is doing is calling witnesses. He is about to make a purchase, so he calls witnesses, that it can be put in the books for the future that this is what was done.

Boaz laid the matter before the kinsman: Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land which was our brother Elimelech's. If thou wilt redeem it, redeem it; but if not, tell me, for there is none to redeem it beside thee, and I am after thee. And the kinsman said, I will redeem it. What is this going back to? The law of the land, the law of inheritance when it comes to land, read back in the book of Numbers. The husband died and the two sons died, and the only person left is the wife with the land; so she instinctively went to Boaz, and Boaz is now conducting the laws of the land of who it should be passed down to, going down the list of inheritance.

What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. Whoever took the land had to take the dead brother's wife with it; Ruth the Moabitess came along as a parcel of the land, to keep the name of Mahlon alive. What law is that going back to? That law goes back to [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25), the duty of the husband's brother: the widow of the dead does not marry without unto a stranger, and the firstborn she bears succeeds in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. This law was taught in full when it was read ahead at [Ruth 1:6-9](/bible/ruth/1#v6) in these notes: the firstborn carries the weight of the name, and the shoe was loosed from him that would not build up his brother's house.

The kinsman said, I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself, for I cannot redeem it. In other words, I already have kids in the way; I cannot do it, I am not doing it.

Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing: for to confirm all things, a man plucked off his shoe and gave it to his neighbour, and this was a testimony in Israel. So the kinsman said unto Boaz, Buy it for thee, and he drew off his shoe. You can read about that shoe back in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25).

Boaz said unto the elders and unto all the people, Ye are witnesses this day that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi; moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place. What law is Boaz exercising in this? Love thy neighbour as thyself. That is what Boaz was putting into place and applying, and that is why he is mentioned in the scriptures.

All the people that were in the gate and the elders said, We are witnesses. They blessed the marriage: the Lord make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel; and let thy house be like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah, of the seed which the Lord shall give thee of this young woman. In that blessing they are prophesying about David to come.

So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife; and when he went in unto her, the Lord gave her conception, and she bare a son. The women said unto Naomi, Blessed be the Lord, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel; he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him.

Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it; and the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying, There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David. Why did Naomi take that child from Ruth the Moabitess? Because it is not the custom of Israel to allow a child to be raised up under the hand of a heathen. Although Ruth was used to keep Mahlon's name alive in Israel, and although she was brought in, she was a vessel; she did not have the same standing of rights as an Israelite woman, and she had no hand in raising the child. Naomi took it and raised it as her own, so that it could learn the ways of Israel.

Now these are the generations of Pharez: Pharez is of Judah, so this is the lineage of Judah, how they came about right down to the king. Pharez begat Hezron, and Hezron begat Ram, and Ram begat Amminadab, and Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon, and Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed, and Obed begat Jesse, and Jesse begat David. We read that lineage in Matthew chapter 1: how David came about, how Solomon came about, ultimately down to Christ.

cases.name: Joseph
cases.charge: Refusing his master's wife: how can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?
cases.summary: Sold by his brothers, bought by Potiphar, tempted daily by his master's wife, Joseph refused, fled, and was jailed on her lie. The Lord was with him in the pit, in the prison, and in the palace, and he became the man through whom the whole house of Israel was kept alive.
cases.offense: The refusal is not a single moment of resistance but a daily one: she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not unto her. His stated ground is the one the case turns on. He names his master's trust first and then goes past it to the real bar, sinning against God, before Sinai, while serving as a Hebrew sold into Egypt (Genesis 39:8-10). Her repeated pressure did not make adultery less wicked. Genesis does not record a hearing at which he answered her accusation; it does record his later insistence that he had done nothing deserving imprisonment (Genesis 40:15). When she caught his garment, he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:11-12). Escape from the sin cost him the appearance of innocence in her story, but he did not recover the garment by surrendering to the demand. In prison he continued serving, noticed the distress of the other prisoners, and directed the interpretation of their dreams to God (Genesis 40:4-8). Faithfulness continued before deliverance came.
cases.judgment: The Lord was with Joseph in Potiphar's house and showed him mercy in prison (Genesis 39:2; Genesis 39:21-23). When he later stood before Pharaoh, he did not claim the interpretation of dreams as his own power: God would give the answer (Genesis 41:16). Favour followed him through service, confinement, and government; it was not measured merely by freedom from hardship. He was raised to govern the country that had bought him and became the means by which the family that sold him survived the famine (Genesis 41:56). His own verdict on the whole sequence is the centre of the case: ye thought evil against me (Genesis 50:20); but God meant it unto good.

When she caught his garment, he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:11-12). verses.text: And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.
And the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
And his master saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand.
And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

And it came to pass from the time that he had made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.
And he left all that he had in Joseph’s hand; and he knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat. And Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured.
And it came to pass after these things, that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.
But he refused, and said unto his master’s wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand;
There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?
And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
And it came to pass about this time, that Joseph went into the house to do his business; and there was none of the men of the house there within.
And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.
But the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
And the keeper of the prison committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners that were in the prison; and whatsoever they did there, he was the doer of it.
The keeper of the prison looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the Lord was with him, and that which he did, the Lord made it to prosper.
And Pharaoh said unto his servants, Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?
And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Forasmuch as God hath shewed thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou art:
Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled: only in the throne will I be greater than thou.
And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, See, I have set thee over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph’s hand, and arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck;
And he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I am Pharaoh, and without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.
And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.
He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:
Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron:
Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.
The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free.
He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance:
To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.
When the righteous was sold, she forsook him not, but delivered him from sin: she went down with him into the pit,

And left him not in bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom, and power against those that oppressed him: as for them that had accused him, she shewed them to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory.
Neither was there a young man born like Joseph, a governor of his brethren, a stay of the people, whose bones were regarded of the Lord.

After two full years Pharaoh dreamed: seven well favoured kine eaten up by seven ill favoured ones, and seven good ears devoured by seven thin ears blasted with the east wind. He saw different variations of the number seven, as the butler and the baker saw variations of three; the dream is a resemblance of one thing to another. His spirit was troubled, and none of the magicians and wise men of Egypt could interpret the dreams unto Pharaoh.

Pharaoh told Joseph he had heard he could understand a dream to interpret it, and Joseph gave all the praise to the Most High: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. The Most High reveals his secrets to his servants, and the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him. That is why the interpretation was with Joseph and not with the magicians of Egypt.

The dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice because the thing is established by God, and God will surely bring it to pass. Joseph did not stop at the interpretation; he gave the counsel: take up the fifth part of the land in the seven plenteous years and store it up, so Egypt could ration food through the years of famine. That shows what was on Joseph: he was wise, understanding, and diligent. A prudent man foresees the evil coming and makes preparation so he is not consumed in it; the simple pass on and are punished. There is treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spends it up; spending irrationally is a spirit of folly.

Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is? Israel has always been a wise and understanding people: Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in ancient Babylon, up until this day, a people responsible for many inventions and cunning arts. The children of Israel brought to Babylon were skilful in all wisdom, cunning in knowledge, understanding science, and able to stand in the king's palace to give counsel; and they were taught the tongue of the Chaldeans, for we have the capability to understand multiple languages as well.

Pharaoh set Joseph over his house and over all the land of Egypt; only in the throne was Pharaoh greater. Without Joseph no man lifted up his hand or foot in all Egypt: nothing moved unless Joseph decreed it. The Most High called for the famine and sent a man before them, even Joseph: sold for a servant, his feet hurt with fetters, laid in iron until the time that his word came; then the king loosed him and made him lord of his house, to bind his princes at his pleasure and teach his senators wisdom. Whether prince or common man, Joseph could bind any man in Egypt.

Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnathpaaneah and gave him Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On to wife. These heathens always like to change our names; that is one reason America is called spiritual Egypt, because they do the same thing that ancient Egypt did.

Joseph called the firstborn Manasseh, forgetting, for God had made him forget all his toil and all his father's house; and the second called he Ephraim, fruitful, for God had caused him to be fruitful in the land of his affliction. Ephraim was the second born, yet Ephraim possessed the kingship: the first king of the Northern Kingdom, Jeroboam, was of the tribe of Ephraim, not of Manasseh. Ephraim is the head tribe of the Northern Kingdom. Jacob set that in place. When Joseph saw his father lay his right hand upon Ephraim's head it displeased him, and he tried to move it to Manasseh's head; but Jacob refused and said, his younger brother shall be greater than he; and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.

The seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said. Another word for dearth is famine: no food, no sustenance to nourish the body. The dearth was in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread, because Joseph had stored up the seven years of plenty. All countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn.

All the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt went up with Joseph and his brethren and his father's house, with chariots and horsemen, a very great company. The Canaanites saw the mourning in the floor of Atad and said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; wherefore the place was called Abelmizraim, which means the mourning of the Egyptians, beyond Jordan. The Israelites and the Egyptians were compared as looking like one people, because the Egyptians are black and the Israelites are black. The Bible dictionary defines Ham as the progenitor of the dark races, and Egypt was of Ham; the people sitting in that land today are not the true ancient Egyptians of the scriptures.

His sons did unto him according as he commanded them, and carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre; and Joseph returned into Egypt, he and his brethren, and all that went up with him.

When Joseph's brethren saw that their father was dead, they said, Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him; for they had sold him as a slave into Egypt. They sent a messenger pleading forgiveness and fell down before his face: Behold, we be thy servants. Joseph wept and answered, Fear not: for am I in the place of God? Joseph dwelt in Egypt and lived an hundred and ten years, and saw the children of Ephraim of the third generation; the children of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees. cases.name: Potiphar's wife
cases.charge: Soliciting her husband's servant day by day, and bearing false witness against him when he fled
cases.summary: She asked Joseph to lie with her and he refused, telling her it would be a great wickedness and a sin against God. When she caught him by the garment and he left it in her hand and fled, she kept the garment and turned it into evidence against him. The record gives her offense and the statute it breaks, and never gives her sentence.
cases.offense: His master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, Lie with me (Genesis 39:7), and she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not unto her (Genesis 39:10), so the solicitation was sustained and not a moment's impulse. His refusal names the offense before any law was written at Sinai: there is none greater in this house than I, neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife; how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God (Genesis 39:9). Adultery was known to be sin from the beginning. Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws (Genesis 26:5), and even a heathen king rebuked Isaac on the same ground, one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us (Genesis 26:10), so the nations themselves knew it carried guilt. Then, on a day when none of the men of the house were within, she caught him by his garment, and he left it in her hand  and fled (Genesis 39:11-12), which is the example the wise man commands: flee from sin as from the face of a serpent, for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee, the teeth  thereof are as the teeth of a lion (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 21:2). The solicitation was followed by false witness. She called the men of her house and said, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us, he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice, and she laid up the garment by her until his lord came home (Genesis 39:14-16). The same mouth that had flattered him turned and accused him: the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil, but her end is bitter as wormwood, and her ways are moveable (Proverbs 5:3-6), and more bitter than death is the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands, whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her (Ecclesiastes 7:26). The later law requires diligent inquiry and directs that a false witness receive the consequence intended for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). That statute identifies the gravity of false accusation; Genesis does not say an Israelite court applied it in Egypt.
cases.judgment: The judgment recorded falls on the innocent man. His master's wrath was kindled, and he took Joseph and put him into the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound (Genesis 39:19-20). No inquiry or hearing of Joseph's defence is described. Proverbs warns of the force of a husband's jealousy: jealousy is the rage of a man, therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance, he will not regard any ransom (Proverbs 6:34-35). Against the woman no later sentence is recorded. Her offense is double under the law, the solicitation and then the false witness, and both stand written with no penalty set against them. What the record does report is where the favour went: the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison (Genesis 39:21), and the psalm carries it on, whose feet they hurt with fetters, he was laid in iron, until the time that his word came, the word of the Lord tried him (Psalms 105:18-19). The prison became part of the road to government, but Joseph's eventual deliverance did not make the accusation true.

Accidents happen, and the Most High put laws in place for when these things happened. If it was for sure an accident, the man is not worthy of death, as the scripture says.

The elders of his own city shall fetch him from there and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die. The landmark establishes the boundaries of a man's property, where it begins and where it ends. A man who keeps nudging his neighbour's landmark over little by little until he has taken an acre is stealing land; the dictionary notes it was considered equal to theft.

verses.text: And it came to pass after these things, that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.
But he refused, and said unto his master’s wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand;
There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?
And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
And it came to pass about this time, that Joseph went into the house to do his business; and there was none of the men of the house there within.
And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
And it came to pass, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and was fled forth,
That she called unto the men of her house, and spake unto them, saying, See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice:
And it came to pass, when he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled, and got him out.
And she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home.
And she spake unto him according to these words, saying, The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me:
And it came to pass, as I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled out.
And it came to pass, when his master heard the words of his wife, which she spake unto him, saying, After this manner did thy servant to me; that his wrath was kindled.
And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.
Thou shalt not commit adultery.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
If a false witness rise up against any man to testify against him that which is wrong;
Then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before the Lord, before the priests and the judges, which shall be in those days;
And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
Then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother: so shalt thou put the evil away from among you.
He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:
Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron:
Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.

cases.name: Job
cases.charge: Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; sinning not with his lips in all his loss
cases.summary: Job of Uz feared God and eschewed evil. Under a trial limited by God's command, he lost his substance, his children, and then his health, yet held fast his integrity. When God answered, Job humbled himself and repented of words beyond his understanding. He prayed for his accusing friends, and the Lord restored him.
cases.offense: The commendation is given by God before the trial and repeated after it began: hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God and escheweth evil (Job 1:8), and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him to destroy him without cause (Job 2:3). The obedience is not endurance only. He acted as a priest for his own household: when the days of their feasting were gone about, and every one had kept his day, Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all, for Job said, it may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts; thus did Job continually (Job 1:5). His defence recalls practical righteousness: when he went out to the gate through the city, the young men saw him and hid themselves, the aged arose and stood, the princes refrained talking, and the nobles held their peace (Job 29:7-10). He delivered the poor that cried and the fatherless, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, searched out a cause he did not know before judging it, and broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the spoil out of his teeth (Job 29:12-17). He also made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). His righteousness included investigation, not merely sympathy: he sought the facts and rescued the oppressed from the wicked. That stands against his friends' readiness to explain his suffering by accusing him without establishing their charge. Satan's charge was that the obedience  was bought: doth Job fear God for nought, hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side (Job 1:9-10). The trial has limits set by God. Satan asked leave and was given it in limits both times: all that he hath is in thy power, only upon himself put not forth thine hand (Job 1:12), and then, behold, he is in thine hand, but save his life (Job 2:6). And when the property, the servants and all ten children were taken in a single day, he worshipped and said, the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord; in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly (Job 1:20-22). After his body was afflicted, his wife urged him to abandon his integrity: dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die (Job 2:9), and he answered her, thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh; what, shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips (Job 2:10).
cases.judgment: The Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before. So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, seven sons and three daughters, and in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job; and he saw his sons' sons, even four generations. James: ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.

entries.commentary: This first verse tells you who Job is, what land he lived in, and his character. Just because he lived in the land of Uz does not mean he was of that nation, because he was a son of God. It is the same thing today: we live in America but we are not Caucasians. There are brothers that live in Europe and they are not Caucasians either, but they are the sons of God.

Job had seven sons and three daughters, and his substance was seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she asses, so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east. His sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day. When it says "every man his day," they were talking about their birthdays. Whenever somebody's birthday came around they would say, "this is my day, this is my day." Now people have gotten to the point where it is, "this is my month, my birthday month, so I am celebrating the whole month." Same thing with this. Job sanctified them and rose up early to offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all, for Job said it may be that his sons had sinned and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually. -

When it says "the sons of God," this is talking about the line, the lineage of Adam. Before we were called Israelites we were called the sons of God, and even still today we are called the sons of the living God. So this is talking about the same thing; it is not just talking about angels alone. -

This is Satan talking to the Lord. The Lord says, have you considered My servant Job, have you ever tried Job, you walking up and down the earth, have you tried My servant, because he is an upright man. It is the same thing with us today. Every time we do more good works, the harder Satan comes at you. When you fast, the trials get worse, because you are showing God that you are upright through your fasting, striving to be that righteous vessel He wants you to be. So in order to see how strong you are, Satan is going to try you, and he is always going to go to the Lord for permission.

Satan said, does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not made a hedge about him and blessed the work of his hands? Satan is telling the Most High that Job is only worshiping Him because He gives him a lot of stuff. That is the same thing with us today. When everything is going good you do not hear nothing from us; as soon as things go bad, that is when we start complaining and moaning and groaning. Satan said put forth thine hand and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face. The Lord said, behold, all that he hath is in thy power, only upon himself put not forth thine hand. In Christianity they teach that Satan and God had a fight and Satan rebelled and took a third of the angels. That does not sound like what is right here. Job was the subject of discussion between Satan and the Lord, and Satan needed permission from the Lord to mess with him. A lot of times in Christianity people think everything bad comes from the devil and everything good comes from God. Wrong. Both good and evil come from the Lord. Satan is not a free spirit out here doing his own thing; he is subject to God, much like us. -

Job lost his oxen: the Sabeans fell upon them, took them away, and slew the servants with the edge of the sword. That is problem number one. While the first messenger was yet speaking, another came: the fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants. That is problem number two. While he was yet speaking, another came: the Chaldeans made out three bands, fell upon the camels, carried them away, and slew the servants. That is problem number three. While he was yet speaking, another came: a great wind from the wilderness smote the four corners of the house and it fell upon the young men and they are dead. Job just lost his cattle, his servants, and his children. Job just lost everything. Why? Because the devil, with the permission of the Lord, was able to put his hand on Job to try him. That is what we need as Israelites; when we do certain things the Lord gives us certain things, and He has to try them to see if the heart is still going to be the same way. -

Job rent his mantle, shaved his head, fell down and worshiped, and said naked came I out of my mother's womb and naked shall I return; the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord. In all this Job sinned not nor charged God foolishly. Job understood it: everything that we have comes from the Lord, everything that we get comes from the Lord. What good is it for us to blame God for stuff that we lose, when He can give it right back to you? There is nothing in this world that you can get yourself without the help of the Lord, unless you serve Satan and he gives it to you, but do you really want to pay that price? Even then it was the Lord that gave it to you, because the Lord handed you over to Satan; He put that stumbling block before you and you fell over it. -

Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also. The Lord said, hast thou considered My servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst Me against him to destroy him without cause. The Lord is bragging, He is boasting: even though you made Me go after Job for no reason at all, he is still standing strong, he is still handling his business. We have to allow God to brag on us. It is the same thing with all our enemies watching online; you have got to give the Lord a chance to brag.

Satan said, skin for skin, all that a man hath will he give for his life, but put forth thine hand now and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face. Possessions are possessions; a brother could lose a car, a job, family members, whatever. But Satan is saying if his health is afflicted, I bet you he will curse you to your face, because that is another thing that gets us. A lot of us, material things are not your stronghold. Even if you lost it today it would not do you nothing, but your health, that is your trial. As soon as you get sick you think it is the end of the world, or you think you did something. Maybe the Lord is doing this to you so you can be a shining light to somebody going through the same thing. A lot of our trials are not just for us. We read the book of Job because Job went through the things that we go through ourselves. The Lord said, behold, he is in thine hand, but save his life. The Lord said touch him but do not kill him. That does not sound like somebody rebellious against God; Satan took orders, just like we take orders.
Satan went forth and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown, and Job took a potsherd to scrape himself withal, and he sat down among the ashes.

Then his wife said, dost thou still retain thine integrity? Curse God, and die. This is the other test that brothers get. Satan is going to come through your woman. If he cannot get to you, he is going to come through her. Look at what he did with Adam: Satan was not going to get past Adam, so he backdoored and went to Eve. Same thing here; Satan was in his woman too. A lot of men, we get emotional behind our woman, and whatever she wants to say we go follow it instead of checking her. Job said, thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh; what, shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips. So he told her, woman, you sound foolish. Are we only going to get good from God and not evil? That is what we tell people all the time. We just read in [Isaiah 45:7](/bible/isaiah/45#v7) that God creates evil and creates peace. God is a man of war; He creates life and death. Nothing happens without the Lord; everything asks for permission.

Job's three friends heard of all this evil that came upon him: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him. When they lifted up their eyes afar off and knew him not, they lifted up their voice and wept, rent every man his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven. They sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word, for they saw that his grief was very great. Much like us, our friends hear of our affliction and come to lend their support, to give correction, to give harsh reality and hard truth. We are not talking about people that butter you up knowing you are in the wrong; we are talking about people that give you straight facts about what is going on with you.

Job continues his parable and remembers the months past when the Most High preserved him, when His candle shined upon his head and by His light Job walked through darkness. These were the days of his youth, when the secret of God was upon his tabernacle, when the Almighty was yet with him and his children were about him, when he washed his steps with butter and the rock poured him out rivers of oil. Remember verse 1 says Job continued his parable. A lot of what Job is talking about, not the entire book but a lot of it, is in parable form, and most of it is above the pay grade.

When Job went out to the gate of the city and prepared his seat in the street, the young men saw him and hid themselves, and the aged arose and stood up. The princes refrained talking and laid their hand on their mouth. The nobles held their peace and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth. When the ear heard him it blessed him, and when the eye saw him it gave witness to him.

Job delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him. The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon him, and he caused the widow's heart to sing for joy. He put on righteousness and it clothed him, his judgment was as a robe and a diadem. He was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the poor, and he searched out the cause he knew not. He broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the spoil out of his teeth.

Then Job said he would die in his nest and multiply his days as the sand. His root was spread out by the waters and the dew lay all night upon his branch. His glory was fresh in him and his bow was renewed in his hand.

Men gave ear to Job and waited and kept silence at his counsel. After his words they spake not again, and his speech dropped upon them. They waited for him as for the rain and opened their mouth wide as for the latter rain. If he laughed on them they believed it not, and the light of his countenance they cast not down. He chose out their way and sat chief, dwelling as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners. This is a deep parable by Job.

Job made a covenant with his eyes, so why then should he think upon a maid? He asks what portion of God is there from above and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high. Is not destruction to the wicked and a strange punishment to the workers of iniquity? This is the chapter where it is clear and obvious that Job is starting to justify himself, which is where he actually made his mistake. He asks that he be weighed in an even balance that God may know his integrity.

If his step turned out of the way, or his heart walked after his eyes, or any blot cleaved to his hands, then let him sow and let another eat, and let his offspring be rooted out. If his heart was deceived by a woman or he laid wait at his neighbor's door, then let his wife grind unto another and let others bow down upon her. Job is saying if he committed adultery let the same come back on him, for this is a heinous crime, a fire that consumeth to destruction and would root out all his increase. -

If Job despised the cause of his manservant or maidservant when they contended with him, what then would he do when God riseth up and visiteth? What would he answer? Did not He that made Job in the womb make his servant also, and did not one fashion them both in the womb?

If Job withheld the poor from their desire, caused the widow's eyes to fail, or ate his morsel alone while the fatherless did not eat, then let judgment come. From his youth the fatherless was brought up with him as with a father, and he guided the widow from his mother's womb. If he saw any perish for lack of clothing, or any poor without covering, whose loins did not bless him when warmed with the fleece of his sheep; if he lifted up his hand against the fatherless when he saw his help in the gate, then let his arm fall from his shoulder blade and be broken from the bone. He is justifying himself, saying I help people, I do this, I do that. For destruction from God was a terror to him and by reason of His highness he could not endure.

If Job made gold his hope or said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence; if he rejoiced because his wealth was great and his hand had gotten much; then it would be iniquity. If he beheld the sun when it shined or the moon walking in brightness, and his heart was secretly enticed, or his mouth kissed his hand, this also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge, for he should have denied the God that is above.

Job did not rejoice at the destruction of him that hated him nor lift up himself when evil found him; neither did he suffer his mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his enemy's soul. The men of his tabernacle did not go unsatisfied; the stranger did not lodge in the street, for he opened his doors to the traveler. He did not cover his transgression as Adam by hiding his iniquity in his bosom, nor did he fear a great multitude or the contempt of families to the point of keeping silence.

Job desires that the Almighty would answer him, and that his adversary had written a book. Surely he would take it upon his shoulder and bind it as a crown, and declare unto Him the number of his steps as a prince. If his land cried against him or its furrows complained, if he ate its fruits without money or caused its owners to lose their life, then let thistles grow instead of wheat and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended.

Job answers the Most High and confesses that He can do everything and that no thought can be withholden from Him. This is a little thing in the scriptures to take heed to: the Most High hears our words and our thoughts, so the hatred or the private spirit a man carries cannot be hidden from Him. He knows the inward parts of men. Job says he uttered what he understood not, things too wonderful for him which he knew not. He had heard of the Most High by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees Him, and therefore he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. Dust and ashes refer to the custom our forefathers had of putting ashes on the head as a sign of sorrow and repentance. -

After the Most High had spoken these words, He tells Eliphaz the Temanite that His wrath is kindled against him and his two friends, because they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right, as His servant Job has. Throughout the book Job's three friends dealt wrongly with him after his children were killed and everything was taken, so they did not deal righteously as their brother Job did. He commands them to take seven bullocks and seven rams and go to Job and offer a burnt offering for themselves, and Job will pray for them, for him will He accept, lest He deal with them after their folly. The sacrifice for their sin had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the situation. This is how the priesthood worked, all the way from Leviticus and the five books throughout history: we brought the sacrifice to the Levites and priests and they did it on our behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, the Most High would deal with him and what he did would not be forgiven. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Most High commanded, and He accepted Job. -

The Most High turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before. It was not the prayer alone that availed, but the prayer of a righteous man, so the Most High deals with those that are dealing in righteousness. Then all his brethren, sisters, and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him, bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil the Most High had brought upon him, and every man gave him a piece of money and an earring of gold. After his captivity was turned his friends returned as well. -

The Most High blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses, along with seven sons and three daughters. He named the daughters Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch, and in all the land were no women found so fair, and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren. Job lived a hundred and forty years after this and saw his sons and his sons' sons, even four generations, and died being old and full of days. He received much more than he had in the beginning, all because he stayed faithful to the Most High through the whole trial. The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and at some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom. -

Certain of the elders of Israel came and sat before Ezekiel, and the word of the Lord said these men have set up their idols in their hearts, setting up something above God, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face. The Most High asks whether He should be inquired of at all by them. Every man of the house of Israel that sets up his idols in his heart and comes to the prophet, the Lord will answer according to the multitude of his idols, that He may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from Him through their idols and spiritual idolatry.

The Most High tells the house of Israel to repent, come back to His laws, and turn themselves from their idols and away from all their abominations. Every one of the house of Israel, or the stranger that sojourns in Israel, who separates himself from Him and sets up idols in his heart and comes to a prophet to inquire, the Lord will answer by Himself and set His face against that man. He will make him a sign and a proverb, meaning a curse, and cut him off from the midst of His people as an example, that they may know He is the Lord.

If a prophet is deceived when he has spoken a thing, the Lord Himself has deceived that prophet; do not try to deceive yourself in this truth, and when we get counsel we should take it and keep it moving. He will stretch out His hand upon that prophet and destroy him from the midst of His people Israel, and both shall bear the punishment of their iniquity. This is so the house of Israel may go no more astray from Him nor be polluted any more with their transgressions, but be His people and He their God. -

The word of the Lord came saying that when a land sins by trespassing grievously, He will stretch out His hand upon it, break the staff of its bread, and send famine to cut off man and beast. Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness. No one can save anyone else; it does not matter who you are or what your status is in Israel, you have to save yourself by your own righteousness.

If He causes noisome beasts to pass through the land and spoil it so that it is desolate and no man may pass through, this is one of His judgments. Though these three men were in it, as the Lord lives they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters; they only shall be delivered by their righteousness, but the land shall be desolate.

If He brings a sword upon that land to cut off man and beast, though these three men were in it, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters. They only shall deliver themselves by their righteousness.

If He sends a pestilence into the land and pours out His fury upon it in blood to cut off man and beast, though Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter. They shall but deliver their own souls by their righteousness; everyone has to work out their own righteousness in fear and trembling, delivering their own soul by keeping the Most High's commandments. -

How much more when the Most High sends His four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, the famine, the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off man and beast; and these are not just for back then but for today. Behold, a remnant shall be left, both sons and daughters, that shall be brought forth unto you, and you shall see their ways and their doings. You shall be comforted concerning the evil the Most High brought upon Jerusalem when you see their ways, and you shall know He has not done without cause all that He has done in it. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry)

verses.text: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters.

His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east.
And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.

And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.
And the Lord said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?
Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped,
And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.

And the Lord said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause.
When the ear heard me, then it blessed me; and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me:
Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him.
The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow’s heart to sing for joy.
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem.
I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame.
I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out.
And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth.
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.

Then came there unto him all his brethren, and all his sisters, and all they that had been of his acquaintance before, and did eat bread with him in his house: and they bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him: every man also gave him a piece of money, and every one an earring of gold.
So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: for he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.
He had also seven sons and three daughters.
And he called the name of the first, Jemima; and the name of the second, Kezia; and the name of the third, Keren–happuch.
And in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job: and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.
After this lived Job an hundred and forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, even four generations.
So Job died, being old and full of days.
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord God.

cases.name: Job's three friends
cases.charge: Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous
cases.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite made an appointment together to come and mourn with Job and to comfort him. They wept, rent their mantles, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they argued for thirty chapters that his suffering proved hidden sin, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind he answered them too, and required them to bring sacrifice to the man they had condemned.
cases.offense: Their first response was compassion. They heard of the evil that was come upon him and came every one from his own place, having made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him (Job 2:11); they wept, rent their mantles, and sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him, for they saw  that his grief was very great (Job 2:12-13). Their presence in his grief was not itself the fault. The fault is in what they concluded and would not abandon. Eliphaz began from a rule that is not always true: who ever perished, being innocent, or where were the righteous cut off (Job 4:7). Bildad argued from God's justice to Job's guilt, doth God pervert judgment, or doth the Almighty pervert justice (Job 8:3), which is a true question put to a false use. Zophar spoke a heavy precept and misapplied it, that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth (Job 11:6), treating unproved guilt as something already established. Then Eliphaz stopped
cases.judgment: My wrath is kindled against thee and against thy two friends, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. They were ordered to bring seven bullocks and seven rams to Job and have him pray for them, lest I deal with you after your folly. He did, and the Lord accepted Job.

entries.commentary: Job answers the Most High and confesses that He can do everything and that no thought can be withholden from Him. This is a little thing in the scriptures to take heed to: the Most High hears our words and our thoughts, so the hatred or the private spirit a man carries cannot be hidden from Him. He knows the inward parts of men. Job says he uttered what he understood not, things too wonderful for him which he knew not. He had heard of the Most High by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees Him, and therefore he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. Dust and ashes refer to the custom our forefathers had of putting ashes on the head as a sign of sorrow and repentance. -

After the Most High had spoken these words, He tells Eliphaz the Temanite that His wrath is kindled against him and his two friends, because they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right, as His servant Job has. Throughout the book Job's three friends dealt wrongly with him after his children were killed and everything was taken, so they did not deal righteously as their brother Job did. He commands them to take seven bullocks and seven rams and go to Job and offer a burnt offering for themselves, and Job will pray for them, for him will He accept, lest He deal with them after their folly. The sacrifice for their sin had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the situation. This is how the priesthood worked, all the way from Leviticus and the five books throughout history: we brought the sacrifice to the Levites and priests and they did it on our behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, the Most High would deal with him and what he did would not be forgiven. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Most High commanded, and He accepted Job. -

The Most High turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before. It was not the prayer alone that availed, but the prayer of a righteous man, so the Most High deals with those that are dealing in righteousness. Then all his brethren, sisters, and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him, bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil the Most High had brought upon him, and every man gave him a piece of money and an earring of gold. After his captivity was turned his friends returned as well. -

The Most High blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses, along with seven sons and three daughters. He named the daughters Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch, and in all the land were no women found so fair, and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren. Job lived a hundred and forty years after this and saw his sons and his sons' sons, even four generations, and died being old and full of days. He received much more than he had in the beginning, all because he stayed faithful to the Most High through the whole trial. The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and at some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom. -
Job responds to what his friends think they know. He tells them the knowledge you think you have, I myself already know, and I am not inferior unto you in understanding.

Job desires to speak to the Almighty and to reason with God directly, not with these friends. He calls them forgers of lies and physicians of no value, because the things they are trying to tell him cannot help him. In verse 5 he is basically telling them to shut up. If they would hold their tongue that would be wisdom in the sight of the Most High, because the things they speak are not true and Job is not ignorant of what is being done to him by the hand of God.

Job warns his friends about speaking wickedly for God and talking deceitfully for Him, accepting God's person to defend their own accusations. He asks whether it is good that God should search them out. If they secretly accept persons and mock God, His excellency will make them afraid and His dread will fall upon them. Their remembrance is like ashes, their bodies like bodies of clay.

Job tells them to hold their peace and let him alone to speak, and let come on him what will. He is content to let whatever is going to happen to him happen by the hand of God. Though he take his flesh in his teeth and put his life in his hand, though God slay him, yet will he trust in Him and maintain his own ways before Him. God also shall be his salvation, for a hypocrite shall not come before Him.
Job asks them to hear his speech diligently. He has ordered his cause and knows that he shall be justified. He asks who will plead with him, for if he holds his tongue he shall give up the ghost.

Job asks God for only two things: withdraw His hand from him, and let not His dread make him afraid. Then let God call and Job will answer, or let Job speak and God answer him. He asks God to make him know how many are his iniquities and sins. Job is pleading with the Most High to show him what sin he is in, if he is in sin at all, for the things he is going through.

Job asks why God hides His face and holds him for an enemy. He feels broken like a leaf driven to and fro and dry stubble pursued. He says God writes bitter things against him and makes him possess the iniquities of his youth, putting his feet in stocks and setting a print upon the heels of his feet, while he consumes away as a rotten and moth-eaten garment.

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answers: can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise is profitable to himself? Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous, or gain that you make your ways perfect? Will he reprove you for fear of you? Will he enter with you into judgment? Is not your wickedness great and your iniquity infinite? Eliphaz throws Job's righteousness back as filthy rags, as if keeping the commandments profits nothing. But Christ told us if we keep the commandments and follow him, we will rule on thrones with him, so there is falsehood in Eliphaz's answer. -

Eliphaz accuses Job: you have taken a pledge from your brother for naught and stripped the naked of their clothing, withheld water from the weary and bread from the hungry, sent widows away empty, and broken the arms of the fatherless. Therefore snares are round about you, and sudden fear troubleth you. Eliphaz claims Job's suffering proves Job was sinning, but the Lord was only trying him. The truth is the opposite: when Job had his riches he dealt righteously, helped people, taught people, and was looked up to like an elder in the city. -

Is not God in the height of heaven? Behold the height of the stars, how high they are. And you say, how doth God know? Can he judge through the dark cloud? Thick clouds are a covering to him that he seeth not, and he walketh in the circuit of heaven. Eliphaz says God is surrounded by thick clouds and cannot judge through them, but that is when God is really looking, when you think he is not. -

Have you marked the old way which wicked men have trodden, which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overthrown with a flood? This points to the men destroyed in the flood. They said unto God, depart from us, and what can the Almighty do for them, yet he filled their houses with good things. But the counsel of the wicked is far from Job. The righteous see it and are glad, and the innocent laugh them to scorn, while their substance is not cut down but the remnant of them the fire consumes.

Acquaint now thyself with him and be at peace; thereby good shall come unto thee. You do not acquaint yourself with God by whispering that you love him; you hear from God through his prophets and his people to whom he gave his word. Receive the law from his mouth and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you shall be built up and put away iniquity far from your tabernacle. This was our job, to build up our people. -

Then you shall have your delight in the Almighty and lift up your face unto God. You shall make your prayer unto him and he shall hear you, for he hears you when you keep the commandments. You shall pay your vow, the original agreement you made in the covenant to keep his commandments. You shall decree a thing and it shall be established, and the light shall shine upon your ways. When men are cast down you shall say there is lifting up, and he shall save the humble person. He shall deliver the island of the innocent, delivered by the pureness of your hands.

A lot of us think, well, I did not do nothing wrong, so why is this happening to me, why me? That is a common fleshly response to a lot of things we go through, but we have to take a step back and see who is in control of everything and for what purpose. Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered: if we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking? Eliphaz is like, you go to visit somebody that is sick and you do not want to say the wrong thing, but we just cannot sit here and say nothing. Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands; thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees. But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. That right there cuts deep. A lot of times we can give other people the scriptures, First Corinthians 10:13, Ecclesiasticus chapter 2, [Deuteronomy 28](/bible/deuteronomy/28), and be the strongest person out there. But then as soon as a trial comes to us, that is when we fall apart. That is what Eliphaz was asking: now trial is coming to you, Job, and now you are falling apart. Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways? Eliphaz is saying, you used to uplift people, and now trouble is coming upon you and you are about to lose your mind. Maybe you did something. Sometimes it is something we did, but a lot of times it is not; it is for us to go through something because we can handle it, and be a shining example to the next person.

Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the righteous cut off? Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed. The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. The old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad.

Now a thing was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a little thereof. In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men. Now it is talking about the dreams that we have. Fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake. Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof; an image was before mine eyes, there was silence, and I heard a voice. Saying, shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his maker? Behold, he put no trust in his servants, and his angels he charged with folly. How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth? They are destroyed from morning to evening; they perish for ever without any regarding it. Doth not their excellency which is in them go away? They die, even without wisdom. Eliphaz is basically telling Job, maybe it is something that you did, something you got going on, something you need to examine yourself with. And that is where it ends. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

Bildad the Shuhite answers: how long will Job speak these things, and how long shall the words of his mouth be like a strong wind? He accuses Job of just talking on and on. Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty pervert justice? Bildad asks if Job is claiming God is being unjust, picking on a man so righteous. If Job's children sinned against Him, He cast them away for their transgression. This points back to Job's children celebrating their days, whom Job sanctified because he knew they might have sinned.

If Job would seek unto God early and make supplication to the Almighty, and if he were pure and upright, then God would awake for him and make the habitation of his righteousness prosperous. Though his beginning was small, his latter end should greatly increase. Bildad promises restoration, but on the false premise that Job is not already upright. -

Inquire of the former age and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers, for we are but of yesterday and know nothing, our days upon earth being a shadow. Shall not they teach thee and tell thee and utter words out of their heart? This is what we do in this truth: search our history, go back into the scriptures, learn our mistakes and our names, and walk in the spirit of strength and prophecy the fathers had.

Can the rush grow up without mire, or the flag grow without water? These are plants by the water; without their source they wither before any other herb while still in their greenness. So are the paths of all that forget God, and the hypocrite's hope shall perish. His hope shall be cut off and his trust shall be a spider's web; any strong thing breaks through it, for it has no foundation. He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand; he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure, because there is no foundation in the one who forgets God.

The wicked is green before the sun, his branch shooting forth in his garden, his roots wrapped about the heap and seeing the place of stones. But if he is destroyed from his place, it shall deny him, saying it never saw him. This is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow in his place.

God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will He help the evildoers. He will yet fill Job's mouth with laughing and his lips with rejoicing. They that hate Job shall be clothed with shame, and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought. Bildad concludes that Job must present his case, for God is a just judge who does what is right to whom it is right. In the chapters to come Job will present his case and the Most High will give His answer. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high)

Zophar the Naamathite answers and asks whether the multitude of words should be left unanswered and whether a man full of talk should be justified. He asks whether Job's lies should make men hold their peace, and whether when Job mocks no man shall make him ashamed. Job has said his doctrine is pure and he is clean in God's eyes, and Zophar is mocking that. Zophar wishes that God would speak and open his lips against Job and show him the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is known; only when the Most High opens your eyes and reveals the secrets of wisdom will you understand. Zophar says God exacteth of Job less than his iniquity deserves; this is a heavy precept, because it means the Most High gives us less than we deserve, so Job has a lot of mercy on him even though he cannot see it. Even so, Job questioned but he did not curse God.

Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? It is as high as heaven, what canst thou do; deeper than hell, what canst thou know. The measure thereof is longer than the earth and broader than the sea; you cannot go high enough, wide enough, or low enough to find out the perfection of God. This is where the song ain't no mountain high enough comes from. If the Most High cut off, shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him? He knoweth vain men and seeth wickedness; will he not then consider it? Vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt.

Zophar tells Job to prepare his heart and stretch out his hands toward the Most High. If iniquity be in thy hand, put it far away, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles; this is Job speaking to us as well, to put off the uncleanliness, the wickedness, the impure minds and ways we had in the world. Not letting wickedness dwell in thy tabernacle means the temple, the spirit here, purifying yourself and dedicating it back to the Most High, reforming your mind on a daily basis. Then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be steadfast and shalt not fear. Thou shalt forget thy misery and remember it as waters that pass away.

Thine age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth and be as the morning. Thou shalt be secure because there is hope; thou shalt dig about thee and take thy rest in safety. Thou shalt lie down and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thee. But the eyes of the wicked shall fail; they shall not escape, and their hope shall be as the giving up of the ghost, which is the breath that leaves the body when they die.
