entries.commentary: The men of Ephraim chode with Gideon sharply: why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? Ephraim has an attitude because they got called late to the battle and wanted in from the beginning. Gideon answers with wisdom: is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what was I able to do in comparison of you? He gave them the best possible situation, the enemy fed right into their hands with nowhere to go, and then their anger was abated toward him.

Gideon and the three hundred pass over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. He asks the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for his men, and the princes of Succoth answer, are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? They try to play neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. Gideon promises Succoth that when the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, he will tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers; and when the men of Penuel answer him the same way, he promises to break down their tower when he comes again in peace.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled, he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host.

Returning from battle, Gideon caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with Zebah and Zalmunna in hand: behold the kings with whom ye did upbraid me. Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them. He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth; he taught them a lesson, that when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.

Zebah and Zalmunna describe the men they slew at Tabor: each one resembled the children of a king. Those were powerful men, and they were Gideon's brethren, the sons of his mother; as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. Gideon tells Jether his firstborn, up, and slay them, but the youth drew not his sword, for he feared, because he was yet a youth. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from pops and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but you see Gideon being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk.

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, both he, his son, and his son's son, for delivering them from the hand of Midian. Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness. It has always been that way, and you see it playing out right here. Gideon refuses: I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.

Gideon requests of every man the earrings of his prey, for the enemy had golden earrings because they were Ishmaelites; and they willingly gave them, a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments, collars, purple raiment, and camel chains of the kings. Gideon made an ephod thereof and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.

Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had threescore and ten sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bare him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age. The sum of the history of Gideon, who is also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

It came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god, and remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side; neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years. That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little bit of freedom, and we go right back to wickedness. The same thing goes on today; we get relaxed, and the Lord has to remind us, putting us right back into hard bondage, that this is not our rest. Because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens in the mountains, and caves, and strongholds; Israel hid in the mountains of their own land.

When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude, destroyed the increase of the earth, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass, and Israel was greatly impoverished. That goes right into the curses.

When Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them: I brought you up from Egypt out of the house of bondage, and I said, fear not the gods of the Amorites in whose land ye dwell, but ye have not obeyed my voice. The judgment came with a reason attached.

An angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak in Ophrah, while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites; that is how hard the oppression sat on the land, that a man hid his own harvest to keep it. The angel greets him: the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon answers, oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us, and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of? A lot of us ask that same question today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over: if we be the chosen people, why does all of this happen to us?

The Lord commissions him: go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites; have not I sent thee? Gideon answers with his pedigree: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, because every one of us was called for a reason, to put a brick in for the kingdom.

The Lord promises, surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man. Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the Lord talking with him; the least in his father's house wanted to be sure he was not talking to himself.

Gideon brings a kid and unleavened cakes, and the angel touches the flesh and the cakes with the end of his staff; fire rises up out of the rock and consumes them, and the angel departs out of his sight, gone just like that. No lighter fluid existed on the earth; the angel made fire come out of the rock, because the angels are made out of that fire.

When Gideon perceived he had seen an angel of the Lord face to face, he feared death, but the Lord said, peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die. Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, which is, the Lord is peace.

The same night the Lord tells him to throw down his own father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove by it, and build an altar unto the Lord in its place. Notice this: even before the split of the kingdom, the tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal, worshipping the Lord in some fashion while holding onto the idol.

In the morning the men of the city found the altar of Baal cast down, and when they inquired, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing. He crept at night, but somebody was peeping out a window; he was doing the right thing and still got told on. The grove they worshipped was a carved tree stump, cut and shaped to look like a particular god; that is the idol Gideon cut down. The men demand his death, but Joash stands up for his son: will ye plead for Baal? If he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Obviously he is no god; he is an idol. So that day Gideon was named Jerubbaal, saying, let Baal plead against him.

The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east gathered and pitched in the valley of Jezreel, but the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon; he blew a trumpet, and Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali came up to meet him. Those tribes are warriors; do not get it twisted. You see how Zebulun and Naphtali, who are in the south Americas right now, get down: that warrior spirit is still in them, only right now it has turned on each other, and the Most High is going to correct it and turn it right again.

Gideon asks the fleece signs: dew on the fleece only with dry earth beside, and then the reverse, dew on all the ground with the fleece dry. The Lord commands the dew, the condensation that falls through the night, to land exactly where he pleases; God can do whatever he wants, infinite power.

Abimelech was the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem. He went to Shechem unto his mother's brethren, his uncles on his mother's side, and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or for one man to reign. Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

His mother's brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem, whispering for their nephew, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, He is our brother. They chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him. Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal. With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.

He went unto his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone. He killed his own family to clear his way to a throne. Notwithstanding, Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem. They endorsed the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers.

When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and cried, Hearken unto me, ye men of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you. This young brother was fearless; he stood up alone and rebuked the men who had made his brothers' killer king. In his parable the trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them. The olive tree would not leave its fatness, wherewith by it they honour God and man; the fig tree would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; the vine would not leave its wine, which cheereth God and man. The profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees. Only the bramble accepted: if in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon. The worthless bush took the crown, and its answer carried the threat of fire.

Jotham applied the parable: if ye have done truly and sincerely in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. He reminded them of what they owed his father: my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian; and ye are risen up against my father's house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother. They did it only because he was kin to them. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech. That is what the parable of the bramble was about: he prophesied that they would destroy one another, and it came to pass.
Jotham ran away and fled to Beer and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother. His brother already had a reputation for killing; he knew he could be next.

When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech. Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of these things, mustering the host, the armies above and below, and he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another. The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.
The men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech. The treachery the Most High sent had begun.

Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren and went over to Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. They went out into the fields, gathered their vineyards, trode the grapes, made merry, went into the house of their god, did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal talked big: who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him? He asked why they should be serving this Israelite at all. Would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. He was talking cash money with wine in him: increase thine army, and come out.

When Zebul the ruler of the city, Abimelech's officer, heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. He sent messengers unto Abimelech privily, saying, Behold, Gaal and his brethren fortify the city against thee. Zebul counselled Abimelech to rise up by night with his people and lie in wait in the field, and in the morning, as soon as the sun was up, to set upon the city. This is the same hand we read of in verse 23; the Lord is in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech and all the people with him rose up by night and laid wait against Shechem in four companies. When Gaal saw the people coming down from the top of the mountains, Zebul told him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men, playing him until it was too late. Then Zebul threw his own words back at him: where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them. All of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Gaal went out before the men of Shechem and fought with Abimelech, and Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many were overthrown and wounded, even unto the entering of the gate. Abimelech dwelt at Arumah, and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

On the morrow the people went out into the field, and it was told Abimelech. He divided his men into three companies, laid wait in the field, rose up against the people, and smote them. Abimelech fought against the city all that day; he took the city, slew the people that was therein, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.

When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard that, they entered into an hold of the house of the god Berith. Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, cut down a bough from the trees with an axe, laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. They cut every man his bough, put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them, so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women. Remember, these are the people whose money and endorsement made him king: I am your brother, make me king. Now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them; the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled to the top of it. Abimelech came unto the tower and went hard unto the door to burn it with fire, and a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull. A millstone is a heavy stone; it crushed his skull. He called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer: draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death earlier in this book. His young man thrust him through, and he died. He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren; and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads. Both sides were judged; for three years they reigned and everything looked good, then the Most High brought the judgment. Upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. Our forefather Jotham, a young man at the time, prophesied their destruction, and it came to pass. We read these accounts for the history, but look deeper and apply them to our lives: if there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, like he judged Abimelech.

An image in itself is not the sin, except for that white image of the beast; making images to bow down to them and serve them is the transgression, for the Lord thy God is a jealous God. Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation: Israel is yet this day in captivity, scattered for a reproach and a curse, according to all the iniquities of the fathers which departed from the Lord. Right now Israel is paying for the sins of the fathers; that is why the people are scattered to the four corners of the earth.

And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments. Judith recounted how the Most High tried the fathers for the examination of their hearts: he tried Abraham and Isaac, and Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria keeping the sheep of Laban, serving twenty years with his wages changed and given Leah when he looked for Rachel. In Judith's day there was no tribe, family, people, nor city that worshipped gods made with hands, as had been aforetime; for that cause she trusted the Lord would not despise the nation. Mercy rests on them that know none other God, not Allah, not Buddha, not a white Jesus.

Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. The word says remember because Israel would forget it: in this captivity the people were forced to serve other gods and their religions, and the Sabbath was lost through forced conversion. verses.text: Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son’s son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian.
And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you.
And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
And they answered, We will willingly give them. And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey.

And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that was on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that were about their camels’ necks.
And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.
And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal–berith their god.
And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:
Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, namely, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.

And it came to pass the same night, that the Lord said unto him, Take thy father’s young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:

And build an altar unto the Lord thy God upon the top of this rock, in the ordered place, and take the second bullock, and offer a burnt sacrifice with the wood of the grove which thou shalt cut down.

Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the Lord had said unto him: and so it was, because he feared his father’s household, and the men of the city, that he could not do it by day, that he did it by night.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
Ye shall not make with me gods of silver, neither shall ye make unto you gods of gold.

cases.name: Abimelech son of Gideon
cases.charge: Murder of seventy brothers on one stone; usurping a crown
cases.summary: Gideon's son by a Shechemite concubine hired vain and light persons with silver from the house of Baal-berith, killed his seventy brothers on one stone, and had himself made king at Shechem. Only Jotham escaped, and his parable from Mount Gerizim pronounced the sentence.
cases.offense: Abimelech appealed to his mother's brethren in Shechem and asked whether they preferred seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man who was their own bone and flesh (Judges 9:1-2). They promoted him because he was their brother. Kinship took the place of judgment, and money from the house of Baal-berith financed the choice: seventy pieces of silver paid the vain and light men who followed him (Judges 9:3-4). He went to his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren upon one stone; Jotham escaped by hiding. Shechem then made the killer king (Judges 9:5-6). Their part was not confined to approving him afterward. They supplied the means by which he established his rule. The blood would be laid upon the man who killed and upon the men who strengthened his hands (Judges 9:24). Jotham spoke from Mount Gerizim. In his parable, the olive, fig, and vine would not forsake their fruitfulness to reign over the trees, but the bramble offered its shadow and threatened fire (Judges 9:7-15). He applied it to the ingratitude shown his father's house: Gideon had risked his life to deliver them, and they had answered by destroying his sons. If their choice was not true and sincere, Abimelech and Shechem would consume one another (Judges 9:16-20).
cases.judgment: Three years passed before the alliance broke. God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem so that the blood of Gideon's sons would be requited upon both parties (Judges 9:22-24). The interval had not erased the murder. Numbers 32:23 warns that sin will find the offender out; a season of apparent success is not acquittal. Shechem dealt treacherously, trusted Gaal, and cursed Abimelech; Abimelech returned with ambush and slaughter. He destroyed the city and burned the stronghold where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge (Judges 9:26-49). The man they had called their brother brought the fire Jotham had pronounced. The god whose treasury financed his rise could not shelter those who fled into its house. At Thebez, Abimelech approached another tower to burn it, but a woman cast a piece of millstone upon his head and crushed his skull. He ordered his armour-bearer to kill him so that men would not say a woman slew him (Judges 9:50-54). Even at death he sought control of his reputation. The history still records the woman and the stone. God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and Shechem's evil upon its own head; Jotham's curse came upon them (Judges 9:56-57). The killer and his backers did not cancel one another's guilt by becoming enemies. Their conflict became the means by which both were repaid.

verses.text: And Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem unto his mother’s brethren, and communed with them, and with all the family of the house of his mother’s father, saying,

Speak, I pray you, in the ears of all the men of Shechem, Whether is better for you, either that all the sons of Jerubbaal, which are threescore and ten persons, reign over you, or that one reign over you? remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.
And his mother’s brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem all these words: and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech; for they said, He is our brother.
And they gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal–berith, wherewith Abimelech hired vain and light persons, which followed him.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
And all the men of Shechem gathered together, and all the house of Millo, and went, and made Abimelech king, by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem.

Now therefore, if ye have done truly and sincerely, in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, and have done unto him according to the deserving of his hands;
(For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian:

And ye are risen up against my father’s house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother;)
If ye then have dealt truly and sincerely with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you:
But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem, and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.
When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel,
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech:

That the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them; and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren.
And Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city, and slew the people that was therein, and beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.
And Abimelech came unto the tower, and fought against it, and went hard unto the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head, and all to brake his skull.

Then he called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer, and said unto him, Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. And his young man thrust him through, and he died.
And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.
Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren:
And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.

Who smote Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? did not a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon him from the wall, that he died in Thebez? why went ye nigh the wall? then say thou, Thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.

entries.commentary: Abimelech was the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem. He went to Shechem unto his mother's brethren, his uncles on his mother's side, and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or for one man to reign. Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

His mother's brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem, whispering for their nephew, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, He is our brother. They chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him. Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal. With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.

He went unto his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone. He killed his own family to clear his way to a throne. Notwithstanding, Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem. They endorsed the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers.

When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and cried, Hearken unto me, ye men of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you. This young brother was fearless; he stood up alone and rebuked the men who had made his brothers' killer king. In his parable the trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them. The olive tree would not leave its fatness, wherewith by it they honour God and man; the fig tree would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; the vine would not leave its wine, which cheereth God and man. The profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees. Only the bramble accepted: if in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon. The worthless bush took the crown, and its answer carried the threat of fire.

Jotham applied the parable: if ye have done truly and sincerely in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. He reminded them of what they owed his father: my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian; and ye are risen up against my father's house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother. They did it only because he was kin to them. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech. That is what the parable of the bramble was about: he prophesied that they would destroy one another, and it came to pass.
Jotham ran away and fled to Beer and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother. His brother already had a reputation for killing; he knew he could be next.

When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech. Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of these things, mustering the host, the armies above and below, and he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another. The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.
The men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech. The treachery the Most High sent had begun.

Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren and went over to Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. They went out into the fields, gathered their vineyards, trode the grapes, made merry, went into the house of their god, did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal talked big: who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him? He asked why they should be serving this Israelite at all. Would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. He was talking cash money with wine in him: increase thine army, and come out.

When Zebul the ruler of the city, Abimelech's officer, heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. He sent messengers unto Abimelech privily, saying, Behold, Gaal and his brethren fortify the city against thee. Zebul counselled Abimelech to rise up by night with his people and lie in wait in the field, and in the morning, as soon as the sun was up, to set upon the city. This is the same hand we read of in verse 23; the Lord is in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech and all the people with him rose up by night and laid wait against Shechem in four companies. When Gaal saw the people coming down from the top of the mountains, Zebul told him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men, playing him until it was too late. Then Zebul threw his own words back at him: where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them. All of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Gaal went out before the men of Shechem and fought with Abimelech, and Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many were overthrown and wounded, even unto the entering of the gate. Abimelech dwelt at Arumah, and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

On the morrow the people went out into the field, and it was told Abimelech. He divided his men into three companies, laid wait in the field, rose up against the people, and smote them. Abimelech fought against the city all that day; he took the city, slew the people that was therein, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.

When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard that, they entered into an hold of the house of the god Berith. Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, cut down a bough from the trees with an axe, laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. They cut every man his bough, put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them, so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women. Remember, these are the people whose money and endorsement made him king: I am your brother, make me king. Now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them; the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled to the top of it. Abimelech came unto the tower and went hard unto the door to burn it with fire, and a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull. A millstone is a heavy stone; it crushed his skull. He called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer: draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death earlier in this book. His young man thrust him through, and he died. He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren; and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads. Both sides were judged; for three years they reigned and everything looked good, then the Most High brought the judgment. Upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. Our forefather Jotham, a young man at the time, prophesied their destruction, and it came to pass. We read these accounts for the history, but look deeper and apply them to our lives: if there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, like he judged Abimelech.

After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child. Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down. David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also. David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city. Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High. It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

cases.name: Jephthah's vow
cases.charge: A rash vow, and its performance on his daughter
cases.summary: Before battle with Ammon, Jephthah vowed that what came from his doors to meet him would be the Lord's. His only daughter came out with timbrels and dances. She accepted the dedication, mourned her virginity, and remained unmarried as her father fulfilled his vow.
cases.offense: The vow itself was the sin: sworn thoughtlessly with the lips, as Leviticus describes, binding himself to a thing God never asked and, on the plain reading, forbade. Ecclesiastes: suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin. The text records that she bewailed her virginity and knew no man; readers have long divided over whether the sacrifice was literal or a life devoted, and the text does not settle it.
cases.judgment: He lost his only child and his line ended with him. The daughters of Israel kept a yearly lament for her. Jephthah is nonetheless counted among the faithful in Hebrews 11, which is the record's own tension.

entries.commentary: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot: and Gilead begat Jephthah. His mother was a harlot, but he himself was a mighty man of valour. Gilead's wife's sons grew up and thrust out Jephthah: thou shalt not inherit in our father's house, for thou art the son of a strange woman. Strange woman here does not mean his mother was of another nation; the scripture says only that she was a harlot. His brothers cast him out of his father's house over his mother, though he had as much right to that house as they did. Jephthah fled from his brethren and dwelt in the land of Tob, and there were gathered vain men to Jephthah, and went out with him. Watch what that shows: when we do our brothers and sisters wrong, when the ones trying to do right do not get the love and support they need from their own family, they go looking for love in the wrong places, and you see the kind of men they gravitate to.

In process of time the children of Ammon made war against Israel, and the elders of Gilead went to fetch Jephthah out of the land of Tob: come and be our captain, that we may fight with the children of Ammon. Now they wanted the man of valour they had cast out. Jephthah answered, Did not ye hate me, and expel me out of my father's house? and why are ye come unto me now when ye are in distress? You hated me, you put me out, and now that trouble has come, you need me. He set the terms: if ye bring me home again to fight against the children of Ammon, and the LORD deliver them before me, shall I be your head? And the elders of Gilead said, The LORD be witness between us, if we do not so according to thy words; they called the Lord to judge them if they broke their word. Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and captain over them: and Jephthah uttered all his words before the LORD in Mizpeh.

Jephthah sent messengers unto the king of the children of Ammon, saying, What hast thou to do with me, that thou art come against me to fight in my land? He wanted to know what Ammon had against Israel. The king of Ammon answered, Because Israel took away my land, when they came up out of Egypt, from Arnon even unto Jabbok, and unto Jordan: now therefore restore those lands again peaceably. That claim was a lie, and Jephthah knew it.

Jephthah sent messengers again and broke down the whole history: Israel took not away the land of Moab, nor the land of the children of Ammon. He knew the record, so nobody could talk him out of it. When Israel came up from Egypt and walked through the wilderness unto the Red sea and came to Kadesh, they sent messengers to the king of Edom and to the king of Moab asking passage, and both refused; so Israel went along through the wilderness, compassed the land of Edom and the land of Moab, came by the east side of the land of Moab, and pitched on the other side of Arnon; but they came not within the border of Moab, for Arnon was the border of Moab. This is why we must know our history. The king of Ammon could have pulled that on somebody ignorant and been given the land; Jephthah said no, that is not what happened, the book of Numbers does not say that. People try to confuse us about the Bible in the street the same way, so prepare yourself to the search of the fathers.

So now the LORD God of Israel hath dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel, and shouldest thou possess it? The Lord moved the Amorites out by moving Israel in; why should Ammon possess what the Most High gave to Israel? Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee? So whomsoever the LORD our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess. You take what your god gives you; we will possess whatever the Most High gives us, and we are not backing down from anybody. Art thou any thing better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them? While Israel dwelt in Heshbon and her towns, and in Aroer and her towns, and in all the cities along the coasts of Arnon, three hundred years, why did ye not recover them within that time? Three hundred years Israel held that land and nobody came to claim it. Wherefore I have not sinned against thee, but thou doest me wrong to war against me: the LORD the Judge be judge this day between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon. The Lord is in the midst of every battle; nothing goes down without the Most High letting it go down. World War One, the Lord was in the midst; World War Two, the Lord was in the midst; whoever he has destined to win is going to win. Howbeit the king of the children of Ammon hearkened not unto the words of Jephthah: the Lord had hardened their hearts not to listen, the same as he did with Sihon. The Most High strengthens nations and weakens nations, and moves peoples in and out of lands to fulfil his word. In this last battle Israel cannot lose so long as we keep the commandments, have faith in Christ, and endure to the end; but if we stay in sin, we die with the heathen.

Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed over Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over unto the children of Ammon. Jephthah vowed a vow unto the LORD: if thou shalt without fail deliver the children of Ammon into mine hands, then whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace, shall surely be the LORD'S, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering. The vow was made before the battle, an offering promised to the Lord for the victory: whatever came out of his doors first would be given over to the Lord.

Jephthah passed over unto the children of Ammon to fight against them, and the LORD delivered them into his hands. He smote them from Aroer even till thou come to Minnith, even twenty cities, with a very great slaughter. Thus the children of Ammon were subdued before the children of Israel.

Jephthah came to Mizpeh unto his house, and behold, his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances; and she was his only child; beside her he had neither son nor daughter. He rent his clothes and said, Alas, my daughter! thou hast brought me very low; for I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back. A vow made to the Most High could not be taken back.

His daughter answered, My father, if thou hast opened thy mouth unto the LORD, do to me according to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth; forasmuch as the LORD hath taken vengeance for thee of thine enemies, even of the children of Ammon. She was not pleading for her life; she accepted that her life was now vowed to the Lord. She asked one thing: let me alone two months, that I may go up and down upon the mountains, and bewail my virginity, I and my fellows. To bewail is to weep and mourn; she went with her companions and mourned her virginity, because being given over to the Lord she would never know a man. Jephthah did not burn his daughter as a human sacrifice. Israel did not do human sacrifices; that was Molech worship among the Canaanites. Read the end of the passage: at the end of two months she returned unto her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed, and she knew no man. If she had been put to death, there would be no reason for the scripture to say she knew no man; her life was committed to the Lord and she remained a virgin. Why would she mourn her virginity if she were about to die? Because the sorrow was that she could never marry or bear children. In those days our women wanted to bring children into the world and continue the lineage; to be without children was counted a shame and a dishonour among the daughters of Israel. A lot of people try to say Jephthah sacrificed his daughter, because our people do not understand the scriptures; keep reading and the text itself answers it. It is a translation difference around the word offering: she was presented to the Lord to serve him, not sent up as a burnt sacrifice. And it was a custom in Israel, that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.

If a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it, if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity. Verse 4 defines the voice of swearing: a soul that swears, pronouncing with his lips to do evil or to do good. If you know and say nothing, your brother's blood is required because you did nothing about it. We are to rebuke one another. Hear no evil, see no evil, speak no evil is a wicked saying; the scriptures say you renounce evil. The watchman does not cover his eyes, because he needs to see, and does not cover his mouth, because he gives the warning; hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me. If you do not apply this verse, you hate your brother in your heart; keeping quiet at his sin, or trimming your ways for him, is hate too. Stand still for the laws of the Most High and do not turn your ways for anybody, even carnal family that puts you out over your beard or your fringes. There is a way to correct: brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness. A soft answer turneth away wrath; you do not render evil for evil and blast a brother, you build him up with a humble mind, and that is how souls are won. The man gathering sticks got the reproof that fit that willful case; meekness fits the brother overtaken in a fault.

Touching any unclean thing, the carcase of an unclean beast or the uncleanness of man, leaves a soul unclean and guilty. This goes into eating, not mere contact; the classes have touched on this already, and it stands. It is the same as telling your son or daughter, get your hand out of the cookie jar: you say do not touch it, not do not eat it, because you know what the intention is. The Lord deals with us the same way; do not be touching that stuff means do not eat it, do not defile yourself. The touching itself pertained to the sacrifice: Israel was separated from their uncleanness that they die not when they defile the tabernacle, so a man that had touched the unclean thing could not come in to sacrifice. There is no more sacrifice, so the touching-defilement laws do not apply today; a brush of boar bristles is not sin.

If a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil or to do good, and it be hid from him, when he knoweth of it he is guilty. Brothers say, I swear to God; watch your mouth. When a man is guilty in one of these things, he shall confess that he hath sinned in that thing, and bring his trespass offering, a female from the flock, a lamb or a kid of the goats, and the priest shall make an atonement for him concerning his sin. A man was held accountable for whatever came out of his mouth; pronouncing with his lips and not performing it was sin. When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it, for better is it that thou shouldest not vow than that thou shouldest vow and not pay; suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin. Christ set the same standard on the mouth: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay.

The offering scaled to what a man could bring: if he be not able to bring a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering; and if he be not able to bring those, the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil and no frankincense upon it, for it is a sin offering. The offerings were the collateral of those times, and families felt the after-effects of always sacrificing: the livestock and the agriculture went for your sins, and the household lacked because of it. Israel took the nourishment of the Lord for granted, and he grew tired of the empty offerings: put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh. He spake not unto our fathers concerning burnt offerings, but this thing commanded he: obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people. He never wanted the sacrifices above obedience; today he does not want an apology or money in the plate, he wants you to obey his voice and repent.

If a soul commit a trespass and sin through ignorance in the holy things of the Lord, he brings a ram without blemish, with thy estimation by shekels of silver after the shekel of the sanctuary; he makes amends for the harm done in the holy thing and adds the fifth part thereto for the priest, and it shall be forgiven him. The scripture that pops up again is the same one: if thou sayest, behold, we knew it not, doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? Worldly family and coworkers that are not keeping the laws talk the same way, not understanding they condemn themselves because they are not repenting; that card cannot be pulled on the Messiah.

If a soul sin against any of the commandments, though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity. Though he is ignorant of it, the iniquity is still there; saying I did not know does not remove sin, and everyone still appears before the judgment seat of Christ when it is all said and done. The priest made an atonement concerning his ignorance wherein he erred and wist it not, for he hath certainly trespassed against the Lord. The remedy is to know the law: let thy mind be upon the ordinances of the Lord, and meditate continually in his commandments. The ordinances are found in the first five books; as these four chapters a day are conducted, meditate and study them continually. As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. The milk is the dos and the don'ts. Many want to run to Revelation and the parables, but the solutions for what is wrong in your spirit, for lust, covetousness, hatred, malice, and envy, sit in the ordinances and the commandments; look up the scriptures on patience, temperance, and how to treat your family correctly. Stay humble with it: Lord, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty; neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me; David behaved and quieted himself as a child that is weaned of his mother. Except ye be converted and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven; so behave yourselves humbly, and the Most High will establish thine heart and increase thy wisdom.

If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth. A vow is promising the Lord you will do a thing. Say a man vows, Lord, if you bring this to pass I will never eat swine again; he must keep that vow, and he cannot go back on it and simply ask forgiveness afterward. If thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee; but that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform. Do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error.

A daughter in her father's house in her youth who vows a vow is under her father's covering. If her father hears her vow and holds his peace, all her vows stand and every bond wherewith she hath bound her soul stands. But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth, not any of her vows or bonds shall stand, and the Lord shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her. That shows the power the Most High put in the man of the house: a father can hear his daughter bind herself and say no, and the Lord releases her.

The same covering passes to the husband. If a woman with a husband vows, or utters ought out of her lips wherewith she binds her soul, and her husband hears it and holds his peace in the day that he hears it, her vows stand. But if her husband disallow her on the day that he heard it, he makes her vow of none effect, and the Lord shall forgive her. A wife could be binding herself to something she cannot perform, and her husband can step in and say, Lord, do not hear that vow, and the Most High releases her because of her husband. That is the power of the head of the house: the husband keeping the commandments stands between his wife and a bond that would jack her up. That is a reason to love your hedge, not to despise it.

Every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her. She has no father or husband to disallow it, so what she vows she must perform. The husband is a hedge of protection; where no hedge is, the possession is spoiled. The married woman has a covering that the widow and the divorced woman do not have.

If a wife vowed in her husband's house and her husband heard it and held his peace and disallowed her not, then all her vows stand. Her husband may establish every vow and every binding oath to afflict the soul, or her husband may make it void. If he altogether holds his peace at her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows and confirms all her bonds, because he held his peace in the day that he heard them. Holding your peace is confirming it. But if he shall any ways make them void after that he hath heard them, then he shall bear her iniquity. He cannot hear her vow, hold his peace day after day, and then come later to void it; he had the power to stop it and did not, so the iniquity falls to him. And this runs one way: a wife cannot disallow or nullify her husband's vow. This is the order of the house: the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church, and he is the saviour of the body; so let the wives be subject to their own husbands in every thing, even in what is vowed in prayer.

These are the statutes which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife, and between the father and his daughter, being yet in her youth in her father's house. The whole chapter is the government of vows inside the house of Israel. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Keep your foot when you go to the house of the Most High and be more ready to hear than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they do not consider that they do evil. Be not rash with your mouth nor let your heart be hasty to utter anything before the Most High, for he is in heaven and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few. This means watch your mouth, which is why Christ said you will give account of every word. -

When you vow a vow to the Most High, do not defer to pay it, for he has no pleasure in fools; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel that it was an error, lest the Most High be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands. This is what Christ meant by not swearing by heaven, earth, or your own head. -

If you see the oppression of the poor and the perverting of judgment and justice in a province, do not marvel, for he that is higher than the highest regards it, and there are higher than they. Do not worry about the wicked that are successful and all they are doing, because there is a God and that God will have his vengeance. This is why the scriptures say vengeance is his and he will repay. -

He that loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he that loves abundance with increase; this also is vanity. When goods increase, those that eat them increase. As one rapper said, more money more problems: the more money most people get, the bigger their family gets, meaning the more food you can buy, the more mouths there are to feed. The sleep of a laboring man is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich will not let him sleep. The rich lose sleep to gain wealth; ask successful entrepreneurs and businessmen and they work off four or five hours of sleep.

There is a sore evil under the sun: riches kept for the owners to their hurt, and those riches perish by evil travail so that the son is left with nothing in his hand. As a man came from his mother's womb naked, so shall he return, and take nothing of his labor to carry away in his hand. In all points as he came, so shall he go, and he has labored for the wind, eating in darkness with much sorrow, wrath, and sickness.

It is good and comely for a man to eat, drink, and enjoy the good of all his labor all the days of his life which the Most High gives him, for it is his portion. Every man to whom the Most High gives riches, wealth, and power to enjoy them and rejoice in his labor, this is the gift of the Most High. He shall not much remember the days of his life, because the Most High answers him in the joy of his heart. Ecclesiastes is a book of regret, and we can learn from it; in the end you see what really matters in this life. Money is a defense, but keep the commandments in the faith of Christ, which is what Solomon was saying. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

These are the statutes and judgments which ye shall observe to do in the land: the Lord gave the fathers a land other nations were living in, and Israel went to war with those nations to take it. The whole book of Deuteronomy is the Lord speaking unto his people Israel; he showed his statutes and his judgments to no other nation.

Utterly destroy all the places wherein the nations served their gods, upon the high mountains, upon the hills, and under every green tree. Even after being warned, Israel was still idolatrous: the children of Israel secretly built high places in all their cities, set up images and groves in every high hill and under every green tree, and burnt incense as did the heathen, the very thing the Lord said ye shall not do. Because Israel served the gods of the nations, the Most High gave those nations the rule over Israel; that is how they became the oppressor, and the word says envy not the oppressor and choose none of his ways. Unlearned and lost brothers and sisters today are still serving other gods, whatever the religion calls itself.
Unto the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there shall ye seek: out of all the tribes he chose Jerusalem as the place for his name and the temple.

Ye are not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance: the rest is when the Lord gives rest from all your enemies round about, so that ye dwell in safety. This is why the scripture is pulled out on the street, this is not our rest: Israel today dwells among its enemies and serves them for food, shelter, and clothing, as [Deuteronomy 28](/bible/deuteronomy/28) declares. Arise ye and depart does not mean to leave physically; it means come up out of the ways of this place, because it is polluted. Israel waits for the time when the third part has repented, the hundred forty and four thousand are sealed, and Christ returns to take his people out of this place and set them back in their own land.

Whatsoever thy soul lusteth after is not license to eat anything: it stays within the guidelines of the clean foods, as of the roebuck and as of the hart, the beasts listed in chapter 14, for the law says thou shalt not eat any abominable thing. The unclean and the clean that may eat thereof are unclean and clean persons, not unclean meats; Israel had servants then and will have servants again.

Take heed that thou be not snared by inquiring after the gods of the nations after they are destroyed, saying, how did these nations serve their gods, even so will I do likewise; Israel has a history of following what the other nations do. The snare fulfilled is written in the psalm: Israel did not destroy the nations, but was mingled among the heathen, learned their works, served their idols, and sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, the very abomination the Lord warned of here. The wrath of the Lord was kindled insomuch that he abhorred his own inheritance; that snare is why Israel is where it is now, scattered among the heathen and serving them.
