verses.text: Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together, and came to Samuel unto Ramah,
And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.
But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, Give us a king to judge us. And Samuel prayed unto the Lord.
And the Lord said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even unto this day, wherewith they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so do they also unto thee.
Now therefore hearken unto their voice: howbeit yet protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them.

And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots.

And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties; and will set them to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and instruments of his chariots.
And he will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers.
And he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants.
And he will take the tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give to his officers, and to his servants.
And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your goodliest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work.
He will take the tenth of your sheep: and ye shall be his servants.
And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the Lord will not hear you in that day.
Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us;
That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.

And ye have this day rejected your God, who himself saved you out of all your adversities and your tribulations; and ye have said unto him, Nay, but set a king over us. Now therefore present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes, and by your thousands.
And when ye saw that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon came against you, ye said unto me, Nay; but a king shall reign over us: when the Lord your God was your king.
Now therefore behold the king whom ye have chosen, and whom ye have desired! and, behold, the Lord hath set a king over you.

Is it not wheat harvest to day? I will call unto the Lord, and he shall send thunder and rain; that ye may perceive and see that your wickedness is great, which ye have done in the sight of the Lord, in asking you a king.
So Samuel called unto the Lord; and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day: and all the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.
And all the people said unto Samuel, Pray for thy servants unto the Lord thy God, that we die not: for we have added unto all our sins this evil, to ask us a king.
And Samuel said unto the people, Fear not: ye have done all this wickedness: yet turn not aside from following the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart;
I gave thee a king in mine anger, and took him away in my wrath.

When thou art come unto the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, and shalt possess it, and shalt dwell therein, and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me;

Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the Lord thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee: thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother.

cases.name: King Saul
cases.charge: Unlawful sacrifice; sparing what was devoted; consulting a medium
cases.summary: A king undone by a pattern of partial obedience. He offered a sacrifice that was not his to offer, spared Agag and the best of the spoil against a direct command, and at the end sought a medium the law condemned.
cases.offense: Saul's fall began with a command displaced by pressure. At Gilgal he saw the people scattering and the Philistines gathering. Samuel had instructed him to wait, but Saul offered the burnt offering and defended himself by naming the circumstances that frightened him (1 Samuel 10:8; 13:8-12). He had not been given authority to change the command because waiting became difficult. The trial exposed whose word governed him when the people grew afraid.
cases.judgment: The kingdom was torn from him and given to another. 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' He died by his own hand on Gilboa the next day, his sons with him.

entries.commentary: Chapter 13 is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the beginning of the proof that he is not fit to be king over Israel. Saul chose three thousand men, two thousand with him in Michmash and mount Bethel and a thousand with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it; Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, and Israel was had in abomination with the Philistines. His son popped off the battle, so now it is war time.

The Philistines gathered thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand on the seashore, far deeper than the three thousand Israel had prepared. When the men of Israel saw they were in a strait, they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, high places, and pits; some Hebrews fled over Jordan, and the people that followed Saul followed him trembling. The sons of God, the mighty men of valor, saw the enemy coming and started hiding. As the chosen people, if we really have faith we should be fearless; the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel in chapter 7. To still fear the enemy shows a lack of faith, that you really do not believe in your God. Nehemiah shows the right spirit. In the Persian captivity he had liberty from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and the enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem plotted to scare him off the work. A hired man urged him to hide in the temple because they were coming to slay him, and Nehemiah refused; operating in the spirit of fear is sin according to the scripture.

Samuel had instructed Saul in chapter 10: when you get to Gilgal, tarry seven days, make no moves until I arrive. Saul tarried seven days according to the set time, but Samuel came not at the moment expected, and the people were scattered from him and acting frantic. Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and he offered the burnt offering, and Saul is not the priest; that is Samuel's office. And it came to pass that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. He was barely late, and Saul could not hold his patience. Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said it would be here at ten, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. Be humble and tarry like you were instructed; it may run some minutes over, and the Lord may be testing your patience.

Samuel asks, What hast thou done? Saul answers with excuses: the people were scattered from me, thou camest not within the days appointed, the Philistines gathered at Michmash, so I forced myself and offered a burnt offering. This is part of Saul's pattern of behavior; he never wants to hold himself accountable, he always deflects onto whoever else.

Samuel does not entertain the excuses: thou hast done foolishly; thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God. Saul thought he was only bending Samuel's word, but disobeying the instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. For now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever; but now thy kingdom shall not continue. For that one act of foolishness the Lord withdrew what he would have given: Saul's lineage ruling Israel. The Lord wants to see whether you will perform what he told you to do even when things do not work out how you planned; that is what proves you faithful in temptation and worthy of being exalted. Saul failed that test in the time of his distress. The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart to be captain over his people. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement; that man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures.

Samuel went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin, and Saul numbered the people present with him, about six hundred men. The Philistines encamped in Michmash, and the spoilers came out of their camp in three companies, toward Ophrah, toward Bethhoron, and toward the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim; three raiding parties sent out to invade Israel.

There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears. The Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his share, his coulter, his axe, and his mattock, so the Philistines knew exactly how disarmed Israel was; all they had was a file for the tools. This is heavy for today. A people that must depend on its adversary for weaponry cannot deliver itself by arms; talk of going to war means nothing when you have to buy your weapons from the very gun store of the ones you say you will fight. Same picture as the scriptures. So in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in the hand of any of the people, but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found; only two men in the army had a blade. In chapter 13 Saul blew the kingdom with his instability in a time of distress. The Most High said, You are not fit; I would have established you, but your replacement is already on the way.

Samuel said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people; now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way when he came up from Egypt. Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers; the generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. This is a specific instruction: kill all of them, spare none. Note that the Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness; that answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows [Leviticus 19:18](/bible/leviticus/19#v18) applies to the children of thy people.

Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah, and laid wait in the valley. Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed. The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment.

Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, and utterly destroyed the people with the edge of the sword; but he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive. He halfway fulfilled the order, reasoning like the king might be valuable as a hostage, as if the Lord forgot that detail. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them; but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. They killed what looked like it deserved killing, so they could say they did some killing, and kept the healthy, good looking animals, telling themselves surely the Lord could not have meant these.

Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel: It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part, understand: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. That is what the Most High is showing us in this story. And it grieved Samuel, and he cried unto the Lord all night. Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost.

Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul came to Carmel and set him up a place, a monument to himself, and is gone down to Gilgal. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name; do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more. Saul greets Samuel first with a cover: Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. The first thing out of his mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed. Samuel answers, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals? Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

Samuel said, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance: when you thought nothing of yourself, with no confidence to be a ruler, the Most High still chose you. And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25). Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

Saul is in denial: Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Samuel breaks down the rebuke and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong. In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

Samuel makes it plain: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in. This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy words; because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, Pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord; take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

Samuel refuses: I will not return with thee; for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. Think it through: Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him; and Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel. This spirit is very real: okay, you are right, but do not let the people see the demotion; make sure they still know I am the king. That is the spirit of vanity, caught up in a rank and a title while forgetting that the title came for pleasing the Lord; once you discontinue pleasing the Lord, the title is going to leave as well. So Samuel turned again after Saul, and Saul worshipped the Lord.

Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately, and said, Surely the bitterness of death is past; with Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was mad at the Amalekites anymore and he was safe. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek's sword had done.

Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah, and Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. The mourning is what makes it sad: Samuel raised Saul up from nothing, saw his potential, and saw the Spirit come upon him in chapter 11 when he stood up as a savior for the people; he had hope in him, and it came to this. Samuel was grieved, and the Lord repented of the appointment. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

What Saul was doing when he went to the woman with the familiar spirit is called necromancy. Look that word up: it is when you go to somebody that conjures up spirits. Saul turned to this because the Lord was departed from him and answered him no more, neither by prophets nor by dreams, so he had Samuel conjured up to tell him what to do.

Samuel asks Saul why he inquires of him, seeing the Lord is departed from him and is become his enemy. The Lord did to Saul exactly as he spake by Samuel: he rent the kingdom out of Saul's hand and gave it to his neighbour, even to David. The reason is stated plainly: because Saul obeyed not the voice of the Lord, nor executed his fierce wrath upon Amalek. The Most High gave a law concerning Amalek, and Saul did not carry it out; that history was read earlier in this book.

Tomorrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me means tomorrow you and your sons are going to die; you are going to be with me. Samuel prophesied from his grave, and he also declared that the Lord would deliver the host of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.

Saul fell straightway all along the earth, sore afraid because of the words of Samuel, and there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all the day nor all the night. The woman reminded Saul that she had put her life in her hand and obeyed his voice, and asked him to let her set a morsel of bread before him that he might have strength for his way. He refused at first, but his servants together with the woman compelled him; she killed the fat calf, baked unleavened bread, and they did eat and went away that night. The chapter in sum: Saul inquired of the Lord and was not answered, so he turned to a woman with a familiar spirit and conjured up Samuel. Samuel told him that because of his disobedience the Lord was not dealing with him anymore, and prophesied that tomorrow Saul and his sons would be with him.

Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. The Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons, and slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons. The battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was sore wounded of the archers.

Saul said unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. What Saul was fearful of is what you see in war, how men will abuse their captives, killing them and abusing their bodies. He was already wounded and could not get away, so instead of being taken captive he told his armourbearer to kill him. His armourbearer would not, for he was sore afraid; therefore Saul took a sword and fell upon it, and when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword and died with him. So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together. Remember what we read in chapter 28: when Saul went and conjured up the spirit of Samuel, Samuel said to him, To morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me. He prophesied unto Saul what was going to happen, and now we read the fulfillment of that prophecy.

When the men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley, and they that were on the other side of Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they forsook the cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

On the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa. They cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish it in the house of their idols and among the people. They put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan.

When the inhabitants of Jabeshgilead heard of that which the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Bethshan, and came to Jabesh and burnt them there. They took their bones and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. So in chapter 31 we read of Saul and his sons and his armourbearer dying at the hands of the Philistines. This concludes the history of Saul coming to an end; the second book of Samuel takes up the rise and much of the history concerning King David. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The Philistines fought Israel, the men of Israel fled and fell slain in mount Gilboa, and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. The battle went hard against Saul, the archers wounded him, and he asked his armourbearer to run him through so the uncircumcised would not abuse him. The armourbearer was too afraid, so Saul fell on his own sword and died. Saul died, his three sons, and all his house together, and when Israel saw it they forsook their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

The next day the Philistines came to strip the slain, found Saul and his sons fallen in Gilboa, took his head and his armour, and sent word throughout their land to carry tidings to their idols and to the people. They put his armour in the house of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. Dagon was the fish god, and its likeness is carried over into false religion in the fish-shaped mitre and the fish symbol.

When Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all their valiant men arose, took the bodies of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, buried their bones under the oak, and fasted seven days. It has always been in Israel to mourn our dead. No matter what a person has done, it does not sit right with us to see our brothers put to death. This is why we pray for all Israel to recover themselves.

Saul died for his transgression against the Most High, for not keeping His word, and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit rather than inquiring of the Most High. Therefore the Most High slew him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse. Saul had gone to a woman with a familiar spirit to bring up Samuel. The left hand of the Most High is real. People who meddle with that get entangled and get spirits put on them. It is not our custom. The last straw for Saul was seeking that familiar spirit. Through Samuel the Most High told him he would join him the next day. The difference is that Samuel died righteously. -

verses.text: And he tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed: but Samuel came not to Gilgal; and the people were scattered from him.
And Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering.
And it came to pass, that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him, that he might salute him.

And Samuel said, What hast thou done? And Saul said, Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash;
Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the Lord: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.

And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever.

But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.

Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at En–dor.

Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it.
And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him.
So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together.

So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the Lord, even against the word of the Lord, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;
And enquired not of the Lord: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.
And before his long sleep he made protestations in the sight of the Lord and his anointed, I have not taken any man’s goods, so much as a shoe: and no man did accuse him.
And after his death he prophesied, and shewed the king his end, and lifted up his voice from the earth in prophecy, to blot out the wickedness of the people.

cases.name: David
cases.charge: A man after the Lord's own heart; keeping his commandments and following him with all his heart, save only in the matter of Uriah
cases.summary: Shepherd, giant-killer, hunted man who twice had Saul in his hand and would not touch the Lord's anointed, king who danced before the ark and would not build a house until told he could. The Lord made a covenant with his house that has a Son sitting on it for ever. His one great fall is its own case; this is the rest.
cases.offense: David was taken from keeping sheep to feed Israel. Samuel first looked upon Jesse's older son, but the Lord corrected the measure: man looks upon appearance; the Lord looks upon the heart (1 Samuel 16:6-13). Psalms 78:70-72 joins David's shepherding of the flock to the integrity and skill with which he fed the nation. The calling required the same care on a greater charge. Before he held the throne, he served the king who would come to hate him. He played for Saul's relief, went where Saul sent him, and behaved wisely while Saul's envy grew (1 Samuel 16:21-23; 18:5-16). Twice Saul was placed within his reach, and twice David refused to kill him. Even cutting the skirt of Saul's robe troubled his heart (1 Samuel 24:4-7; 26:8-12). He would not use a promised kingdom to justify taking the life of the Lord's anointed.
cases.judgment: Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever. Therefore the Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight. The sure mercies of David. He gave them a king, David, to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will. Of this man's seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus.

He would not use a promised kingdom to justify taking the life of the Lord's anointed.

entries.commentary: Chapter 13 is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the beginning of the proof that he is not fit to be king over Israel. Saul chose three thousand men, two thousand with him in Michmash and mount Bethel and a thousand with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it; Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, and Israel was had in abomination with the Philistines. His son popped off the battle, so now it is war time.

The Philistines gathered thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand on the seashore, far deeper than the three thousand Israel had prepared. When the men of Israel saw they were in a strait, they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, high places, and pits; some Hebrews fled over Jordan, and the people that followed Saul followed him trembling. The sons of God, the mighty men of valor, saw the enemy coming and started hiding. As the chosen people, if we really have faith we should be fearless; the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel in chapter 7. To still fear the enemy shows a lack of faith, that you really do not believe in your God. Nehemiah shows the right spirit. In the Persian captivity he had liberty from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and the enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem plotted to scare him off the work. A hired man urged him to hide in the temple because they were coming to slay him, and Nehemiah refused; operating in the spirit of fear is sin according to the scripture.

Samuel had instructed Saul in chapter 10: when you get to Gilgal, tarry seven days, make no moves until I arrive. Saul tarried seven days according to the set time, but Samuel came not at the moment expected, and the people were scattered from him and acting frantic. Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and he offered the burnt offering, and Saul is not the priest; that is Samuel's office. And it came to pass that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. He was barely late, and Saul could not hold his patience. Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said it would be here at ten, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. Be humble and tarry like you were instructed; it may run some minutes over, and the Lord may be testing your patience.

Samuel asks, What hast thou done? Saul answers with excuses: the people were scattered from me, thou camest not within the days appointed, the Philistines gathered at Michmash, so I forced myself and offered a burnt offering. This is part of Saul's pattern of behavior; he never wants to hold himself accountable, he always deflects onto whoever else.

Samuel does not entertain the excuses: thou hast done foolishly; thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God. Saul thought he was only bending Samuel's word, but disobeying the instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. For now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever; but now thy kingdom shall not continue. For that one act of foolishness the Lord withdrew what he would have given: Saul's lineage ruling Israel. The Lord wants to see whether you will perform what he told you to do even when things do not work out how you planned; that is what proves you faithful in temptation and worthy of being exalted. Saul failed that test in the time of his distress. The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart to be captain over his people. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement; that man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures.

Samuel went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin, and Saul numbered the people present with him, about six hundred men. The Philistines encamped in Michmash, and the spoilers came out of their camp in three companies, toward Ophrah, toward Bethhoron, and toward the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim; three raiding parties sent out to invade Israel.

There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears. The Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his share, his coulter, his axe, and his mattock, so the Philistines knew exactly how disarmed Israel was; all they had was a file for the tools. This is heavy for today. A people that must depend on its adversary for weaponry cannot deliver itself by arms; talk of going to war means nothing when you have to buy your weapons from the very gun store of the ones you say you will fight. Same picture as the scriptures. So in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in the hand of any of the people, but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found; only two men in the army had a blade. In chapter 13 Saul blew the kingdom with his instability in a time of distress. The Most High said, You are not fit; I would have established you, but your replacement is already on the way.

Coming out of the prior chapters, Saul was hunting after David to kill him. When Saul returned from following the Philistines and was told David was in the wilderness of Engedi, he took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel to seek David and his men upon the rocks of the wild goats. Saul went into the cave to cover his feet: that means he was in there relieving himself. See the vulnerable position Saul was in, and yet David spared his life; that is why David could say, thou wast delivered into my hand, but I did not take thy life.

Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand: who is being referred to as the enemy? His own people; Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and David was of the tribe of Judah. On the skirt: the Zondervan Compact Bible Dictionary (page 136) shows the basic garments in general use among men of biblical times were the inner tunic, the tunic coat, the girdle, and the cloak, with the headdress and sandals. The word skirt in the KJV usually refers to an article of male, not female, clothing, with meanings of extremity and corner. Where we have our fringes attached to the borders of our garments, that is the bottom part of Saul's robe that David cut off privily.

When Saul rose out of the cave, David went out after him, cried, My lord the king, and stooped with his face to the earth and bowed himself. He reverenced Saul even though Saul was trying to kill him; that is why the Most High said David is a man after mine own heart. David maintained his integrity. David laid the proof before Saul: this day thine eyes have seen how the Lord delivered thee into mine hand in the cave, and some bade me kill thee, but mine eye spared thee, for he is the Lord's anointed. See the skirt of thy robe in my hand: I cut off the skirt and killed thee not; there is neither evil nor transgression in mine hand, yet thou huntest my soul to take it. David left the judgment with the Most High: the Lord judge between me and thee, and the Lord avenge me of thee, but mine hand shall not be upon thee; as saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked. After whom is the king of Israel come out? after a dead dog, after a flea.

Saul lifted up his voice and wept, and said to David, Thou art more righteous than I, for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil; if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? Saul made an acknowledgement there because he saw the righteousness of David: I know well that thou shalt surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in thine hand.

Saul asked David to swear that he would not cut off his seed after him nor destroy his name out of his father's house, and David sware unto Saul; Saul went home, and David and his men gat them up unto the hold. David showed so much restraint and respect unto his elder; that is something some of us struggle with today, and we need to use this as an example. The Most High was dealing with David: even though he saw Saul acting wickedly and strangely with him, when he had the opportunity to kill Saul he would not do it.

The Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon? Right here we are going back: chapter 26 is picking up on what we read in chapter 23, when the Ziphites first went up to Saul to deliver David into the king's hand.

David beheld the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host; Saul lay in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster, and the people pitched round about him as protection to the king. David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai the son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp? and Abishai said, I will go down with thee; and they came to the people by night, and all lay sleeping.

Abishai said, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day; let me smite him, I pray thee, with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not smite him the second time. But David said, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless? David left Saul's end with the Most High: as the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish; the Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. They took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster and got them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the Lord was fallen upon them.

David went over to the other side, stood on the top of an hill afar off, and cried to Abner: Art not thou a valiant man? and who is like to thee in Israel? wherefore then hast thou not kept thy lord the king? for there came one of the people in to destroy the king thy lord. As the Lord liveth, ye are worthy to die, because ye have not kept your master, the Lord's anointed; and now see where the king's spear is, and the cruse of water that was at his bolster.

Saul knew David's voice and said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And David said, Wherefore doth my lord thus pursue after his servant? for what have I done? or what evil is in mine hand? Let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the Lord: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.

Saul said, I have sinned: return, my son David, for I will no more do thee harm, because my soul was precious in thine eyes this day: behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly. Saul was acknowledging once more David's righteousness, because again David had an opportunity to kill Saul and did not put forth his hand. David answered, The Lord render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness: for the Lord delivered thee into my hand to day, but I would not stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. Again he showed compassion, restraint, and the fear of the Most High. That is what we have to get to as far as brotherly love: when we see each other, we see Christ in each other. That is what our nation is lacking, and that is why we have to be that example, as David was in sparing Saul's life.

When the king sat in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies round about, David said to Nathan the prophet that he dwelt in a house of cedar while the ark of God dwelt within curtains. David was not seeking his own riches but a place for the ark. Nathan told David to do all that was in his heart, for the Lord was with him. But that night the word of the Lord came to Nathan. The Lord asked, Shalt thou build me a house to dwell in? He had not dwelt in any house since bringing Israel out of Egypt but had walked in a tent and a tabernacle, and had never asked any tribe why they built Him not a house of cedar.

The Lord reminded David that He took him from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over His people Israel, and was with him whithersoever he went, cutting off all his enemies and making him a great name. The Most High promised to appoint a place for His people Israel and to plant them that they might dwell in a place of their own and move no more, and that the children of wickedness should afflict them no more. The Lord calls the nations the children of wickedness, the same as when it is taught that Esau is of the wicked one. He also promised David rest from all his enemies, and that the Lord Himself would make David a house.

The Lord said that when David's days were fulfilled and he slept with his fathers, He would set up his seed after him, proceeding out of his bowels, and establish his kingdom; that seed would build a house for the Lord's name. The word reaches past Solomon. Solomon built the house and sat on the throne, but his kingdom was not established for ever; his son Rehoboam would not hear counsel, and the kingdom split into two nations. The phrase "for ever" points to Jesus Christ the black Messiah, who came through David's lineage. The Lord said He would be his father and he His son, and if he committed iniquity He would chasten him with the rod of men. Solomon was not chastened with the rod of men in his lifetime; the one smitten with the rod upon the cheek was Jesus the Christ, who did no sin, though it was Solomon who sinned. The Lord promised that His mercy would not depart from him as it did from Saul, and that David's house, kingdom, and throne would be established for ever. The Lord did not make the Bible easy in every place, that He might see who would research and learn precept upon precept.

Nathan spoke to David according to all these words and this vision. Then David went in and sat before the Lord and said, Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto? David marveled that the Lord had spoken of his house for a great while to come, for there is none like the Most High, neither is there any God beside Him, according to all Israel had heard with their ears. David asked what one nation in the earth is like Israel, whom God went to redeem for a people to Himself, to make Him a name and to do great and terrible things. He did not redeem one man alone but a whole people, and He will bring them out again as a people. The teaching applies: though a brother or sister may have a difference, we must forgive one another and come back together, for the Most High chose us as one people. We lost our heritage in captivity, and coming back to it we must let go of grudges. The northern and southern kingdoms are to be made one nation again under one king and one shepherd. The one king is Jesus Christ, called the throne of David because David ruled over all twelve tribes; David will be present but is not the king. The chief shepherd, the great shepherd, the good shepherd who lays down his life is Christ, and he gathers the elect from the four winds and brings them up out of the land.

David prayed that the Lord would establish for ever the word He had spoken concerning His servant and his house, and do as He had said. He asked that the Lord's name be magnified for ever, that men would say, The Lord of hosts is the God of Israel, and that the house of His servant David be established before Him. Because the Lord of hosts had revealed to David that He would build him a house, David found in his heart to pray this prayer. He rested on the truth of the Lord's word, that with the Lord's blessing the house of His servant would be blessed for ever.

David smote the Philistines and subdued them, taking Methegammah out of their hand, and smote Moab, measuring them with a line, casting them to the ground. Our forefather David was a mighty warrior, subduing two different nations, which nations do not usually do at once. With two lines he measured Moab to death and with one full line to keep alive; the Moabites became David's servants and brought gifts. War was not about killing everyone, for the living become servants and pay tribute; the fear was put in the nations so they would not fight back. David smote Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates, taking a thousand chariots, seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen, houghing the chariot horses but reserving a hundred chariots. When the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, David slew twenty and two thousand of them and put garrisons in Syria, and the Syrians became servants and brought gifts. The Lord preserved David whithersoever he went. David took the shields of gold and much brass and carried them to Jerusalem.

When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer, he sent his son Joram to salute and bless David, because Hadadezer had had wars with Toi. Joram brought vessels of silver, gold, and brass. This is the making of allies: when a stronger king removes an enemy you could never beat, the wise thing is to ally with him. David's kingdom made allies, but not by serving their idols or giving sons and daughters in marriage; the alliances served needful things, as Hiram later helped build the temple. David dedicated the silver and gold to the Lord, along with that dedicated from all the nations he subdued: Syria, Moab, the children of Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, and the spoil of Hadadezer. David got a name when he returned from smiting the Syrians in the valley of salt, eighteen thousand men. He put garrisons throughout all Edom, and all they of Edom became David's servants, and the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went.

David reigned over all Israel and executed judgment and justice unto all his people. This is the mark of a real king and ruler: to lead the people in true judgment according to the commandments. The prayer of a servant is to one day have the spirit of King David, to lead brothers and sisters in justice and truth, and for all the brothers to become such leaders, each praying that those under them be better than themselves. David set his officers: Joab over the host; Jehoshaphat the recorder; Zadok and Ahimelech the priests; Seraiah the scribe; Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David's sons were chief rulers. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem and walks in all the sins of his father, his heart not perfect with the Most High as David's was. The children did what they saw their fathers do, not merely what was said, which is why the Most High teaches His people to be different. Yet for David's sake the Most High gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, because David did right all his days save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, a wrong from which David repented. -

After Abijam dies, Asa his son reigns forty-one years and does right in the eyes of the Most High as David his father did. Asa takes the sodomites out of the land, removes the idols his fathers made, and even removes his own mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, which he destroys and burns at the brook Kidron. Though the high places are not removed, Asa's heart is perfect with the Most High all his days, and he brings dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into the house of the Most High.

There is war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel, who builds Ramah to cut off passage to and from Asa. Asa takes silver and gold from the house of the Most High and the king's house and sends it to Benhadad of Syria to break his league with Baasha, and Benhadad smites cities of Israel so Baasha stops building Ramah. Asa uses the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. In his old age he is diseased in his feet, then sleeps with his fathers, and Jehoshaphat his son reigns in his place.

Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel two years and does evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha conspires against him, kills him, and reigns in his place, then smites all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite. This fulfills, years later, the judgment that Jeroboam's descendants would be destroyed for the sins by which he made Israel to sin.

Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah and does evil, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin by which he made Israel to sin. The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

David loves the Most High, his strength, his rock, fortress, deliverer, buckler, the horn of his salvation and his high tower. He calls upon the Lord who is worthy to be praised, and so is saved from his enemies.

The sorrows of death compassed him and the floods of ungodly men made him afraid; the sorrows of hell compassed him and the snares of death prevented him. The sorrows of death describe the curses of the scattering. -

The earth shook and the foundations of the hills moved and were shaken because the Most High was wroth. Smoke went out of his nostrils and fire out of his mouth devoured. He bowed the heavens and came down with darkness under his feet; he rode upon a cherub and did fly upon the wings of the wind. He made darkness his secret place, dark waters and thick clouds his pavilion; at his brightness the clouds passed with hailstones and coals of fire. The Lord thundered in the heavens, the Most High gave his voice, and sent out his arrows and lightnings to scatter and discomfit his enemies. The channels of waters were seen and the foundations of the world were discovered at his rebuke, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.

He sent from above and drew David out of many waters, delivering him from his strong enemy and from them which hated him, for they were too strong for him. We are still looking for that deliverance from our strong enemy and them that hate us. -

The Lord rewarded David according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands, because he kept the ways of the Lord and did not wickedly depart from his God. We get clean by taking heed to the word and the commandments, not by water baptism. -

With the merciful the Most High shows himself merciful, with the upright man upright, with the pure pure, and with the froward he shows himself froward. He will save the afflicted people but bring down high looks. Israel is the afflicted people the scripture is talking about. -

The Most High lights David's candle and enlightens his darkness; by his God he has run through a troop and leaped over a wall. As for God, his way is perfect and the word of the Lord is tried; he is a buckler to all that trust in him. -

He teaches David's hands to war so that a bow of steel is broken by his arms; he gives him the shield of his salvation, his right hand holds him up, and his gentleness makes him great. He enlarges David's steps under him so his feet do not slip; David pursues his enemies, overtakes them, and does not turn again till they are consumed. -

His enemies cry but there is none to save them, even unto the Lord, but he answers them not; David beats them small as the dust before the wind and casts them out as dirt in the streets. The Most High delivers him from the strivings of the people and makes him the head of the heathen; a people whom he has not known shall serve him. -

The Lord liveth, blessed be his rock, and let the God of his salvation be exalted; it is God that avenges David and subdues the people under him. He delivers David from his enemies and lifts him above those that rise against him, delivering him from the violent man. The enemies are not just going to and fro; there is a people who serve satan, the so-called white man, to make it plain. -

Therefore David gives thanks among the heathen and sings praises to the Most High's name. Great deliverance he gives to his king and shows mercy to his anointed, to David and to his seed forevermore. -

Everyone that thirsts is called to the waters, and he that has no money is told to come, buy, and eat wine and milk without money and without price. The invitation is free. He asks why they spend money for that which is not bread and their labour for that which does not satisfy. They are told to hearken and eat that which is good, and let the soul delight itself in fatness. If they incline their ear and come, their soul will live, and He will make an everlasting covenant with them, even the sure mercies of David. David is given for a witness to the people, a leader and a commander. A nation not known will be called, and nations that did not know her will run to her because of the Most High, who has glorified her.

Seek the Most High while He may be found, call upon Him while He is near. The wicked is to forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and return to the Most High, who will have mercy and abundantly pardon. His thoughts are not our thoughts, and His ways are not our ways. As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are His ways and His thoughts higher than ours.

As the rain and snow come down from heaven and do not return without watering the earth, causing it to bring forth seed and bread, so His word does not return to Him void but accomplishes what He pleases. His people will go out with joy and be led forth with peace; the mountains and hills will break forth into singing and the trees of the field will clap their hands. Instead of the thorn will come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle tree, and this will be to the Most High for a name and an everlasting sign that will not be cut off.

verses.text: But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.

And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily.
And it came to pass afterward, that David’s heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
And he said unto his men, The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord’s anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the Lord.
So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul. But Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed, and be guiltless?
David said furthermore, As the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish.
The Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord’s anointed: but, I pray thee, take thou now the spear that is at his bolster, and the cruse of water, and let us go.
Now therefore so shalt thou say unto my servant David, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel:
And I was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and have cut off all thine enemies out of thy sight, and have made thee a great name, like unto the name of the great men that are in the earth.

Moreover I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in a place of their own, and move no more; neither shall the children of wickedness afflict them any more, as beforetime,
And as since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, and have caused thee to rest from all thine enemies. Also the Lord telleth thee that he will make thee an house.
And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.
He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever.
I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men:
But my mercy shall not depart away from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away before thee.
And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
And David reigned over all Israel; and David executed judgment and justice unto all his people.
Because David did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, and turned not aside from any thing that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me.
For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not wickedly departed from my God.
For all his judgments were before me, and I did not put away his statutes from me.
I was also upright before him, and I kept myself from mine iniquity.
Therefore hath the Lord recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight.
Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.

And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.
Of this man’s seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus:
As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.
He played with lions as with kids, and with bears as with lambs.
Slew he not a giant, when he was yet but young? and did he not take away reproach from the people, when he lifted up his hand with the stone in the sling, and beat down the boasting of Goliath?
For he called upon the most high Lord; and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty warrior, and set up the horn of his people.
So the people honoured him with ten thousands, and praised him in the blessings of the Lord, in that he gave him a crown of glory.
For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and brought to nought the Philistines his adversaries, and brake their horn in sunder unto this day.
In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made him.
He set singers also before the altar, that by their voices they might make sweet melody, and daily sing praises in their songs.
He beautified their feasts, and set in order the solemn times until the end, that they might praise his holy name, and that the temple might sound from morning.
The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.

cases.name: Saul's rash oath, and the people at the blood
cases.charge: A rash oath that snared the army; the people eating flesh with the blood; the son who unknowingly broke the oath
cases.summary: Saul adjured the people to eat nothing until evening, and the army fainted in the pursuit. Jonathan, who had not heard, ate honey; the people, famished, fell on the spoil and ate with the blood; and when the lot fell on Jonathan the people would not let the king kill the man who had wrought the day's salvation.
cases.offense: Jonathan went against the Philistine garrison trusting that the Lord could save by many or by few. The attack was followed by trembling throughout the host and the enemy turning its swords against itself (1 Samuel 14:6-23). In the midst of that deliverance, Saul placed the army under a curse against eating until evening, so that he might be avenged upon his enemies (1 Samuel 14:24). His added command deprived the pursuing men of strength. Honey lay within reach, but the people feared the oath. Jonathan, who had not heard it, tasted honey and was refreshed. When told, he said his father had troubled the land and that the army could have done more had it eaten (1 Samuel 14:25-30). The distinction matters: he had not knowingly broken a charge he heard. Saul's command had nonetheless brought the deliverer himself within the danger of the curse. The famished people fell upon the spoil and ate with the blood (1 Samuel 14:31-33). Their hunger did not repeal the commandment. Leviticus 17:10-14 forbids eating blood because the life of the flesh is in it. A ruler's imprudent burden and the people's unlawful response both belong to the history; correcting the one did not make the other righteous.
cases.judgment: Saul was told, The people sin against the Lord, in that they eat with the blood, and he rolled a great stone and had the beasts slain on it, and built his first altar. Then the Lord answered him not, and the lot taken to find the cause fell on Jonathan. Saul swore he should surely die; the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not, on the witness that he had wrought with God that day. The oath was Saul's; the mercy was the people's; the silence was the Lord's.

entries.commentary: Jonathan said unto the young man that bare his armor, Come, let us go over to the Philistines' garrison on the other side; but he told not his father. Saul tarried under a pomegranate tree in Migron with about six hundred men, with Ahiah the priest wearing an ephod, and the people knew not that Jonathan was gone.

Between the passages were two sharp rocks, Bozez and Seneh, one facing Michmash and the other Gibeah. Jonathan said, Come, let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised; it may be that the Lord will work for us: for there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few. The Lord put that spirit on Jonathan. That is how the Most High operates: he loves to show his power by having a small number defeat a very large number. That is why it will be the 144,000 taking over the whole world; that is just how he rolls.

His armor bearer said, Do all that is in thine heart: behold, I am with thee according to thy heart. Jonathan set the sign: we will discover ourselves unto them; if they say, Tarry until we come to you, we will stand still in our place; but if they say, Come up unto us, then we will go up, for the Lord hath delivered them into our hand. That is how they would know the Lord had given the green light.

Both of them showed themselves to the garrison, and the Philistines said, Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of the holes where they had hid themselves; and the men of the garrison said, Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing. The sign came to pass exactly; the Lord had delivered them into the hand of Israel. Jonathan climbed up upon his hands and upon his feet, his armor bearer after him, and that first slaughter was about twenty men within about half an acre of land. Two men against a garrison. Some hold a doctrine that Jonathan was a homosexual; this act answers it. Scaling a rock face to rush a garrison two-deep is a bold, manly act of war that most men are not cut out for; he carried himself like a real man.

There was trembling in the host, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison and the spoilers also trembled, and the earth quaked, so it was a very great trembling. The Philistines got caught off guard and panicked. The watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude melted away, and they went on beating down one another; in their panic and confusion the Philistines started beating on each other.

Saul numbered the people and found Jonathan and his armor bearer missing. While Saul talked with the priest, the noise in the host of the Philistines went on and increased, and when Israel came to the battle, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture; the enemies were destroying each other, and Israel did not have to put in the work. The Hebrews that were with the Philistines from the country round about turned to be with the Israelites that were with Saul and Jonathan, and the men of Israel which had hid themselves in mount Ephraim followed hard after them in the battle when they heard the Philistines fled. So the Lord saved Israel that day, and the battle passed over unto Bethaven.

Saul had adjured the people, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies; so none of the people tasted any food. Saul put out a strange order, and the men of Israel were distressed that day. All they of the land came to a wood, and there was honey upon the ground, and the honey dropped, but no man put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath. But Jonathan heard not when his father charged the people with the oath; he was not there when the order came out.

Jonathan dipped the end of his rod in an honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightened; like the first taste after a long fast, he felt like a whole new creature. Then one of the people told him his father straitly charged the people with an oath, and the people were faint. Jonathan said, My father hath troubled the land: see how mine eyes have been enlightened, because I tasted a little of this honey; how much more, if haply the people had eaten freely of the spoil of their enemies, had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines? He began to convince the people that eating was the better idea and that the king's order was folly.

They smote the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint. Then the people flew upon the spoil, took sheep, oxen, and calves, slew them on the ground, and did eat them with the blood; too faint to prepare the meat, they ate it raw with the blood, and that was the transgression Jonathan's talk led the people into. When they told Saul, he said, Ye have transgressed: roll a great stone unto me this day; bring every man his ox and his sheep, slay them here, and eat, and sin not against the Lord in eating with the blood. And Saul built an altar unto the Lord, the first altar that he built unto the Lord.

Saul proposed going down after the Philistines by night to spoil them until morning, and the people agreed; then said the priest, Let us draw near hither unto God. And Saul asked counsel of God, Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into the hand of Israel? But he answered him not that day. If you are spiritual, when the Lord ignores you, you understand at that point what it reveals: it is sin. It has to be; the scriptures give only that reason.

Saul said, Draw ye near, all the chief of the people, and know and see wherein this sin hath been this day; for as the Lord liveth, which saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die. But there was not a man among all the people that answered him. Saul said unto the Lord God of Israel, Give a perfect lot; and Saul and Jonathan were taken, but the people escaped. Then they cast lots between Saul and Jonathan, and Jonathan was taken. Jonathan told him, I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in mine hand, and, lo, I must die. And Saul answered, God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan. Saul was ready to kill his own son over the oath.

The people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not; they kept him from the wrath of his father. Think about the contrast, and why the scripture says to get the love of the congregation. In chapter 13 Saul was the one disobeying the voice of the Lord and getting rebuked, while Jonathan was brave and mighty and had just saved Israel out of the hand of its enemies; now the coward wants to kill the deliverer. In some situations you have to weigh it like the people did: yes, he made a mistake and crossed the order, but he just saved all our lives.

Saul took the kingdom over Israel and fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the children of Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines; and whithersoever he turned himself, he vexed them. He gathered an host, smote the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of them that spoiled them. The chapter closes with his house: his sons Jonathan, Ishui, and Melchishua; his daughters Merab and Michal, whom we will learn about later; his wife Ahinoam; and Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle, captain of his host. There was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul, and when Saul saw any strong man or any valiant man, he took him unto him.

*1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 Speak unto Aaron, and unto his sons, and unto all the children of Israel, and say unto them; This is the thing which the LORD hath commanded, saying, 3 What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp, 4 And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, to offer an offering unto the LORD before the tabernacle of the LORD; blood shall be imputed unto that man; he hath shed blood; and that man shall be cut off from among his people: 5 To the end that the children of Israel may bring their sacrifices, which they offer in the open field, even that they may bring them unto the LORD, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, unto the priest, and offer them for peace offerings unto the LORD. 6 And the priest shall sprinkle the blood upon the altar of the LORD at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, and burn the fat for a sweet savour unto the LORD. 7 And they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, after whom they have gone a whoring. This shall be a statute for ever unto them throughout their generations. 8 And thou shalt say unto them, Whatsoever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers which sojourn among you, that offereth a burnt offering or sacrifice, 9 And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, to offer it unto the LORD; even that man shall be cut off from among his people. 10 And whatsoever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, that eateth any manner of blood; I will even set my face against that soul that eateth blood, and will cut him off from among his people. 11 For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul. 12 Therefore I said unto the children of Israel, No soul of you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger that sojourneth among you eat blood. 13 And whatsoever man there be of the children of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, which hunteth and catcheth any beast or fowl that may be eaten; he shall even pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust. 14 For it is the life of all flesh; the blood of it is for the life thereof: therefore I said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall eat the blood of no manner of flesh: for the life of all flesh is the blood thereof: whosoever eateth it shall be cut off. 15 And every soul that eateth that which died of itself, or that which was torn with beasts, whether it be one of your own country, or a stranger, he shall both wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even: then shall he be clean. 16 But if he wash them not, nor bathe his flesh; then he shall bear his iniquity.* --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Keep your foot when you go to the house of the Most High and be more ready to hear than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they do not consider that they do evil. Be not rash with your mouth nor let your heart be hasty to utter anything before the Most High, for he is in heaven and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few. This means watch your mouth, which is why Christ said you will give account of every word. -

When you vow a vow to the Most High, do not defer to pay it, for he has no pleasure in fools; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel that it was an error, lest the Most High be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands. This is what Christ meant by not swearing by heaven, earth, or your own head. -

If you see the oppression of the poor and the perverting of judgment and justice in a province, do not marvel, for he that is higher than the highest regards it, and there are higher than they. Do not worry about the wicked that are successful and all they are doing, because there is a God and that God will have his vengeance. This is why the scriptures say vengeance is his and he will repay. -

He that loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he that loves abundance with increase; this also is vanity. When goods increase, those that eat them increase. As one rapper said, more money more problems: the more money most people get, the bigger their family gets, meaning the more food you can buy, the more mouths there are to feed. The sleep of a laboring man is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich will not let him sleep. The rich lose sleep to gain wealth; ask successful entrepreneurs and businessmen and they work off four or five hours of sleep.

There is a sore evil under the sun: riches kept for the owners to their hurt, and those riches perish by evil travail so that the son is left with nothing in his hand. As a man came from his mother's womb naked, so shall he return, and take nothing of his labor to carry away in his hand. In all points as he came, so shall he go, and he has labored for the wind, eating in darkness with much sorrow, wrath, and sickness.

It is good and comely for a man to eat, drink, and enjoy the good of all his labor all the days of his life which the Most High gives him, for it is his portion. Every man to whom the Most High gives riches, wealth, and power to enjoy them and rejoice in his labor, this is the gift of the Most High. He shall not much remember the days of his life, because the Most High answers him in the joy of his heart. Ecclesiastes is a book of regret, and we can learn from it; in the end you see what really matters in this life. Money is a defense, but keep the commandments in the faith of Christ, which is what Solomon was saying. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)
