cases.name: Agag king of the Amalekites
cases.charge: The sword that made women childless
cases.summary: The Lord had sworn war with Amalek from generation to generation for what they did to Israel on the way out of Egypt. Saul was sent to finish it and spared Agag. Samuel did not: as thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.
cases.offense: The command against Amalek reached back to its assault upon Israel in the wilderness. Amalek struck the hindmost, the feeble, and the weary, without fear of God; Israel was commanded to remember and blot out that memory when the Lord gave rest (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Exodus 17:14-16 placed the matter before succeeding generations. The passage of time had not discharged the word.
cases.judgment: Samuel said, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites, and hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The sentence pronounced at Rephidim was carried out by a prophet's hand when the king's hand failed.

entries.commentary: At Rephidim there was no water, and the people did chide with Moses: wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst? At the first sign of trial the people jumped off the Lord's bandwagon again, the same as we do today when tribulation comes. Moses cried unto the Lord, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me. They were ready to kill the prophet over water, blaming the brother for what only the Most High controls; we have to build our faith up like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who trusted the Lord even when trials came.

The Lord stood before Moses upon the rock in Horeb; Moses smote the rock, and water came out of it in the sight of the elders of Israel. He called the place Massah and Meribah, temptation and chiding, because they tempted the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us, or not? That is wickedness: He had just made Egypt dark, slain their firstborn, and sent His angel in the chariot to guide us, and the people still asked whether He was with them. The mercy of the Most High in bearing that is beyond us.

Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt; Amalek was Esau's grandson, born to Eliphaz of Timna the concubine, a duke in the land of Edom. When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed; when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands until the going down of the sun. Moses was about eighty years old holding a rod above his head all day; the fathers were mighty men, stronger than we are today. The sign shewed the people whose hand their life was in: Moses is the man to hearken to, so do not speak against him. And Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword; Joshua was a mighty warrior even then.

Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Moses wrote it, and [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25) is that rehearsal: remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way. Amalek smote the hindmost, all that were feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he feared not God. He did not meet the mighty men in the front; he went to the back to slay the women, the children, and the old ones. That same spirit works against the nation's young and old today. The Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation. By the time Moses rehearsed it in Deuteronomy, forty years had passed and the children of Amalek had done nothing themselves; hundreds of years after that the Lord sent Saul by Samuel to smite Amalek for what was done coming out of Egypt. God be true and every man a liar: the nations do not get away with what they did to His people, and the judgment carries to the seed. Saul did not finish Agag's line, and in Esther's day Haman the Agagite of that same seed rose against Israel; the war truly runs from generation to generation. Today that seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, robbing Israel of identity and prospering off the oppression. The Lord says He will make them come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee. The whole world is set up between Jacob and Esau, and Esau is the end of this world, the so-called white man, with Amalek leading; it is not speaking of the Arab man, for if Ishmael had a rulership still to come, Israel would have another captivity to enter, and Christ has already redeemed us from the curse of the law. The enmity was set from the garden between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed. They bruised Christ's heel, but at the end of the world Jacob bruises the head: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.

If there be a controversy between men, the judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked; the wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine, for the labourer is worthy of his reward. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

If brethren dwell together and one of them die and have no child, the wife of the dead was not to marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother took her to wife, and the firstborn she bare succeeded in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife. It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt: he met thee by the way and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not. At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

Samuel said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people; now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way when he came up from Egypt. Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers; the generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. This is a specific instruction: kill all of them, spare none. Note that the Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness; that answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows [Leviticus 19:18](/bible/leviticus/19#v18) applies to the children of thy people.

Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah, and laid wait in the valley. Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed. The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment.

Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, and utterly destroyed the people with the edge of the sword; but he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive. He halfway fulfilled the order, reasoning like the king might be valuable as a hostage, as if the Lord forgot that detail. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them; but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. They killed what looked like it deserved killing, so they could say they did some killing, and kept the healthy, good looking animals, telling themselves surely the Lord could not have meant these.

Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel: It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part, understand: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. That is what the Most High is showing us in this story. And it grieved Samuel, and he cried unto the Lord all night. Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost.

Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul came to Carmel and set him up a place, a monument to himself, and is gone down to Gilgal. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name; do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more. Saul greets Samuel first with a cover: Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. The first thing out of his mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed. Samuel answers, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals? Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

Samuel said, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance: when you thought nothing of yourself, with no confidence to be a ruler, the Most High still chose you. And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25). Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

Saul is in denial: Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Samuel breaks down the rebuke and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong. In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

Samuel makes it plain: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in. This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy words; because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, Pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord; take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

Samuel refuses: I will not return with thee; for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. Think it through: Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him; and Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel. This spirit is very real: okay, you are right, but do not let the people see the demotion; make sure they still know I am the king. That is the spirit of vanity, caught up in a rank and a title while forgetting that the title came for pleasing the Lord; once you discontinue pleasing the Lord, the title is going to leave as well. So Samuel turned again after Saul, and Saul worshipped the Lord.

Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately, and said, Surely the bitterness of death is past; with Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was mad at the Amalekites anymore and he was safe. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek's sword had done.

Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah, and Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. The mourning is what makes it sad: Samuel raised Saul up from nothing, saw his potential, and saw the Spirit come upon him in chapter 11 when he stood up as a savior for the people; he had hope in him, and it came to this. Samuel was grieved, and the Lord repented of the appointment. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

cases.name: Goliath of Gath
cases.charge: Defying the armies of the living God, morning and evening, forty days
cases.summary: Six cubits and a span, with a spear like a weaver's beam, Goliath stood in the valley of Elah and reproached Israel for forty days. A shepherd boy came in the name of the Lord of hosts and took his head with his own sword.
cases.offense: Goliath stood before Israel morning and evening for forty days. His height, armour, spear, and shield-bearer made his challenge formidable, but his words defined the offense: he defied the armies of Israel and demanded a man to fight him (1 Samuel 17:4-16). Saul and the people answered the spectacle with fear. They measured the champion while forgetting whose army they were. David heard the same challenge and called it reproach against the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:26, 36). Deuteronomy 20:1-4 commanded Israel not to fear a greater host when the Lord went with them. David's answer was therefore not confidence that youth was stronger than experience. It was confidence that the enemy's equipment did not determine the Lord's power. Eliab accused him, and Saul questioned his ability, but David rehearsed the deliverance from the lion and bear. The Lord who preserved him with the sheep could preserve him in the valley (1 Samuel 17:28-37). When Goliath saw him, he despised him, cursed him by his gods, and promised his body to the birds and beasts (1 Samuel 17:41-44). Contempt for the messenger did not answer the God in whose name he came.
cases.judgment: David rejected armour he had not proved and went with his staff, sling, and stones. He declared that the battle belonged to the Lord, who would make the earth know there was a God in Israel and the assembly know that he saved without sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:38-47). Zechariah 4:6 places the work in the Lord's Spirit rather than man's might. The weapon was in David's hand; the deliverance was not confined to the weapon. David ran to meet Goliath, struck him in the forehead with a stone, and brought him down. He then took the champion's sword and cut off his head (1 Samuel 17:48-51). The very sword that had helped present Goliath as invincible was used at his death.

entries.commentary: As we covered before, the Philistines always wanted smoke with the Israelites; they would not leave us alone. They gathered to battle at Shochoh and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah. Saul and the men of Israel pitched by the valley of Elah and set the battle in array; the Philistines stood on a mountain on one side, Israel on a mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.

Out of the camp of the Philistines came a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span; the heavyweight champion of the Philistines. He wore a helmet of brass and a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels of brass, greaves of brass on his legs, a target of brass between his shoulders, a spear like a weaver's beam with a head of six hundred shekels of iron; a big man in a mighty costume of armor. He did not even carry his own shield; one bearing a shield went before him.

Goliath cried to the armies of Israel: choose you a man and let him come down to me. If he kills me, we will be your servants; if I prevail and kill him, ye shall be our servants. And he said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man that we may fight together. When Saul and all Israel heard the words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid. They were in a carnal spirit, measuring his height, his armor, and his reach; the spirit had departed, and fear is not the spirit of the Most High. The Most High put laws in the book about going to battle, and this fear showed that Saul and the people lacked faith; the same God that destroyed Pharaoh and the Egyptians who pursued Israel was with them, and a trial of faith was set before them in the form of one big intimidating man with a big mouth.

David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehemjudah named Jesse, who had eight sons. The three eldest, Eliab, Abinadab, and Shammah, followed Saul to the battle; the same three the Most High refused in chapter 16. David, the youngest, went and returned from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem. The Philistine drew near morning and evening and presented himself forty days; forty days straight of talking his big talk to try to scare Israel.

Jesse sent David to the camp with parched corn and ten loaves for his brethren and ten cheeses for their captain of the thousand, to see how his brethren fared and take their pledge. Saul and all the men of Israel were in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines; David was sent on an errand to get his brothers some supplies and check on them.

David rose early, left the sheep with a keeper, and came to the trench as the host was shouting for the battle; while he saluted his brethren, the champion came up and spake according to the same words, the same daily smack talk, and David heard them. All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were sore afraid. Think on it: the whole nation's freedom, everything they possessed, was on the line, and they ran scared. This is why the Most High said in chapter 16 that he had refused David's brothers: they were there and did not have the spirit to rise up; they were among the ones who fled.

The men of Israel said that the man who killeth Goliath, the king will enrich with great riches, give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel; a prize was on Goliath's head. Compare Caleb, who made a like offer in the book of Joshua. David asked, What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine and taketh away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God? The soldiers themselves did not understand that they were the armies of the living God; David, a sheep keeper sent on an errand, knew it. Israel is the army of the Most High, and every army requires order; that is why there are captains and officers, and despising that order is despising the army of the living God.

Eliab, the eldest brother, heard David and his anger was kindled: why camest thou down hither, and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride and the naughtiness of thine heart; thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle. A big brother talking down to a little brother, accusing him of sneaking out to watch. David answered, What have I now done? Is there not a cause? The men are scared, nobody will step up; what is the problem? And he turned to another and spake after the same manner.

David's words were rehearsed before Saul, and Saul sent for him. David told Saul, Let no man's heart fail because of him; thy servant will go and fight with this Philistine. Nobody panic; I will handle it. Saul answered, Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth. Young people coming into this truth: if the Most High is dealing with you in a special way, do not let anybody discourage you or tell you that you are too young to be a mighty man of the Lord. Do not let it deter you.

David gave Saul his resume: keeping his father's sheep, when a lion and a bear took a lamb out of the flock, he went out after him, smote him, and delivered it out of his mouth; when he arose against him, David caught him by his beard and slew him. He might have looked small, but he was killing lions and bears behind his sheep. David said, The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. Same God, no difference. And Saul said, Go, and the Lord be with thee.

Saul armed David with his own armor, a helmet of brass and a coat of mail, and David girded his sword upon the armor and assayed to go; but he had not proved it, and he said, I cannot go with these, and put them off him. Instead of the helmet and the brass, David took his staff, chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, put them in a shepherd's bag, and took his sling in his hand. What he put on instead was the whole armour of God: the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit.

When the Philistine looked about and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and of a fair countenance: Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves? And the Philistine cursed David by his gods and promised to give his flesh to the fowls of the air and the beasts of the field. David answered, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. Again the record shows who the army of the Most High is: Israel. David understood he did not need the sword, the spear, or the shield; he had the spirit of the living God. It is no amount of carnal firepower that overcomes the enemies of Israel; this is spiritual warfare, and our forefather David understood that.

David prophesied the outcome before the fight: this day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand, and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. All this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord's. The Most High fights how he wants to fight, not how man thinks it must be done.

David hasted and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine, took a stone from his bag, slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead, and he fell upon his face to the earth. David had precise aim and power; that stone left the sling with the velocity of a bullet, and it took one shot. David prevailed with a sling and with a stone, and there was no sword in the hand of David; he ran and stood upon the Philistine, drew Goliath's own sword out of the sheath, slew him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled. They ran from a young youth because they knew something supernatural was going on; he was in the spirit of the Lord.

When Saul saw David go forth against the Philistine, he asked Abner, the captain of the host, Whose son is this youth? And Abner could not tell; in the shock of it they forgot whose son the young man was. As David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine with the head of the Philistine in his hand, Abner brought him before Saul, and David answered, I am the son of thy servant Jesse the Bethlehemite. That is the history of David and Goliath: when the mighty men of Israel ran afraid, a young youth stood up bold in the spirit of the Lord and took the giant down.

verses.text: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.
And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass.
And he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders.
And the staff of his spear was like a weaver’s beam; and his spear’s head weighed six hundred shekels of iron: and one bearing a shield went before him.

And he stood and cried unto the armies of Israel, and said unto them, Why are ye come out to set your battle in array? am not I a Philistine, and ye servants to Saul? choose you a man for you, and let him come down to me.
If he be able to fight with me, and to kill me, then will we be your servants: but if I prevail against him, and kill him, then shall ye be our servants, and serve us.
And the Philistine said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together.
When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.

And as he talked with them, behold, there came up the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, out of the armies of the Philistines, and spake according to the same words: and David heard them.
And all the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him, and were sore afraid.

And the men of Israel said, Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, that the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free in Israel.

And David spake to the men that stood by him, saying, What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine, and taketh away the reproach from Israel? for who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
And the Philistine came on and drew near unto David; and the man that bare the shield went before him.
And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance.
And the Philistine said unto David, Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves? And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
And the Philistine said to David, Come to me, and I will give thy flesh unto the fowls of the air, and to the beasts of the field.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.

This day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.
And all this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord’s, and he will give you into our hands.
And it came to pass, when the Philistine arose, and came and drew nigh to meet David, that David hasted, and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.
And David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.
So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.

Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.

And the men of Israel and of Judah arose, and shouted, and pursued the Philistines, until thou come to the valley, and to the gates of Ekron. And the wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even unto Gath, and unto Ekron.
And the children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines, and they spoiled their tents.
And David took the head of the Philistine, and brought it to Jerusalem; but he put his armour in his tent.
He played with lions as with kids, and with bears as with lambs.
Slew he not a giant, when he was yet but young? and did he not take away reproach from the people, when he lifted up his hand with the stone in the sling, and beat down the boasting of Goliath?
For he called upon the most high Lord; and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty warrior, and set up the horn of his people.

cases.name: Jonathan
cases.charge: Stripping himself of his robe for the man whom the Lord would make king; and thou shalt be king, and I shall be next unto thee
cases.summary: The king's son and heir made a covenant with the shepherd who had just killed Goliath, and gave him his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle. He warned him of his father's intent, spoke for him and was nearly killed for it, and met him in the wood at Ziph to strengthen his hand in God. He said outright that David would be king and he himself would be next. He died with his father on Gilboa.
cases.offense: Jonathan's confidence in the Lord preceded his covenant with David. At the Philistine garrison he declared that no restraint could keep the Lord from saving by many or by few, and went forward with his armour-bearer (1 Samuel 14:6-14). He had already risked his life for Israel when David came into the history as its champion. Their bond joined men who had acted upon the same trust. Jonathan loved David as his own soul, made a covenant with him, and gave him his robe, garments, sword, bow, and girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). His conduct was the opposite of Saul's envy. As David's honour increased, Jonathan did not treat another servant's calling as an injury to himself. Colossians 2:2 speaks of hearts knit together in love; shared faith strengthens service instead of dividing it by rivalry. When Saul ordered David killed, Jonathan warned him and argued his innocence before the king. David had risked his life and done Saul good; killing him without cause would shed innocent blood (1 Samuel 19:1-7). Later Saul explicitly connected David's survival to Jonathan's loss of the kingdom and threw a javelin at his own son (1 Samuel 20:30-33). Jonathan would not purchase a throne through the murder of his friend. He met David in the wood and strengthened his hand in God, acknowledging that David would be king (1 Samuel 23:16-18). The threatened man needed more than information about Saul's movements. He needed a brother who would stand with the Lord's purpose when doing so cost him advantage. Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 6:14 calls a faithful friend a strong defence; Jonathan supplied that defence in counsel, warning, and covenant.

cases.name: Saul and Doeg at Nob
cases.charge: Slaughter of the priests of the Lord on an informer's report
cases.summary: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, told the king that Ahimelech had given David bread and Goliath's sword. Saul summoned the priests, condemned them unheard, and when his own guard refused to strike them, Doeg killed eighty-five men in linen ephods and then the whole city of Nob.
cases.offense: Doeg reported to Saul that Ahimelech had received David at Nob, enquired for him, given him food, and supplied Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul treated help given to David as conspiracy against himself. Ahimelech answered that David was the king's faithful servant and son in law and that he knew nothing of a plot (1 Samuel 22:11-15). His defence was heard but rejected. The king's suspicion had taken the place of a righteous judgment. Saul ordered the priests killed. His servants refused to stretch out their hands against the priests of the Lord, but Doeg obeyed, killing eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. He then smote Nob, including its households and animals (1 Samuel 22:16-19). The refusal of the guard shows that the king's order did not remove the responsibility of those commanded. Doeg did what others would not do. Exodus 23:1 forbids joining a false report or becoming an unrighteous witness; verse 7 forbids slaying the innocent and righteous. Psalms 52 names the malicious tongue that loves evil rather than good. Speech and violence worked together at Nob: the report furnished an occasion, the king supplied the order, and the willing hand carried it through.
cases.judgment: Psalms 52:5-7 pronounces the overthrow of the man who trusted in riches and strengthened himself in wickedness. He would be plucked from his dwelling and rooted out of the land of the living. His apparent strength was not a refuge from the God whose priests had been struck. The righteous would see and fear: the wealth and royal favour he trusted could not establish his house against the Lord.

His defence was heard but rejected. The king's suspicion had taken the place of a righteous judgment.

Saul ordered the priests killed. His servants refused to stretch out their hands against the priests of the Lord, but Doeg obeyed, killing eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. He then smote Nob, including its households and animals (1 Samuel 22:16-19). The refusal of the guard shows that the king's order did not remove the responsibility of those commanded. Doeg did what others would not do.

Exodus 23:1 forbids joining a false report or becoming an unrighteous witness; verse 7 forbids slaying the innocent and righteous. entries.commentary: The priest gave David hallowed bread, for there was no bread there but the shewbread that was taken from before the Lord. Remember David had been out in the field three days, fearful of king Saul, when he came to Nob in need. Link this history with the words of Christ: when the Pharisees challenged his disciples for plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, Christ recounted this very history of David and the shewbread. Precept this in your bibles if you do not have it already.

David fled that day for fear of Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath, and the servants of Achish knew him by the song, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. David laid up these words in his heart and was sore afraid of Achish, so he changed his behaviour and feigned himself mad, scrabbling on the doors of the gate and letting his spittle fall down upon his beard. David was playing crazy; he was fearful, and Achish dismissed him as a mad man.

Here you see that Saul had placed an Edomite over his servants: Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, answered and reported that David had come to Nob and that Ahimelech had inquired of the Lord for him, given him victuals, and given him the sword of Goliath the Philistine. The scriptures tell us we are never supposed to trust our enemies, yet what we are reading is Saul with an Edomite set over his servants.

Saul commanded his footmen to turn and slay the priests of the Lord, but the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord. Saul was able to get the Edomite to do what his own men would not do: Doeg turned and fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod, and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword. Go back to Genesis and see the spirit that has been placed on this man from the beginning: Esau comforted himself with the purpose of killing his brother Jacob. Just as in the time of Saul, even to this very day, when Israel suffers violence at the hands of the other nations, especially Esau, he gets comfort out of killing us; when Saul appointed Doeg to that task, you can best believe he was quite happy over it and most likely found much pleasure in killing the priests.

To the chief musician, Maschil, a Psalm of David, written when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul that David had come to the house of Ahimelech. Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? The man of sin has to be revealed, and our people still do not want to acknowledge that Esau is the devil, not Christ. The white picture of Jesus is a deception; the Bible says nothing like that. -
Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs, like a sharp razor, working deceitfully. -

Thou lovest evil more than good, and lying rather than to speak righteousness. You thought he loved black people; he loves evil, and lying rather than righteousness. So-called blacks, Hispanics, and Native Americans are a reminder of how the Most High really looks and that Esau sold his birthright.
Thou lovest all devouring words, O thou deceitful tongue.

God shall likewise destroy thee for ever; he shall take thee away and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. There will be no white people in the kingdom; there will be a period of slavery, and then they die and it is over.
The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him. -
Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness. He trusted in his slave trades and his riches. -
But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God; I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever. -
I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it; and I will wait on thy name, for it is good before thy saints. -

Thou shalt not raise a false report, nor put thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness: basically, thou shalt not lie. If you did not see it, do not make up a story like you were there; keep your mouth shut. Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil. Enter not into the path of the wicked; sinners entice, saying come with us, cast in thy lot among us, but walk not thou in the way with them, for their feet run to evil and make haste to shed blood. Many of our young men's lives end short because they follow a multitude to do evil. To be in the midst of the singing, like the whole school hollering fight, fight, fight, is to be in the multitude the Most High warns of; a soul without knowledge of the laws of God hastes with his feet and sins.

Neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause. This deals with judgment: do not be a respecter of persons because a man is poor, as if he is automatically wrong when he brings a matter against a rich man. The judges were charged to hear the small as well as the great. In this corrupt system in Babylon, how innocent or guilty you come out depends on how much lawyer you can afford. Our law was holy and righteous because none of that made a difference: either you were right or you were wrong, whether poor or rich. The Pharisees learned the ways of the heathen and began respecting persons, which the book of James speaks against.

If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again; if thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, thou shalt surely help with him. This enemy that hates you is your brother, your own nation, not the other nations as [Matthew 5:44](/bible/matthew/5#v44) is misconstrued to mean. [Deuteronomy 22:1-4](/bible/deuteronomy/22#v1) proves it, saying the same law with thy brother in the place of thine enemy: thou shalt not see thy brother's ox or sheep go astray; in any case, no matter how you feel, bring them again unto thy brother. And if thou know him not, keep it in thine own house until thy brother seek after it. He is still your brother even if you never grew up with him; that is real love for your own people. Deuteronomy means the second law; it speaks the law plain in case you did not understand it here. Keep [Deuteronomy 22:1-4](/bible/deuteronomy/22#v1) and [Leviticus 19:17-18](/bible/leviticus/19#v17) in your hip pocket with this verse.

Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause: verse six explains verse three again in case you did not catch it, do not be partial in judgment. Keep thee far from a false matter; the innocent and righteous slay thou not, for the Most High will not justify the wicked. Thou shalt take no gift, for the gift blindeth the wise and perverteth the words of the righteous: do not take a bribe when it comes to judgment; be upright and honest.

Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger, for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. This is speaking about us, as [Exodus 22:21](/bible/exodus/22#v21) already laid out with [Leviticus 25:35](/bible/leviticus/25#v35).

Six years thou shalt sow thy land, but the seventh year thou shalt let it rest and lie still, that the poor of thy people may eat, and the beasts of the field after them; likewise the vineyard and the oliveyard. That is mercy from the Lord: in the seventh year the land itself fed the poor. The seventh year ties into the count of the jubilee: seven sabbaths of years to the forty-ninth year, and in the fiftieth year no plowing of the land, which the law takes up later.

Six days do thy work, and on the seventh day rest, that thine ox and thine ass may rest, and the son of thy handmaid and the stranger may be refreshed. The stranger here can be another nation working for you: they too get their due rest on the sabbath. When the Lord sets Israel back up to rule, the nations will kick and scream at first, but once these laws are applied there will be righteousness reigning over the earth like they have never seen, and all will be refreshed on the sabbath, spiritually and physically.

Make no mention of the name of other gods is not saying you cannot pronounce the names Buddha, Allah, Krishna, Ra. Christ himself named Beelzebub, the chief of the devils, a name derived from the Philistine god of Ekron, and Christ did no sin; so the verse cannot mean the bare saying of a name. The Lord says this same thing three ways in this one chapter, and the other two places show the meaning: verse 24, thou shalt not bow down to their gods nor serve them nor do after their works; and verses 32 and 33, thou shalt make no covenant with them nor with their gods, for if thou serve their gods it will surely be a snare unto thee. Make no mention means do not learn how to serve and worship them. Joshua and Deuteronomy double it: neither make mention of the name of their gods, nor cause to swear by them, neither serve them, nor bow yourselves unto them; and if thy brother or son or wife entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, thou shalt not consent. Wherever you are, do not go trying to find out how the nations worship their gods.

Three times thou shalt keep a feast unto me in the year: all the males appeared before the Lord God three times in the year. The feast of unleavened bread is the Passover, kept in the time appointed of the month Abib, the first month of the year, as it is written, the feast of unleavened bread drew nigh, which is called the Passover. None shall appear before me empty: you could not come empty-handed. You brought the tenth of your oil, your wine, whatever was required, for the priests to replenish the storehouses. The feast of harvest, the firstfruits of thy labours, is also known as Pentecost and the feast of weeks; and the feast of ingathering, in the end of the year, is also known as the feast of tabernacles and the feast of booths.

Thou shalt not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread, neither shall the fat of my sacrifice remain until the morning. The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the Lord thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk: the Lord repeats what was read at [Exodus 22:30](/bible/exodus/22#v30), that the young one was not to be taken too young and too soon; it stayed its seven days with his dam before it was given.

Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared. Beware of him, obey his voice, provoke him not, for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him. That Angel is speaking of Christ. If thou indeed obey his voice, I will be an enemy unto thine enemies and an adversary unto thine adversaries. These enemies are not the same enemy of verse four: the enemy of verse four is your brother whom you must help and shew mercy; these enemies in verse 22 the Lord himself deals with and destroys for you.

The Angel goes before Israel unto the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, to cut them off. Thou shalt not bow down to their gods nor serve them nor do after their works, but utterly overthrow them and quite break down their images. Serve the Lord your God, and he shall bless thy bread and thy water, take sickness away from the midst of thee, none casting their young nor barren in the land, and the number of thy days he will fulfil. He drives the nations out by little and little, lest the land become desolate and the beasts multiply, until Israel be increased and inherit the land. The bounds are set from the Red Sea even unto the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert unto the river, the river Euphrates. That little sliver on the map today is not how big Israel is supposed to be: the land was to encompass all the way out to the Euphrates by Babylon, taking in parts of what is Iraq and Iran, and it will be filled one day.

Thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor with their gods. They shall not dwell in thy land, lest they make thee sin against me: for if thou serve their gods, it will surely be a snare unto thee. This is the third way the Lord states the command of verse 13 in this chapter: no learning their worship, no serving, no covenant.

verses.text: Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the Lord; and his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul.
Then answered Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, and said, I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.
And he enquired of the Lord for him, and gave him victuals, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.

And Saul said unto him, Why have ye conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread, and a sword, and hast enquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?
Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, And who is so faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king’s son in law, and goeth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house?

Did I then begin to enquire of God for him? be it far from me: let not the king impute any thing unto his servant, nor to all the house of my father: for thy servant knew nothing of all this, less or more.
And the king said, Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou, and all thy father’s house.

And the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the Lord; because their hand also is with David, and because they knew when he fled, and did not shew it to me. But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord.

And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod.
And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep, with the edge of the sword.
And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David.
And Abiathar shewed David that Saul had slain the Lord’s priests.
And David said unto Abiathar, I knew it that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father’s house.
Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life: but with me thou shalt be in safeguard.
Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? the goodness of God endureth continually.
Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.
Thou lovest evil more than good; and lying rather than to speak righteousness. Selah.
Thou lovest all devouring words, O thou deceitful tongue.
God shall likewise destroy thee for ever, he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah.
Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.

cases.name: Nabal
cases.charge: Churlish refusal of hospitality; railing on the Lord's anointed
cases.summary: David's men had guarded Nabal's shepherds all season. At sheep-shearing David asked for provision; Nabal, churlish and evil in his doings, answered, who is David? and sent them away. Abigail's wisdom stopped David's sword. The Lord did not stop his own.
cases.offense: Nabal possessed three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. At sheep-shearing David sent a peaceful request for provision, reminding him that his shepherds and goods had been safe among David's men (1 Samuel 25:2-9). Nabal's own servant confirmed their conduct: they had been a wall by night and day, and nothing had gone missing (1 Samuel 25:14-16). The benefit was known within the household before the request arrived. Nabal answered with contempt, asking who David was and comparing him to a servant breaking away from his master. He would not give his bread, water, and meat to these men (1 Samuel 25:10-11). His repeated claim upon his possessions ignored the protection through which he had enjoyed them. Wealth had become the reason to close his hand rather than the means to supply a need. His servant described him as a man who could not be reasoned with (1 Samuel 25:17). That spirit made correction difficult before the danger arrived. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 forbids hardening the heart and shutting the hand against a needy brother. Nabal joined refusal to railing, repaying good with evil while his household prepared to feast.
cases.judgment: David armed four hundred men and intended to destroy the males of the household. Abigail intervened with provision and counsel, keeping him from avenging himself by bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:13, 18-35). Nabal's guilt did not authorize every act David's anger proposed. The Lord's restraint of David was mercy toward his servant and those his sword would have struck.
offenseFull: Nabal possessed three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. At sheep-shearing David sent a peaceful request for provision, reminding him that his shepherds and goods had been safe among David's men (1 Samuel 25:2-9). Nabal's own servant confirmed their conduct: they had been a wall by night and day, and nothing had gone missing (1 Samuel 25:14-16). The benefit was known within the household before the request arrived.

Nabal answered with contempt, asking who David was and comparing him to a servant breaking away from his master. He would not give his bread, water, and meat to these men (1 Samuel 25:10-11). His repeated claim upon his possessions ignored the protection through which he had enjoyed them. Wealth had become the reason to close his hand rather than the means to supply a need.

His servant described him as a man who could not be reasoned with (1 Samuel 25:17). That spirit made correction difficult before the danger arrived. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 forbids hardening the heart and shutting the hand against a needy brother. Nabal joined refusal to railing, repaying good with evil while his household prepared to feast.

entries.commentary: Samuel died, and all the Israelites gathered together and lamented him and buried him in his house at Ramah; and David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran. There was a very great man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, shearing his sheep in Carmel. His name was Nabal, and his wife was Abigail, a woman of good understanding and of a beautiful countenance; but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb.

David heard in the wilderness that Nabal did shear his sheep and sent ten young men to greet him in peace: peace be to thee, to thine house, and to all that thou hast. The request was righteous: thy shepherds were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them all the while they were in Carmel; ask thy young men and they will shew thee. We come in a good day; give whatsoever cometh to thine hand unto thy servants and to thy son David.

Nabal answered, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master. He was talking much smack, as if he did not even know who David was, and refused to give of his bread, his water, and his flesh to men he knew not. When his young men told David, he said, Gird ye on every man his sword; about four hundred men went up after David, and two hundred abode by the stuff.

One of the young men told Abigail: David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master, and he railed on them. But the men were very good unto us; we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing as long as we were conversant with them; they were a wall unto us both by night and day while we were keeping the sheep. David's men had been giving Nabal's shepherds protection from their enemies. Evil is determined against our master and against all his household, for he is such a son of Belial that a man cannot speak to him. Some of us know people like that: you cannot talk to them, they will not reason with you. Consider that Nabal was rich, a very wealthy man, and a lot of times what comes with that is an arrogant spirit.

Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, clusters of raisins, and cakes of figs, laid them on asses, and sent her servants on before her; but she told not her husband Nabal. David had said, Surely in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness; he hath requited me evil for good. He swore to leave Nabal none by the morning light of any that pisseth against the wall; David was coming with intent to destroy the men of that house.

When Abigail saw David she hasted, lighted off the ass, fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be. She was not the one who did anything wrong, but she took that iniquity upon herself; she was being that pillar of her house, using wisdom to protect it, for the scripture says she was a woman of good understanding. She did not turn her lord over to be destroyed, as some women today would be ready to do; instead she pleaded, Let not my lord regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. She had not seen the young men David sent, or she would have stepped in then to protect their house.

Abigail said, The Lord hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood and from avenging thyself with thine own hand; now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal. She asked, Forgive the trespass of thine handmaid; it was Nabal who was out of the spirit, but again that chaste conversation, stepping up for her household. The soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God, and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out as out of the middle of a sling. When the Lord shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel, this shall be no grief unto thee, that thou hast shed blood causeless or that my lord hath avenged himself; then remember thine handmaid.

David said, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me, and blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood and from avenging myself with mine own hand. David received of her hand that which she had brought him and said, Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice and have accepted thy person.

Abigail came home and Nabal held a feast in his house like the feast of a king, and his heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken; so she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. Remember he had railed, Who is David? but when he sobered up and heard that the coming king had come down to destroy everybody in his house, his heart died within him. About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. Then David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife. Abigail bowed herself on her face to the earth and said, Behold, let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord, and she arose and washed the feet of the servants who delivered the good tidings; that is a very humble act. She was probably very joyous and glad to go: a woman living with a man who is hard to deal with, who will not listen, will not take advice, arrogant, maybe verbally abusive, was relieved of that thing when Nabal died, and she hasted and arose with five damsels of hers and became David's wife.
David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they were also both of them his wives; but Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which was of Gallim.

At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release: every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it, and shall not exact it of his neighbour or of his brother, because it is called the Lord's release. Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release. The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25).

If thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the Most High to observe all these commandments, thou shalt lend unto many nations but thou shalt not borrow, and thou shalt reign over many nations but they shall not reign over thee. This is the blessing that was to come upon us. Since we broke the commandments of the Most High, the other nations lend to us and we borrow from them; we go to them for loans and everything else.

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren, thou shalt not harden thine heart nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother. It is a commandment to us to help our brothers: open thine hand wide unto him and lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.

Beware that there be not a thought in thy wicked heart saying, The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand, and thine eye be evil against thy poor brother and thou givest him nought; if he cry unto the Lord against thee, it is sin unto thee. Give him surely, and let not thine heart be grieved when thou givest, for because of this thing the Most High shall bless thee in all thy works. Notice that Esau had this Bible, these commandments and these laws, yet worked us to death for over four hundred years, and when they released us we did not go out with anything. They had these laws written before them and did not do them. The poor shall never cease out of the land; Christ said the same, that the poor are always going to be among us. That is why no campaign can fight poverty out of existence: Christ said it will always be among us.

If thy brother, an Hebrew man or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee and serve thee six years, then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free, and thou shalt not let him go away empty. When people say slavery was taking place in Africa among us, it was not slavery like we suffered: it was people among us that fell poor and sold themselves to their brothers, the very case this law and [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25) govern. Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress; he must leave blessed, with some of the flock, the corn, and the wine. He cannot go out poor the way he came in; that shows you the Most High is a good God. The reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

If the servant say, I will not go away from thee, because he loveth thee and thine house and is well with thee, then thou shalt take an aul and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever; likewise unto thy maidservant. It shall not seem hard unto thee when thou sendest him away free, for he hath been worth a double hired servant to thee in serving thee six years. A double hired servant: reading this makes you think about slavery and how many years they had us. We were double hired servants unto them, and we still serve them even to this day.

All the firstling males of thy herd and of thy flock thou shalt sanctify unto the Most High: thou shalt do no work with the firstling of thy bullock, nor shear the firstling of thy sheep. The firstlings were to do no work at all; they were to be sacrificed to the Most High, and thou shalt eat it before the Lord thy God year by year in the place which the Lord shall choose. If there be any blemish therein, as if it be lame or blind, thou shalt not sacrifice it unto the Lord thy God; thou shalt eat it within thy gates, the unclean and the clean person alike, as the roebuck and as the hart. Only thou shalt not eat the blood thereof; thou shalt pour it upon the ground as water.

Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he railed on them.
But the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields:
They were a wall unto us both by night and day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore know and consider what thou wilt do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his household: for he is such a son of Belial, that a man cannot speak to him.

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.

And Abigail came to Nabal; and, behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; and Nabal’s heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken: wherefore she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light.
But it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.

And David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife.

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother:
But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.

cases.name: Abigail
cases.charge: Keeping David from shedding blood and avenging himself with his own hand
cases.summary: Her husband Nabal railed on David's men; David strapped on his sword to kill every male of the house by morning. Abigail met him on the road with two hundred loaves and a speech that is one of the wisest in scripture, and turned him back. Ten days later the Lord smote Nabal, and David sent for her.
cases.offense: Abigail heard from a servant what Nabal had done and what David's men had done for the household. The men had protected the shepherds; Nabal had railed upon their messengers; now destruction threatened the house (1 Samuel 25:14-17). She did not make loyalty to her husband mean agreement with his folly. She acted to preserve the household he had placed in danger. She prepared substantial provision and went to meet David without first telling Nabal. David had already armed his men and sworn to leave no male of the house alive (1 Samuel 25:18-22). Her haste addressed a danger that could not wait for the husband described as unwilling to hear reason. The food answered the need; her speech addressed the wrath. She humbled herself, took the burden of pleading upon herself, and named Nabal's folly without disguising it. Then she directed David toward the future the Lord had promised him. When he ruled Israel, he should not carry the grief of causeless bloodshed or self-avenging violence (1 Samuel 25:23-31). She appealed to his calling against the conduct his anger was about to produce. Wise counsel did not flatter the armed man; it stopped him. Proverbs 14:1 says that a wise woman builds her house. Abigail's conduct protected more than its possessions. It preserved lives and called the approaching king back to the fear of the Lord. She neither approved Nabal's railing nor answered it by delivering him to David's sword.
cases.judgment: David blessed the Lord who sent her, blessed her advice, and acknowledged that she had kept him from shedding blood and avenging himself. He accepted the provision and sent her home in peace (1 Samuel 25:32-35). Her counsel succeeded because he received correction while there was still time to turn from the act. At home she again governed the moment of speaking. Nabal was drunk, so she waited until morning. After he heard what had happened, he became as a stone, and about ten days later the Lord smote him (1 Samuel 25:36-38). The household was spared David's intended slaughter; Nabal's own judgment remained with the Lord. David then sought Abigail as his wife, and she answered with the same humility that had marked her appeal (1 Samuel 25:39-42). The blessing follows a woman of understanding who brought provision, spoke truth, and preserved another from sin. Her wisdom was not merely knowledge of what was right. It was the ability to bring that knowledge to bear before blood was shed.

Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul. When Ishbosheth charged him over Rizpah, Saul's concubine, Abner was very wroth, saying he had shown kindness to the house of Saul and not delivered them to David, and now was charged with a fault concerning this woman. Abner swore to do to himself and more, to translate the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba. Ishbosheth could not answer him a word, because he feared him. Abner was through with Ishbosheth and turned to go with David and the Lord.

Abner sent messengers to David offering to bring all Israel to him. David agreed to make a league, but required that Michal, Saul's daughter, first be brought to him, and he sent to Ishbosheth to deliver his wife whom he had espoused for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines. verses.text: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he railed on them.
But the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields:
They were a wall unto us both by night and day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore know and consider what thou wilt do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his household: for he is such a son of Belial, that a man cannot speak to him.

Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses.
And she said unto her servants, Go on before me; behold, I come after you. But she told not her husband Nabal.
And when Abigail saw David, she hasted, and lighted off the ass, and fell before David on her face, and bowed herself to the ground,
And fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be: and let thine handmaid, I pray thee, speak in thine audience, and hear the words of thine handmaid.

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.

Now therefore, my lord, as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, seeing the Lord hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand, now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal.
And now this blessing which thine handmaid hath brought unto my lord, let it even be given unto the young men that follow my lord.

I pray thee, forgive the trespass of thine handmaid: for the Lord will certainly make my lord a sure house; because my lord fighteth the battles of the Lord, and evil hath not been found in thee all thy days.

Yet a man is risen to pursue thee, and to seek thy soul: but the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God; and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out, as out of the middle of a sling.
And it shall come to pass, when the Lord shall have done to my lord according to all the good that he hath spoken concerning thee, and shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel;

That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, either that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself: but when the Lord shall have dealt well with my lord, then remember thine handmaid.
And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me:
And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand.

For in very deed, as the Lord God of Israel liveth, which hath kept me back from hurting thee, except thou hadst hasted and come to meet me, surely there had not been left unto Nabal by the morning light any that pisseth against the wall.
So David received of her hand that which she had brought him, and said unto her, Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice, and have accepted thy person.

And Abigail came to Nabal; and, behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; and Nabal’s heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken: wherefore she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light.
But it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
And it came to pass about ten days after, that the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.

And when David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. And David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife.
And when the servants of David were come to Abigail to Carmel, they spake unto her, saying, David sent us unto thee, to take thee to him to wife.
And she arose, and bowed herself on her face to the earth, and said, Behold, let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.
And Abigail hasted, and arose, and rode upon an ass, with five damsels of hers that went after her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife.
And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.

cases.name: Saul and the witch of Endor
cases.charge: Seeking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, after cutting them off out of the land himself
cases.summary: With the Philistines encamped and the Lord not answering him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets, Saul disguised himself, went by night to a woman at Endor, and asked her to bring up Samuel. He had himself put the mediums out of the land. He was told he and his sons would be with Samuel the next day, fell on the earth, and died on Gilboa. Chronicles names this as a cause of his death.
cases.offense: Saul had removed those with familiar spirits and wizards from the land. When the Philistine host frightened him and the Lord answered neither by dreams, Urim, nor prophets, he sought a woman with a familiar spirit himself (1 Samuel 28:3-7). He knew the prohibition because he had enforced it. The silence he encountered did not give him permission to seek an answer by a forbidden means. He disguised himself and went by night. The woman feared a trap because of Saul's own earlier action, but he swore by the Lord that no punishment would come upon her for the deed (1 Samuel 28:8-10). The name of the Lord was invoked to reassure someone in the performance of what his law condemned. An oath cannot make disobedience holy. Leviticus 19:31 forbids seeking familiar spirits; Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids the necromancer and places these practices among the abominations Israel was to reject. Saul sought counsel while continuing the course for which counsel had condemned him. His need was not another voice agreeing to direct him, but obedience to the word already received.
cases.judgment: Samuel's answer did not open another course. The Lord had departed from Saul and had done what was previously announced: torn the kingdom from him and given it to David. The refusal to execute the word against Amalek was named again (1 Samuel 28:15-18). Going to the forbidden source had not removed the command he had rejected.

He disguised himself and went by night. The woman feared a trap because of Saul's own earlier action, but he swore by the Lord that no punishment would come upon her for the deed (1 Samuel 28:8-10). Leviticus 19:31 forbids seeking familiar spirits; Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids the necromancer and places these practices among the abominations Israel was to reject.
