verses.text: Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the Lord. And the Lord answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.

And the king called the Gibeonites, and said unto them; (now the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites; and the children of Israel had sworn unto them: and Saul sought to slay them in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah.)
Wherefore David said unto the Gibeonites, What shall I do for you? and wherewith shall I make the atonement, that ye may bless the inheritance of the Lord?
And the Gibeonites said unto him, We will have no silver nor gold of Saul, nor of his house; neither for us shalt thou kill any man in Israel. And he said, What ye shall say, that will I do for you.
And they answered the king, The man that consumed us, and that devised against us that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the coasts of Israel,
Let seven men of his sons be delivered unto us, and we will hang them up unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, whom the Lord did choose. And the king said, I will give them.
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the Lord’s oath that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.

But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the Lord: and they fell all seven together, and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.

And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.
And it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.

And David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh–gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth–shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, when the Philistines had slain Saul in Gilboa:
And he brought up from thence the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son; and they gathered the bones of them that were hanged.

And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land.
And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.
But all the princes said unto all the congregation, We have sworn unto them by the Lord God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them.
This we will do to them; we will even let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath which we sware unto them.
So ye shall not pollute the land wherein ye are: for blood it defileth the land: and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that is shed therein, but by the blood of him that shed it.
The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.

The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

entries.commentary: There was a famine in the days of David, three years, year after year, and David inquired of the Lord. The Lord answered that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Saul broke his word. The Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites, and Israel had sworn unto them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal. David asked the Gibeonites what he should do and wherewith he should make the atonement. The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites who are of Ammon; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine. The Gibeonites would take no silver nor gold of Saul nor of his house, but asked for seven of Saul's sons to be hanged unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul. The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the whole house paid for it.

The king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the Lord's oath that was between David and Jonathan. David did not go back on his oath; earlier he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David's table as long as there was family of the lineage of Jonathan. But the king took the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal and delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the Lord. They fell all seven together and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.

Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, took sackcloth and spread it upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and she suffered neither the birds of the air by day nor the beasts of the field by night to touch them. When David was told, he went and took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hanged them when Saul was slain in Gilboa. Jonathan's body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. David buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father, and performed all that the king commanded. After that the Most High was entreated for the land.

The Philistines had war again with Israel, and David went down and waxed faint. Ishbi-benob, of the sons of the giant, thought to slay him, but Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him and killed the Philistine. Then the men of David swore that he should go no more out with them to battle, that he quench not the light of Israel; he was getting up in age and it was time to sit on the throne. There were further battles at Gob and at Gath. Sibbechai slew Sippai, Elhanan slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam, and Jonathan the son of Shimeah, David's brother, slew a man of great stature with six fingers on every hand and six toes on every foot. These four were born to the giant in Gath and fell by the hand of David and his servants. These giants were tall men, one about eight or nine feet, not the twenty foot giants of fairy tales. Goliath had kin, and eventually they were all served by David and his servants.

The kings on this side Jordan, in the hills, in the valleys, and in all the coasts of the great sea over against Lebanon: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite. These are Hamites, better known as Nilotic Africans. When they heard what had been done, they gathered themselves together to fight with Joshua and with Israel with one accord.

The inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, and they did work wilily: they made as if they had been ambassadors, with old sacks upon their asses, wine bottles old and rent and bound up, old shoes and old garments, and bread dry and mouldy. They came to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal saying, We be come from a far country: now therefore make ye a league with us. Israel was commanded to destroy all the inhabitants of the land, the very nations listed in verse 1, so the Gibeonites' only hope was to pretend they were not of the land.

The men of Israel were suspicious at first: peradventure ye dwell among us, and how shall we make a league with you? Joshua pressed them, Who are ye, and from whence come ye? The Gibeonites leaned on the fame of the Most High: we have heard all that he did in Egypt, and to Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites beyond Jordan. Their props sold the story. In ancient times wine did not come in bottles like ours; wine came in bags, sometimes made of leather, and they would rend through wear and tear over time.

The men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. That is the first mistake, and not asking counsel of the Most High at this moment ended up being a snare and a trap to us as a people, as the rest of the scriptures show. Let reason think on whether it is the right move, and even before you reason within yourself, the Most High says counsel, counsel, counsel before every action. This type of ordeal will play out again in the times when Christ returns: the sons of strangers shall come to build up Israel's walls, their kings shall minister unto Israel, and the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish. There is nothing new under the sun.

At the end of three days Israel heard that they were their neighbours, dwelling among them. The children of Israel smote them not, because the princes of the congregation had sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel. All the congregation murmured against the princes, but the princes held the line: we have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel, now therefore we may not touch them. Our forefathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding up to their word.

We will even let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath which we sware unto them. A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile. Let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation. Hewers of wood and drawers of water means slaves. This is according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations. If you just read the Old Testament, there was no equality among the nations, and there is still no equality among nations: they were made for a certain purpose. The reason they are not in that purpose now is because we have sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places.

Joshua called for them: wherefore have ye beguiled us, saying, We are very far from you, when ye dwell among us? Now therefore ye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen, and hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God. They were servants all the way up and through.

The Gibeonites answered honestly: it was certainly told thy servants how the LORD thy God commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants, therefore we were sore afraid of our lives because of you. Behold, we are in thine hand. So did he unto them, and delivered them out of the hand of the children of Israel, that they slew them not; and Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day.

Moses commands the tribes to separate cities out of their own inheritance for the Levites to dwell in, with suburbs round about them. The Levites needed cities inside every tribe's territory because the Most High took them from among the children of Israel as a gift, to do the service of the tabernacle of the congregation. Every tribe needed that service done among them, so the Levites had to be spread out through all the children of Israel. The commandment was fulfilled when Israel came into the land: the heads of the fathers of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and Joshua at Shiloh and claimed the cities the Lord commanded by the hand of Moses.

The cities were for the Levites to dwell in, and the suburbs were for their cattle, their goods, and all their beasts. The suburbs were measured out: a thousand cubits from the wall of the city round about, and two thousand cubits on the east, south, west, and north sides, with the city in the midst.

Among the Levite cities six were set apart for refuge, appointed for the manslayer to flee there, with forty and two more added: forty and eight cities in all, given from every tribe according to its inheritance, many from them that had many and few from them that had few. Why would the Lord permit a manslayer refuge? The Most High gave Moses the understanding of how to discern manslaughter from murder. For murder there was no refuge, but for manslaughter cities of refuge were given. The law itself was already instituted in [Exodus 21](/bible/exodus/21); [Numbers 35](/bible/numbers/35) answers where the manslayer goes: the Most High appointed him a place to flee.

Killeth any person unawares means he did not mean to do it; it was an accident that resulted in a death. Accidental deaths are of the Lord, beyond our control. Refuge means a condition of being safe or sheltered from pursuit, danger, or trouble. The cities of refuge exist because the manslayer is being pursued: someone has the right to avenge the death of the one who was killed. The city of refuge keeps the manslayer alive until he stands before the congregation in judgment, so the trial can discern between murder and manslaughter before the avenger reaches him.

Six cities of refuge stood, three on this side Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, and they served the children of Israel, the stranger, and the sojourner among them alike. The chapter lays out three categories when someone dies by the hand of another: he meant to hurt him but not kill him, yet he died, and that is murder; he hated him and killed him with premeditation, and that is murder; or he had no quarrel and never meant it, and that is manslaughter, not worthy of death.

Smite him with an instrument of iron, with a stone, or with a hand weapon of wood so that he die, and he is a murderer: even if the intent was only to hurt him and not to kill him, if he dies, the judgment is death. This is a precept for the street: the music culture glorifies slinging an iron, but the word says if you sling that iron and the brother dies, you are a murderer and your judgment is to die.

The revenger of blood himself slays the murderer when he meets him; there was no refuge and no mercy for murder. This is the law given to Israel at that time, an understanding of those judgments; it is not license for anyone to go about killing today.

Laying of wait means he was lurking and stalking, waiting to catch him slipping because of hatred between them; that is premeditated murder. Even without a weapon, smiting him in enmity with the hand so that he dies is murder; he that smote him shall surely be put to death.

The law repeats its key words on purpose, the way legal statutes do, because the details decide the case: suddenly, without enmity, without laying of wait, and seeing him not. Seeing him not matters because it is nearly impossible to kill a man by accident while looking straight at him; the victim was out of sight when the thing flew and struck him. He was not his enemy and sought not his harm: there could be no documented past hatred, and he could not even have been seeking to harm him, since seeking only to harm still makes the death murder. Then the congregation judges between the slayer and the revenger of blood according to these judgments.

Once the congregation clears him of murder, it delivers the slayer out of the hand of the revenger and restores him to his city of refuge; he still must abide there. He stays within the city until the death of the high priest which was anointed with the holy oil, whoever held that office when the incident happened.

If the slayer steps outside the borders of his city of refuge before that high priest dies and the revenger of blood finds him there and kills him, the revenger is not guilty of blood, because the slayer was instructed to remain within the borders. After the death of the high priest the slayer returns to the land of his possession, and the avenger can no longer touch him.

The murderer is put to death by the mouth of witnesses, plural: multiple people must testify, and their stories must match in the details for the murder to be established. One witness alone cannot cause a man to die, because a single witness could lie in the interest of the avenger and put an innocent man to death. The rule stood first for sins worthy of death and then had to become the principle for every matter: two or three witnesses establish any accusation of iniquity or sin.

The judges could take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer guilty of death, and no satisfaction for the manslayer to come home before the death of the high priest; a guilty man cannot buy himself off. No matter who stands before the judge or what money is offered, if they are guilty of death they are guilty of death; a gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous. Israel's judges later fell into exactly this: they became covetous and took bribes to clear the guilty and turn aside the poor in the gate.

Blood defileth the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood shed in it but by the blood of him that shed it; the murderer who escapes his judgment leaves the land polluted. That judgment was instituted back in the days of Noah, and Moses carried it forward in the statutes given to Israel, for the Lord himself dwells among the children of Israel.

When a man hath taken a wife and she find no favour in his eyes because he hath found some uncleanness in her, then let him write her a bill of divorcement, give it in her hand, and send her out of his house. Christ magnified this law: when the Pharisees asked why Moses then commanded to give a writing of divorcement, he said, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery; and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.

If the latter husband hate her and write her a bill of divorcement, or if the latter husband die, her former husband which sent her away may not take her again to be his wife after that she is defiled, for that is abomination before the Lord. The question is whether a woman who leaves her husband and becomes another man's wife can be joined to the first again; the prophet asks the same thing: shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?

When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business; he shall be free at home one year and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken. Make it plain: the first year, stay at home and make a baby. Husband and wife render due benevolence to one another; benevolence means good, it is a good thing. The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge, for he taketh a man's life to pledge. The millstone is a tool for grinding meal: the manna was gathered and ground in mills or beaten in a mortar and baked into cakes. Taking a man's tool takes away his living, like somebody stealing your tools so you cannot make a living. It is better that they steal your money, because with your tools you can go back and make more money.

Remember what the Lord thy God did unto Miriam by the way, after that ye were come forth out of Egypt: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married, and Miriam was not supposed to be speaking against Moses. The anger of the Lord was kindled against them, the cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow. The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding.

When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge; stand abroad, and let the man bring the pledge out unto thee. If the man be poor, thou shalt not sleep with his pledge; deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment and bless thee, and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the Lord thy God. The law was already given: if thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, deliver it by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only, and when he crieth unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious. The history shows how wicked we were to each other: Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god, instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness. That is why the Lord was judging us.

The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin. The example: as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in Amaziah's hand, he slew his servants which had slain the king his father, but the children of the murderers he slew not, according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses. The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.

The word of the Most High asks what they mean by the proverb, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. As the Most High lives, they shall no more use this proverb in Israel, for all souls are His; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is His. The soul that sinneth, it shall die, setting the theme of individual accountability.

If a man be just and do that which is lawful and right, has not eaten upon the mountains nor lifted his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, nor oppressed any, but restored the debtor his pledge and given his bread to the hungry, he is just and shall surely live. He has not given forth upon usury nor taken increase, has withdrawn his hand from iniquity, executed true judgment between man and man, and walked in the Most High's statutes.

If that just man beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, who eats upon the mountains, defiles his neighbour's wife, oppresses the poor and needy, spoils by violence, and lifts his eyes to idols, committing abomination. Such a son who gives forth upon usury and takes increase shall not live; he has done all these abominations and shall surely die, and his blood shall be upon him.

If that wicked man beget a son that sees all his father's sins, considers, and does not do likewise, but gives his bread to the hungry, covers the naked, takes off his hand from the poor, and keeps the Most High's judgments and statutes. That son shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live, but the father, because he cruelly oppressed and spoiled his brother, shall die in his own iniquity.

They ask why the son does not bear the iniquity of the father, when the son has done that which is lawful and right and kept the statutes; he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous is upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked upon him.

If the wicked turn from all his sins, keep all the Most High's statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live and not die; his transgressions shall not be mentioned unto him. The Most High has no pleasure that the wicked should die, but that he return from his ways and live; yet if the righteous turn away from his righteousness and commit iniquity, all his righteousness shall not be mentioned, and he shall die in his sin.

Yet the house of Israel says the way of the Lord is not equal; the Most High answers, Are not your ways unequal. When a righteous man turns from his righteousness and dies in his iniquity, it is for the iniquity he has done; when a wicked man turns from his wickedness and does that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive.

Therefore the Most High will judge the house of Israel, everyone according to his ways; repent and turn yourselves from all your transgressions, so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away all your transgressions and make you a new heart and a new spirit, the heart being the mind, for the Most High has no pleasure in the death of him that dies; wherefore turn yourselves and live. This reading taught repentance, how our enemies take the chief of our young men and women to leave the nation base, and that the Most High has a plan to use the lowly and base to confound the wise, so let your light shine rather than look for any slither of hope to unite with our oppressors. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant)

cases.name: David's numbering of the people
cases.charge: Numbering Israel in pride; a plague on the nation
cases.summary: David commanded Joab to number Israel and Judah. Joab objected; the king's word prevailed. When the count came in, David's heart smote him: I have sinned greatly. Gad offered three judgments, and David chose to fall into the hand of the Lord.
cases.offense: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and David was moved to number the people; Chronicles names Satan as the one who stood up against Israel and provoked him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The provocation did not make David an unwilling bystander. He gave the command and pressed it against objection. Joab wished that the Lord would multiply the people a hundredfold and asked why David delighted in this thing. Chronicles records his warning that the act would bring trespass upon Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). The king's word prevailed, and the officers went through the land (2 Samuel 24:2-8). Authority could compel the count without making the purpose acceptable. Numbering itself was not absent from the law. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom for each man when Israel was numbered, that there be no plague among them. The people were the Lord's, not a measure of strength for a ruler to possess independently of him. Joab's protest and the prescribed warning both stood against treating the census as a harmless exercise of royal pleasure. Afterward David's heart smote him. He confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). He did not place the guilt upon the officers who had obeyed him. The recognition came after the command had already carried its work through the kingdom.
cases.judgment: Pestilence: seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beersheba in three days. The angel stood at Araunah's threshingfloor with drawn sword when the Lord said, it is enough. David bought the floor and built an altar; it became the temple site.

entries.commentary: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah. This was the Most High wanting to judge Israel; he used David and used Satan to provoke him to do it. Joab objected, asking why the king delighted in this thing, for numbering the people was not the king's job but the work of the Levites. Notwithstanding, the king's word prevailed against Joab and the captains, and they went out to number the people. Joab did not understand that behind it all, verse one, the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; it was of the Most High that this happened.

Joab and the captains passed over Jordan and went through all the land, from Aroer and Gad and Gilead, to Dan-jaan, to Zidon, to the stronghold of Tyre and the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites, and out to the south of Judah to Beersheba. It took them nine months and twenty days to count all of Israel. Joab gave the sum to the king: there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men that drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men. This did not count the women and the children.

David's heart smote him after he had numbered the people, and he said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly; take away the iniquity of thy servant, for I have done very foolishly. As soon as it was done it hit him, because it was not the king's job but the Levites' to number the people. In the morning the word of the Lord came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, offering David three things to choose one: seven years of famine, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence. David was in a great strait and said, Let us fall now into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, and let me not fall into the hand of man. He had two prophets, Gad and Nathan, who ministered to him.

The Lord sent the pestilence upon Israel from the morning to the time appointed, and there died seventy thousand men from Dan to Beersheba. When the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord repented him of the evil and said to the angel, It is enough, stay now thine hand; and the angel was by the threshing place of Araunah the Jebusite. David saw the angel that smote the people, something we cannot see today, for the Most High has blinded our eyes to it and this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. David spoke unto the Lord, Lo, I have sinned and done wickedly, but these sheep, what have they done; let thine hand be against me and against my father's house. Remember the reason for the seventy thousand is verse one, the Most High was angry at Israel.

Gad told David to rear an altar unto the Lord in the threshing floor of Araunah, and David went up as the Lord commanded. Araunah bowed himself before the king and offered to give the floor, the oxen, and the instruments freely for the burnt sacrifice, saying, The Lord thy God accept thee. David refused to take it for nothing, saying he would not offer burnt offerings unto the Lord his God of that which cost him nothing, and bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. He built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, so the Lord was entreated for the land and the plague was stayed from Israel. True worship costs us something. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number the people; David commanded Joab to number Israel from Beersheba to Dan. Joab objected, asking why the king would require this thing and be a cause of trespass to Israel, but the king's word prevailed. Joab numbered the people: a thousand thousand and a hundred thousand men that drew sword in Israel, and four hundred threescore and ten thousand in Judah. Joab left Levi and Benjamin uncounted because the king's word was abominable to him.

The Most High was displeased with the numbering and smote Israel; David confessed he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly and begged that the iniquity be taken away. The Most High sent Gad the seer to offer David three choices: three years of famine, three months of destruction before his foes, or three days of pestilence with the destroying angel. David chose to fall into the hand of the Most High rather than the hand of man, saying very great are His mercies, for he knew man would not show him the mercy the Most High would.

The Most High sent pestilence, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell; the angel was sent to destroy Jerusalem, but the Most High beheld it, repented of the evil, and told the angel it was enough to stay his hand. David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Most High standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword stretched over Jerusalem, and he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces. David pleaded that he alone had sinned by commanding the numbering, asking that the hand be on him and his father's house but not on the people, who as sheep had done nothing. Our forefathers had the pleasure of seeing such acts of the Most High in their midst; in these last days we walk by faith in what the scriptures say, for the war is now of a different kind.

The angel commanded Gad to tell David to set up an altar in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, and David went up at the word spoken in the name of the Most High. Ornan, threshing wheat, turned and saw the angel and hid with his four sons, then saw David and bowed to the ground; David asked to buy the threshingfloor for the full price so the plague might be stayed. Ornan offered to give it all, the place, the oxen, the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat, but David refused to take what was another man's or to offer burnt offerings without cost. David paid six hundred shekels of gold, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the Most High answered him by fire from heaven and commanded the angel to sheathe his sword. David paid the full price rather than take the offering for free, and this is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something. -

When David saw that the Most High answered him at the threshingfloor of Ornan, he sacrificed there. The tabernacle Moses made and the altar of burnt offering were then at the high place in Gibeon. David could not go to Gibeon to inquire of the Most High because he was afraid of the sword of the angel, so he worshipped at the new altar instead. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The altar to burn incense upon was made of shittim wood, a cubit in length and a cubit in breadth, foursquare, and two cubits high, with horns of the same. A cubit has been read to be about seventeen inches, so this stood about waist high. It was overlaid with pure gold, the top, the sides round about, and the horns, with a crown of gold round about, two golden rings under the crown, and staves of shittim wood overlaid with gold. The staves through the rings were how the priests bore it as Israel moved through the wilderness.

The altar was put before the vail that is by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat where the Most High would meet with Moses. Aaron burned sweet incense on it every morning when he dressed the lamps, and again at even when he lighted the lamps, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout the generations; it burned continually, morning and evening. No strange incense went on it, and no burnt sacrifice, meat offering, or drink offering; this altar was for one specific incense only. The service had to be exactly as prescribed, and deviation carried death, which is a reason to thank the Lord for Christ.

Aaron made an atonement upon the horns of it once in a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements; it is most holy unto the Lord. This altar served the day of atonement. On the tenth day of the seventh month Israel afflicted their souls and did no work at all, and the priest made an atonement for the sanctuary, the tabernacle, the altar, the priests, and all the people of the congregation, to cleanse them from all their sins before the Lord; an everlasting statute, once a year. The priests went always into the first tabernacle accomplishing the service of God, but into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood. Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, so the day of atonement is still kept by afflicting the soul and doing no work, but without the animal sacrifice, because Christ took the place of the animal.

Numbering the children of Israel was not done lightly; when they were counted, every man gave a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, that there be no plague among them when they were numbered. The ransom was half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary, from every one that passed among them that were numbered, from twenty years old and above; the rich gave no more and the poor gave no less, to make an atonement for their souls. The atonement money was appointed for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation. The gold, the wood, the curtains, and the fabrics all had to be bought and kept up, and the tabernacle moved with the nation through the wilderness; that is the same reason offerings are gathered in the congregation today, because the house of the Most High cannot be built or kept without it.

The laver of brass, with his foot also of brass, stood between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, with water in it; a great brass bowl set on a brass base. Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet thereat when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation and when they came near to the altar to minister, that they die not; the priests could not go in unclean. It was a statute for ever to Aaron and to his seed throughout their generations.

The holy anointing oil was compounded of principal spices, pure myrrh five hundred shekels, sweet cinnamon two hundred and fifty, sweet calamus two hundred and fifty, cassia five hundred after the shekel of the sanctuary, and oil olive an hin, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary, which is a maker of perfume. With it were anointed the tabernacle of the congregation, the ark of the testimony, the table and all his vessels, the candlestick and his vessels, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all his vessels, and the laver and his foot, that they be most holy; whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy. Aaron and his sons were anointed and consecrated with it to minister in the priest's office. It was not poured upon man's flesh, and none was to be made like it after the composition of it; whosoever compounded any like it, or put any of it upon a stranger, was cut off from his people. The Most High gave specific orders down to the spices and the weights, and none could deviate from them or they would die. Our forefathers carried out that tedious, exact work, yet we complain about the smallest things set in place for order, the uniform, the new moon, and not cooking on the sabbath; the spirit has to get right.

The perfume was made of sweet spices, stacte, onycha, and galbanum, with pure frankincense, of each a like weight, tempered together, pure and holy, a confection after the art of the apothecary. Part of it was beaten very small and put before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation; unto you it shall be most holy. The Most High wanted the tabernacle anointed and smelling sweet, everything done one specific way. It was for the Lord alone; ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof, and whosoever made like unto it, to smell thereto, was cut off from his people. There were no knockoffs of the holy things; a copy carried death.

*1 Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand. 2 Over the first course for the first month was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 3 Of the children of Perez was the chief of all the captains of the host for the first month. 4 And over the course of the second month was Dodai an Ahohite, and of his course was Mikloth also the ruler: in his course likewise were twenty and four thousand. 5 The third captain of the host for the third month was Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, a chief priest: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 6 This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son. 7 The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 8 The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 9 The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 10 The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 11 The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 12 The ninth captain for the ninth month was Abi-ezer the Anetothite, of the Benjamites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 13 The tenth captain for the tenth month was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 14 The eleventh captain for the eleventh month was Benaiah the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 15 The twelfth captain for the twelfth month was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 16 Furthermore over the tribes of Israel: the ruler of the Reubenites was Eliezer the son of Zichri: of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maachah: 17 Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok: 18 Of Judah, Elihu, one of the brethren of David: of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael: 19 Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: 20 Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: 21 Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: 22 Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel. 23 But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. 24 Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David. 25 And over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah: 26 And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub: 27 And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite: 28 And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baal-hanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash: 29 And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai: 30 Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite: 31 And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s. 32 Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: 33 And Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor: and Hushai the Archite was the king’s companion: 34 And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar: and the general of the king’s army was Joab.*

verses.text: And again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.

For the king said to Joab the captain of the host, which was with him, Go now through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beer–sheba, and number ye the people, that I may know the number of the people.

And Joab said unto the king, Now the Lord thy God add unto the people, how many soever they be, an hundredfold, and that the eyes of my lord the king may see it: but why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?

Notwithstanding the king’s word prevailed against Joab, and against the captains of the host. And Joab and the captains of the host went out from the presence of the king, to number the people of Israel.

And David’s heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O Lord, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.
For when David was up in the morning, the word of the Lord came unto the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
Go and say unto David, Thus saith the Lord, I offer thee three things; choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.

So Gad came to David, and told him, and said unto him, Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land? or wilt thou flee three months before thine enemies, while they pursue thee? or that there be three days’ pestilence in thy land? now advise, and see what answer I shall return to him that sent me.
And David said unto Gad, I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the Lord; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man.
So the Lord sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning even to the time appointed: and there died of the people from Dan even to Beer–sheba seventy thousand men.

And David spake unto the Lord when he saw the angel that smote the people, and said, Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house.
And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.
And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, Go, number Israel from Beer–sheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.

And Joab answered, The Lord make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?
Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem.

And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword.
But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.
And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel.
And David said unto God, I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.
So the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men.

And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the Lord beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, It is enough, stay now thine hand. And the angel of the Lord stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.

And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the Lord stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces.

And David said unto God, Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered? even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed; but as for these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, O Lord my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.
And king David said to Ornan, Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the Lord, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.
So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight.
And David built there an altar unto the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the Lord; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering.

When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them.
But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the Lord had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens.
Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David.

cases.name: Adonijah
cases.charge: Exalting himself to be king; asking for the king's concubine
cases.summary: David's fourth son exalted himself, saying, I will be king, and gathered chariots, horsemen, Joab, and Abiathar for a coronation feast at En-rogel while David lay dying. Solomon was anointed the same day. Pardoned once, Adonijah then asked for Abishag the Shunammite.
cases.offense: Adonijah exalted himself, saying that he would be king, and prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. David had not displeased him by asking why he acted so (1 Kings 1:5-6). The display of succession grew without the father's correction, but display was not appointment. Joab and Abiathar supported him. He made a sacrificial feast and invited the king's sons and servants while leaving out Solomon, Nathan, Benaiah, and the mighty men (1 Kings 1:7-10). The invitations divided the house according to the claim he intended to establish. Religious sacrifice accompanied a decision made without the king's declaration. Nathan and Bathsheba brought the matter before David, who confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign. Solomon was placed upon the king's mule and anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan (1 Kings 1:28-40). David also declared that the Lord had chosen Solomon to sit upon the throne (1 Chronicles 28:5). Adonijah's seniority among the surviving sons did not overrule that choice. When the news reached his feast, the guests rose in fear and departed. Adonijah caught hold of the horns of the altar and sought assurance that Solomon would not kill him (1 Kings 1:41-51). The man who had announced himself king now depended upon the king's mercy.
cases.judgment: Solomon had spared him on condition of worthiness. The second offense was the end of it: Benaiah fell upon him and he died. Abiathar was banished and Joab executed in the same purge.

Nathan and Bathsheba brought the matter before David, who confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign. entries.commentary: David is old and cannot stay warm, so his servants seek a fair young woman to lie in his bosom and give him heat. This is one of the things that happens with age, when the body no longer produces heat as it did in youth and strength. Abishag the Shunammite is found and ministers to the king, but he does not know her. That means he did not have relations with her; she was there only to keep him warm. -
Adonijah exalts himself, saying he will be king, and prepares chariots and horsemen to promote himself. He takes the throne to himself rather than receiving it from the Most High.
David repeats the oath he swore by the Lord God of Israel, that Solomon his son shall reign after him and sit upon his throne in his stead. The throne belongs to Solomon by that sworn word. -

David commands that Solomon be set on the king's own mule and brought to Gihon, where Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him king over Israel. The people come up rejoicing so that the earth rings with the sound.

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

David said, This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel. He commanded to gather together the strangers that were in the land of Israel and set masons to hew wrought stones to build the house of God. These strangers were brought in to help with the building of the temple. David prepared iron in abundance for the nails and for the joinings, brass in abundance without weight, and cedar trees in abundance. The Zidonians and they of Tyre brought much cedar wood to David.

David said that Solomon his son was young and tender, and the house to be built for the Lord must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and glory throughout all countries, so he prepared abundantly before his death. He called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the Lord God of Israel.

David told Solomon that it was in his mind to build a house unto the name of the Lord, but the word of the Lord came to him saying he should not build it because he had shed blood abundantly and made great wars. Because of all the wars and fighting David had done, the Most High did not allow him to build the temple. The Lord promised David a son who would be a man of rest, to whom he would give rest from all his enemies round about, whose name would be Solomon, and in whose days he would give peace and quietness unto Israel. This son would build the house for the Most High's name, and the Most High would establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.

David charged Solomon that the Lord be with him and prosper him to build the house of the Lord his God, and asked that the Lord give him wisdom and understanding and charge concerning Israel that he might keep the law of the Lord. He said Solomon would prosper if he took heed to fulfill the statutes and judgments which the Lord charged Moses with concerning Israel. This is the same message the Most High gives us today: we will prosper as long as we obey the commandments. Be strong and of good courage; dread not, nor be dismayed.

In his trouble David prepared for the house of the Lord a hundred thousand talents of gold and a thousand thousand talents of silver, and brass and iron without weight, and timber and stone in abundance, telling Solomon he might add thereto. Without weight means they gave in such abundance they were not counting it. There were workmen with him in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber and all manner of cunning men for every kind of work. David told Solomon to arise and be doing, and the Lord be with him.

David commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son, asking whether the Lord their God was not with them and had not given them rest on every side, for he had given the inhabitants of the land into David's hand and the land was subdued before the Lord. This is what David was there to do: he subdued all the nations by the power of the Most High. He charged them to set their heart and soul to seek the Lord their God, to arise and build the sanctuary of the Lord God, and to bring the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels of God into the house that was to be built. Earlier David had moved the ark from place to place, and that is when he desired to build a house for it before the Lord.

*1 And David assembled all the princes of Israel, the princes of the tribes, and the captains of the companies that ministered to the king by course, and the captains over the thousands, and captains over the hundreds, and the stewards over all the substance and possession of the king, and of his sons, with the officers, and with the mighty men, and with all the valiant men, unto Jerusalem. 2 Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building: 3 But God said unto me, Thou shalt not build an house for my name, because thou hast been a man of war, and hast shed blood. 4 Howbeit the LORD God of Israel chose me before all the house of my father to be king over Israel for ever: for he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler; and of the house of Judah, the house of my father; and among the sons of my father he liked me to make me king over all Israel: 5 And of all my sons, (for the LORD hath given me many sons,) he hath chosen Solomon my son to sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. 6 And he said unto me, Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. 7 Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day. 8 Now therefore in the sight of all Israel the congregation of the LORD, and in the audience of our God, keep and seek for all the commandments of the LORD your God: that ye may possess this good land, and leave it for an inheritance for your children after you for ever. 9 And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the LORD searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever. 10 Take heed now; for the LORD hath chosen thee to build an house for the sanctuary: be strong, and do it. 11 Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat, 12 And the pattern of all that he had by the spirit, of the courts of the house of the LORD, and of all the chambers round about, of the treasuries of the house of God, and of the treasuries of the dedicated things: 13 Also for the courses of the priests and the Levites, and for all the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and for all the vessels of service in the house of the LORD. 14 He gave of gold by weight for things of gold, for all instruments of all manner of service; silver also for all instruments of silver by weight, for all instruments of every kind of service: 15 Even the weight for the candlesticks of gold, and for their lamps of gold, by weight for every candlestick, and for the lamps thereof: and for the candlesticks of silver by weight, both for the candlestick, and also for the lamps thereof, according to the use of every candlestick. 16 And by weight he gave gold for the tables of shewbread, for every table; and likewise silver for the tables of silver: 17 Also pure gold for the fleshhooks, and the bowls, and the cups: and for the golden basons he gave gold by weight for every bason; and likewise silver by weight for every bason of silver: 18 And for the altar of incense refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot of the cherubims, that spread out their wings, and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. 19 All this, said David, the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern. 20 And David said to Solomon his son, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the LORD God, even my God, will be with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, until thou hast finished all the work for the service of the house of the LORD. 21 And, behold, the courses of the priests and the Levites, even they shall be with thee for all the service of the house of God: and there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service: also the princes and all the people will be wholly at thy commandment.*

When David was past the top of the hill, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with saddled asses, two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. When David asked where his master's son was, Ziba said Mephibosheth abode in Jerusalem, saying the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father. So David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth. Ziba came with gifts, and when David asked about Mephibosheth, Ziba claimed Mephibosheth thought the kingdom was about to be restored to him, which was not true. On that word David handed Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth.

As David came to Bahurim, a man of the house of Saul named Shimei the son of Gera came out, cursing and casting stones at David and all his servants. Shimei cursed, calling David a bloody man and a man of Belial, saying the Most High had returned upon him all the blood of the house of Saul, and delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom his son, and taken him in his mischief because he was a bloody man. Shimei was of the house of Saul, and Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David; it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. That is the mindset of some people in Israel as well.

Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and offered to go take off his head. But the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Most High hath said unto him, Curse David; who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? David rolled with mighty men of war, so Abishai was ready to take Shimei's head off his shoulders. But David said to let him curse, for if it was of the Most High, then let him do it. Just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and try to bring confusion, it is of the Most High, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

David said to Abishai and all his servants, Behold, my own son who came forth out of my bowels seeketh my life, how much more now may this Benjamite do it? Let him alone and let him curse, for the Most High hath bidden him. It may be that the Most High will look on his affliction and requite him good for the cursing this day. David reasoned that if his own son sought his life, this Benjamite was nothing; the Most High was doing this, so let him curse. It may be the Most High will look on all that was done to David and bless him in front of them, the same as when people try to bring us down and the Most High blesses us before them, which is why this congregation has grown exponentially.

David and his men went by the way while Shimei went along the hillside cursing, throwing stones, and casting dust; and they came weary and refreshed themselves. Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom saying, God save the king, Absalom asked why he went not with his friend, and Hushai answered that he would serve whom the Most High and Israel chose, and would serve in the presence of the son as he served the father. Hushai put into action the plan he and David made. Absalom challenged him, asking, Is this thy kindness to thy friend? Why wentest thou not with thy friend? This is a real friend, not a friendish one; a true friend tells you when you are wrong and full of it, not the one who only strokes your head and pats your back like Absalom did to steal the people's hearts.

Absalom asked Ahithophel for counsel, and Ahithophel said, Go in unto thy father's concubines whom he left to keep the house, and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father, and the hands of all with thee shall be strong. So they spread Absalom a tent on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God. Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.
