entries.commentary: The burden of the valley of vision falls on a city gone up to the housetops, a tumultuous and once joyous city whose slain men are not slain with the sword nor dead in battle. Its rulers are fled together and bound, and the prophet turns away to weep bitterly and will not be comforted.

It is a day of trouble, of treading down, and of perplexity by the Most High of hosts in the valley of vision, with the walls broken down and a crying to the mountains. Elam bears the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield, so the choicest valleys are full of chariots set in array at the gate.

The people look to their defenses in that day: the breaches of the city of David, the gathering of the waters of the lower pool, the numbering and breaking down of houses to fortify the wall, and a ditch made between the two walls for the water of the old pool. Yet they have not looked unto the Maker thereof nor had respect unto Him that fashioned it long ago.

In that day the Most High of hosts calls to weeping, mourning, baldness, and girding with sackcloth, but instead there is joy and gladness, slaying oxen and eating flesh, saying "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die." The Most High reveals that this iniquity shall not be purged from them till they die.

The word comes against Shebna, the treasurer over the house, who has hewn himself out a sepulchre on high and graved a habitation for himself in a rock. The Most High will carry him away with a mighty captivity, toss him like a ball into a large country where he shall die, and drive him from his station and pull him down from his state.

In Shebna's place the Most High calls His servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, clothing him with the robe and girdle and committing the government into his hand, so he is a father to Jerusalem and to Judah with the key of the house of David laid upon his shoulder to open and shut. He is fastened as a nail in a sure place for a glorious throne, yet in that day the nail shall be removed, cut down, and fall, and the burden upon it cut off.

Hezekiah son of Ahaz begins to reign over Judah in the third year of Hoshea, the last king of Israel before the captivity. He does that which is right according to all that David his father did, removing the high places, breaking the images, and cutting down the groves. He breaks in pieces the brazen serpent Moses made in the wilderness, which had stood from that time and was now being burned incense to, and he calls it Nehushtan.

Hezekiah trusts in the Most High so that none among the kings of Judah, before or after, was like him. He clave to the Most High, kept the commandments, and the Most High was with him so that he prospered. Prospering here does not mean a mansion or luxury, but the blessing that comes from keeping and doing the commandments. He rebels against the king of Assyria and smites the Philistines even unto Gaza. -

In Hezekiah's fourth year Shalmaneser besieges Samaria, and after three years, in Hezekiah's sixth year, Samaria is taken. Israel was not removed all at once but carried away in stages into Assyria. The reason given again is that they obeyed not the voice of the Most High but transgressed His covenant and all Moses commanded. -

Sennacherib king of Assyria comes up against the fenced cities of Judah and takes them. Hezekiah sends to Lakish acknowledging offense and agrees to bear whatever tribute is laid on him. Assyria appoints three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, so Hezekiah gives all the silver of the house of the Most High and even cuts the gold from the temple doors.

The king of Assyria sends Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem, and they stand by the conduit of the upper pool. Rabshakeh challenges Hezekiah's confidence, mocking his trust and calling Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of any who lean on it. He argues that because Hezekiah removed the high places, even Judah's own worship is now confined to one altar, twisting the reform into a weakness. He boasts that Assyria came up against the land by the word of the Most High Himself, claiming divine backing to destroy it.

Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah ask Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language so the people on the wall will not understand, but he refuses. Rabshakeh cries aloud in the Jews' language, warning the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them or make them trust in the Most High. He promises the people their own vines, fig trees, and waters if they surrender, then a land like their own, seeking to turn them from their king. He asks whether the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah delivered their lands, claiming no god can deliver Jerusalem out of his hand. The people hold their peace and answer not a word, for Hezekiah had commanded silence. Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come to Hezekiah with their clothes rent and tell him the words of Rabshakeh. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)
Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.

Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. Fear him which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell. Not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Things happen to a man that no one else sees; they are not unseen.

Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God. Unto him that blasphemeth against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven. When they bring you unto the synagogues, and unto magistrates, and powers, take ye no thought how or what thing ye shall answer, for the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say.

A man asks him to make his brother divide the inheritance, and is answered, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you? Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. He discerned the thoughts of both men in that dispute. The rich man pulls down his barns to build greater, and is told, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee. So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.

Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, and God feedeth them. Consider the lilies: Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. After all these things do the nations of the world seek: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things. But rather seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you.

Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. Provide yourselves treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning, and be like men that wait for their lord. Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching. Be ye therefore ready also: for the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not.

The faithful and wise steward gives the household their portion of meat in due season, and is made ruler over all his lord hath. The servant that says in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming, and begins to beat the menservants, has his portion appointed with the unbelievers. That servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, shall be beaten with many stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished. He was in anguish of mind over it. He knew what he had come to do.

Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division. The division named here is inside a house: father against son, mother against daughter, mother in law against daughter in law. Coming into this truth is where that starts.

Ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth; but how is it that ye do not discern this time? Men who can read the weather and every other sign will not read the one in front of them. Agree with thine adversary in the way, lest he hale thee to the judge, and thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite.

verses.text: Thus saith the Lord God of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say,
What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?

And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father’s house.
And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons.

In that day, saith the Lord of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the Lord hath spoken it.
And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully:
And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.

cases.name: Sennacherib and Rabshakeh
cases.charge: Reproaching the living God; setting him among the gods of the nations that could not save
cases.summary: Rabshakeh stood by the conduit of the upper pool and told Jerusalem in the Jews' language that no god of any nation had ever delivered a land from the king of Assyria. Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord. That night an angel slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib went home to be murdered by his sons in the house of his god.
cases.offense: Rabshakeh addressed Jerusalem's people in their own language to shake their confidence. He promised provision if they surrendered and compared the Lord with the gods of cities Assyria had already taken (2 Kings 18:28-35). Past victories were used as evidence that no power could now deliver Judah. Sennacherib's letters repeated the railing. The offense was not merely confidence in his army, but the claim that the God of Israel could be measured by defeated idols (2 Chronicles 32:17-19). Assyria's strength was real; the conclusion drawn from it was false.
cases.judgment: Hezekiah brought the letter before the Lord. Through Isaiah the answer identified the one they had reproached: the Holy One of Israel. The Lord knew Sennacherib's rage and would turn him back by the way he came (2 Kings 19:14-28). An angel struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returned to Nineveh and was later killed by his sons while worshipping in the house of Nisroch (2 Kings 19:35-37). The commander who said no god could save Jerusalem could not be preserved in his own god's house. His return and death answered the word; Jerusalem's deliverance did not depend upon matching the host he had displayed.

verses.text: Then Rab–shakeh stood and cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ language, and spake, saying, Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria:
Thus saith the king, Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you out of his hand:
Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, saying, The Lord will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.

Hearken not to Hezekiah: for thus saith the king of Assyria, Make an agreement with me by a present, and come out to me, and then eat ye every man of his own vine, and every one of his fig tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his cistern:

Until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of oil olive and of honey, that ye may live, and not die: and hearken not unto Hezekiah, when he persuadeth you, saying, The Lord will deliver us.
Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered at all his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?
Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of mine hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem out of mine hand?
And Hezekiah received the letter of the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up into the house of the Lord, and spread it before the Lord.

And Hezekiah prayed before the Lord, and said, O Lord God of Israel, which dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; thou hast made heaven and earth.
Lord, bow down thine ear, and hear: open, Lord, thine eyes, and see: and hear the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent him to reproach the living God.
Of a truth, Lord, the kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations and their lands,
And have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them.
Now therefore, O Lord our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord God, even thou only.
Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, That which thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard.
This is the word that the Lord hath spoken concerning him; The virgin the daughter of Zion hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee.
Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? even against the Holy One of Israel.

By thy messengers thou hast reproached the Lord, and hast said, With the multitude of my chariots I am come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon, and will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the lodgings of his borders, and into the forest of his Carmel.
I have digged and drunk strange waters, and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of besieged places.
Hast thou not heard long ago how I have done it, and of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.

Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded; they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up.
But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me.
Because thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.
Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it.
By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the Lord.
For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.

And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh.

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.
And his servants spake yet more against the Lord God, and against his servant Hezekiah.

He wrote also letters to rail on the Lord God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, As the gods of the nations of other lands have not delivered their people out of mine hand, so shall not the God of Hezekiah deliver his people out of mine hand.
Then they cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city.
And they spake against the God of Jerusalem, as against the gods of the people of the earth, which were the work of the hands of man.
And for this cause Hezekiah the king, and the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, prayed and cried to heaven.

And the Lord sent an angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he was come into the house of his god, they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword.
Thus the Lord saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib the king of Assyria, and from the hand of all other, and guided them on every side.
Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it.
By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the Lord.
For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.
Then the angel of the Lord went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh.

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esar–haddon his son reigned in his stead.

And if the king Sennacherib had slain any, when he was come, and fled from Judea, I buried them privily; for in his wrath he killed many; but the bodies were not found, when they were sought for of the king.
And when one of the Ninevites went and complained of me to the king, that I buried them, and hid myself; understanding that I was sought for to be put to death, I withdrew myself for fear.
Then all my goods were forcibly taken away, neither was there any thing left me, beside my wife Anna and my son Tobias.

And there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons killed him, and they fled into the mountains of Ararath; and Sarchedonus his son reigned in his stead; who appointed over his father’s accounts, and over all his affairs, Achiacharus my brother Anael’s son.

Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come to Hezekiah with their clothes rent and tell him the words of Rabshakeh. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

When Hezekiah hears the reproach of Assyria he rends his clothes, covers himself with sackcloth, and goes into the house of the Most High, then sends his servants to Isaiah the prophet. He calls it a day of trouble, rebuke, and blasphemy, and asks Isaiah to lift up prayer for the remnant that is left. This follows chapter 18, where Rabshakeh the messenger of Sennacherib told Judah their God was no different from the gods of the nations Assyria had already destroyed. Isaiah, Micah, and Hosea prophesied in this same period, so much of what is read in one is found in the others. Isaiah returns the word of the Most High: fear not the blasphemy, for the Most High will send a blast upon Sennacherib, and he shall hear a rumor, return to his own land, and fall by the sword there.

Rabshakeh returns and finds the king of Assyria warring against Libnah, having departed from Lachish. Hearing that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight against him, Sennacherib sends messengers again to Hezekiah with a threatening letter. The letter mocks Judah's trust, listing the nations and kings Assyria destroyed, saying their gods could not deliver them, so Jerusalem will not be delivered either.

Hezekiah receives the letter, reads it, goes up to the house of the Most High, and spreads it before Him. He prays acknowledging the Most High as God alone of all the kingdoms of the earth, maker of heaven and earth, and asks Him to bow down His ear and hear the words that reproached the living God. He confesses that the gods Assyria cast into the fire were no gods but the work of men's hands, wood and stone, and asks the Most High to save them so all the nations may know He alone is the Lord God. The prayer of Hezekiah is that the Most High show His power and prove His people are the chosen and that He is the one true living God. This is a righteous prayer, the same praying for the downfall of enemies and for righteous judgment to come upon them.

Isaiah sends word that the Most High has heard the prayer against Sennacherib, and the virgin daughter of Zion despises and laughs him to scorn. The Most High asks whom Sennacherib has reproached and blasphemed, for he has lifted up his eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel. Israel is laughing at the enemy, for it is already written that they lose. Assyria boasted with the multitude of his chariots to cut down cedars and dry up rivers, the same as a nation today boasting of its army, military, and political system. The Most High answers that He did it and formed it of ancient times; He gave Assyria the very ability to lay fenced cities waste as ruinous heaps for His own purpose. Because their rage and tumult came up to His ears, the Most High will put His hook in Sennacherib's nose and His bridle in his lips, and turn him back the way he came, which joins with the blast promised in verse 7. -

The sign given to Hezekiah is that they shall eat what grows of itself two years, and in the third year sow, reap, and plant vineyards. The remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward, for out of Jerusalem and Mount Zion a remnant shall escape. This is twofold: a remnant came out of Assyria and into Babylon, and it also speaks of the remnant today, for the zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform it.

The Most High declares the king of Assyria shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it. By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and he shall not enter the city. The Most High will defend the city to save it for His own sake and for His servant David's sake; what He did to Samaria He will not do to Jerusalem.

That night the angel of the Most High goes out and smites the camp of the Assyrians, killing a hundred fourscore and five thousand, all dead corpses by morning. A score is twenty, so this is a hundred and eighty-five thousand slain. Israel did not lift a finger; the Most High handled the battle for them, for it is not by might but by His spirit. This is praying for the death of the enemy and for righteous judgment. Sennacherib departs and dwells at Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smite him with the sword and flee, and Esarhaddon his son reigns in his stead, fulfilling the word of verse 7. -

After these acts of faithfulness Sennacherib king of Assyria enters Judah and encamps against the fenced cities, thinking to win them for himself. Hezekiah takes counsel to stop the waters of the fountains outside the city, repairs the broken wall, raises towers, builds another wall, and makes darts and shields in abundance. Our people are resourceful and skilled, doing the work themselves. He sets captains over the people and comforts them: be strong and courageous, for there be more with us than with him; with him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God to help us and fight our battles. -

Sennacherib sends servants to Jerusalem asking on what the people trust that they abide in the siege, and claims Hezekiah is persuading them to die by famine and thirst. He mocks that Hezekiah took away the high places and altars and commanded worship at one altar, twisting obedience to the commandment into a weakness. He argues that no god of any nation delivered its people from his hand, so neither will the God of Hezekiah. This is the same seed the world plants to make Israel weary and turn a people off one accord. -

Sennacherib's servants speak yet more against the Lord God and against his servant Hezekiah, and he writes letters to rail on the Lord God of Israel. They cry with a loud voice in the Jews' speech to the people on the wall to frighten and trouble them so they might take the city. They speak against the God of Jerusalem as against the gods of the peoples of the earth, which were only the work of men's hands. The one true God is the God of Israel, not an idol like the false gods of the nations.

Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amos, pray and cry to heaven over this railing. The Lord sends an angel that cuts off all the mighty men of valour, leaders, and captains in the camp of Assyria, so Sennacherib returns with shame to his own land, and his own sons slay him with the sword in the house of his god. Thus the Lord saves Hezekiah and Jerusalem and guides them on every side, and many bring gifts to the Lord and presents to Hezekiah, so he is magnified in the sight of all nations, a picture of the gifts the nations will bring back to Israel in the kingdom.

In those days Hezekiah is sick to death, prays to the Lord, and is given a sign. But Hezekiah renders not according to the benefit done to him, for his heart is lifted up in pride, and wrath comes upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem. When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. Then Hezekiah humbles himself for the pride of his heart, he and the people of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord does not come upon them in his days. -

Hezekiah has exceeding riches and honour, making treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, and spices, and storehouses for corn, wine, oil, and cattle, for God gives him very much substance. He stops the upper watercourse of Gihon and brings it straight down to the west side of the city of David, and prospers in all his works, the plumbing he built for Jerusalem. When the ambassadors of Babylon come to inquire of the wonder, God leaves him to try him and know his heart. Hezekiah then sleeps with his fathers, is buried in honour among the sons of David, and Manasseh his son reigns in his stead. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

When Hezekiah hears the words, he rends his clothes, covers himself with sackcloth, and goes into the house of the Most High. He turns to the Most High rather than to Egypt or to fear. He sends Eliakim, Shebna, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet. He calls it a day of trouble, rebuke, and blasphemy. He asks that Isaiah pray for the remnant that is left, hoping the Most High will hear the words of Rabshakeh, who was sent to reproach the living God. Hezekiah seeks the prophet's intercession.

Isaiah answers the servants: tell your master, Be not afraid of the words with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me. The Most High answers the blasphemy directly. Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land. This is the prophecy that Sennacherib would be killed at home. This is exactly what happened: Sennacherib was killed in his own land by his own sons, showing the word of the Most High through Isaiah came to pass. No nation can stand against Israel when the Most High has spoken against it.

Rabshakeh returns and finds the king of Assyria warring against Libnah, for he had departed from Lachish. Word comes of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia coming out to make war. Sennacherib sends messengers again to Hezekiah, telling him not to let the God in whom he trusts deceive him that Jerusalem will not be given into his hand. He renews the same threat and mockery. He points to all the lands and kings that Assyria destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the rest, asking whether they were delivered. He counts Jerusalem as one more city to fall.

Hezekiah receives the letter, reads it, goes up to the house of the Most High, and spreads it before Him. He lays the whole threat out before the Most High in prayer. He calls on the Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who dwells between the cherubims, as the God alone of all the kingdoms of the earth, who made heaven and earth. He asks Him to incline His ear and hear the words of Sennacherib that reproach the living God. He acknowledges that Assyria has laid waste the nations and cast their gods into the fire, but those were no gods, only the work of men's hands, wood and stone. He asks the Most High to save them, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that He alone is the Lord.

Isaiah sends to Hezekiah that the Most High has heard his prayer against Sennacherib. The virgin daughter of Zion has despised and laughed him to scorn. Sennacherib reproached and blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, boasting by his chariots that he climbed the mountains and cut down the cedars and dried up the rivers. His pride is set against the Most High Himself. The Most High declares that He formed and brought it to pass of ancient times, that Sennacherib should lay waste the defended cities, and that the inhabitants were weak because the Most High allowed it. Because of his rage against the Most High, He will put His hook in his nose and His bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came.

The sign to Hezekiah is that this year they eat what grows of itself, the second year what springs of the same, and the third year they sow, reap, plant vineyards, and eat the fruit. The Most High promises restoration and provision. The remnant that escapes of the house of Judah takes root downward and bears fruit upward, for out of Jerusalem goes forth a remnant. The zeal of the Lord of hosts performs this.

Concerning the king of Assyria, the Most High says he shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it. Jerusalem is not going to be touched. By the way he came, by the same he shall return, and shall not come into the city. The Most High will defend the city to save it for His own sake and for His servant David's sake.

The angel of the Most High goes forth and smites the camp of the Assyrians, a hundred and eighty-five thousand, and in the morning they are all dead corpses. One angel destroys the whole army, proving no nation stands against Israel when the Most High defends it. Sennacherib departs and returns and dwells at Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smite him with the sword and escape into Armenia. The prophecy of [Isaiah 37:7](/bible/isaiah/37#v7) is fulfilled: he falls by the sword in his own land, killed by his own children. Esarhaddon his son reigns in his stead. The Most High's word stands from beginning to end. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

cases.name: Hezekiah and the ambassadors of Babylon
cases.charge: Showing all his treasures to Babylon in the pride of his heart
cases.summary: Healed of a mortal sickness and given fifteen years, Hezekiah received envoys from Babylon and showed them the house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the armor, everything. Isaiah asked what they had seen. Nothing hidden, said the king.
cases.offense: After receiving healing and a sign, Hezekiah did not render according to the benefit done to him, because his heart was lifted up (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). Mercy received became an occasion for self-regard instead of gratitude. The Babylonian envoys came with letters and a present, and he showed them his treasures, armour, and all that was in his dominion (2 Kings 20:12-15). Chronicles says that God left him to try him and disclose what was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). The trial came through honour and interest, not only through an enemy's threat. The king who had sought the Lord under siege also had to remember him amid admiration.
cases.judgment: Isaiah declared that the treasures would be carried to Babylon and that descendants of the king would serve in its palace (2 Kings 20:16-18). What he displayed as the strength of his house was named as another kingdom's future spoil. Hezekiah and Jerusalem humbled themselves, and the wrath did not come in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). The delay was mercy within the sentence. The lesson reached beyond whether the king could survive an immediate danger: the blessings entrusted to him required humility after the danger had passed, and the future of his house could not be measured only by peace during his own remaining years.

verses.text: At that time Berodach–baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah: for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.

And Hezekiah hearkened unto them, and shewed them all the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.
Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country, even from Babylon.
And he said, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All the things that are in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.
And Isaiah said unto Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord.
Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day, shall be carried into Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.
And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.
Then said Hezekiah unto Isaiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken. And he said, Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?
In those days Hezekiah was sick to the death, and prayed unto the Lord: and he spake unto him, and he gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem.
Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah.

Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
At that time Merodach–baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered.

And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.

Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.
Then said he, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.
Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord of hosts:
Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.
And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.
Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days.
In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it.

And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God: which he carried into the land of Shinar to the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god.
And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes;

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king’s palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.

entries.commentary: Hezekiah falls sick unto death, and Isaiah brings the word to set his house in order, for he shall die and not live. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays, asking the Most High to remember how he walked before Him in truth and with a perfect heart, and he weeps sore. Before Isaiah leaves the middle court the word returns: the Most High has heard his prayer and seen his tears, will heal him, add fifteen years, and defend the city for His own sake and for David's sake. Isaiah applies a lump of figs to the boil and Hezekiah recovers, showing that remedies and herbs go together with prayer, for healing is in the hand of the Most High. -

Hezekiah asks for a sign that the Most High will heal him and that he shall go up to the house of the Most High on the third day. Isaiah offers the shadow going forward ten degrees or back ten degrees, and Hezekiah answers that going forward is a light thing, but let it return backward ten degrees. Isaiah cries to the Most High and He brings the shadow ten degrees backward on the dial of Ahaz, reversing the natural course of the sun as proof of His power.

Berodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sends letters and a present to Hezekiah, having heard he had been sick; this is the introduction of Babylon, still only a province under Assyria at this time. Hezekiah hearkens to them and shows them all his precious things, his silver, gold, spices, ointment, and armor, holding nothing back, trusting his enemies because of the gift. Isaiah asks what the men saw and where they came from, then declares that all in the house shall be carried into Babylon, and Hezekiah's own sons shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. Hezekiah answers that the word of the Most High is good, content that peace and truth be in his days. This same account is given in [Isaiah 39](/bible/isaiah/39). -

The rest of the acts of Hezekiah, including how he made a pool and a conduit and brought water into the city, are written in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Bringing water into the city is vision and planning like no other; this is nation building. Hezekiah sleeps with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigns in his stead.

They speak against the God of Jerusalem as against the gods of the peoples of the earth, which were only the work of men's hands. Thus the Lord saves Hezekiah and Jerusalem and guides them on every side, and many bring gifts to the Lord and presents to Hezekiah, so he is magnified in the sight of all nations, a picture of the gifts the nations will bring back to Israel in the kingdom.

In those days Hezekiah is sick to death, prays to the Lord, and is given a sign. But Hezekiah renders not according to the benefit done to him, for his heart is lifted up in pride, and wrath comes upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem. When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. Then Hezekiah humbles himself for the pride of his heart, he and the people of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord does not come upon them in his days. -

He stops the upper watercourse of Gihon and brings it straight down to the west side of the city of David, and prospers in all his works, the plumbing he built for Jerusalem. Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah, having heard he had been sick and recovered. Hezekiah was glad of them and showed them all the house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the spices, the ointment, and all his armor, holding nothing back in all his dominion. Isaiah came and asked what the men had said and where they came from. When Hezekiah answered that they came from Babylon and had seen everything among his treasures, Isaiah declared the days would come when all in his house, and what his fathers had stored up, would be carried to Babylon with nothing left. The prophecy adds that Hezekiah's own sons that issue from him would be taken and made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. Hezekiah called the word of the Lord good because there would be peace and truth in his days. -

In the third year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it, and the Most High gave Jehoiakim into his hand with part of the vessels of the house of God. Nebuchadnezzar carried those vessels into the land of Shinar to the house of his god and put them in his treasure house. This came to pass exactly as the prophets had warned. -

The king commanded to bring certain of the children of Israel, of the king's seed and of the princes: young men without blemish, well favoured, skilful in all wisdom, cunning in knowledge, understanding science, and able to stand in the king's palace. They took the best and the most educated among us, taught them the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans, and set them to build up their kingdom. It is the same thing today, where our people serve in the governments and the congresses and are used to build up a system that is not our own. Often those who are chosen are not loyal to their own people; they are assimilated to believe they are a part of the system and accepted by that society, and they are well rewarded for it. When our people were carried over in the dark ages they were a civilized, educated people, engineers and men of every profession, and they were used to serve and build up Babylon. Israel is the greatest nation the earth has known, and Babylon benefited off our wisdom and our knowledge. The king also appointed them a daily provision of the king's meat and of the wine which he drank.

Among those taken were of the children of Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The prince of the eunuchs gave them new names, Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, part of assimilating them into the king's service.

cases.name: Isaiah
cases.charge: Answering the Lord’s call; prophesying judgment and redemption through persecution and rejection
cases.summary: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up upon a throne, with seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy. His unclean lips were cleansed with a coal from the altar, and he answered, Here am I; send me. He walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia, counseled Hezekiah against Sennacherib, and prophesied the angel that smote 185,000 Assyrians in one night.
cases.offense: In the year that King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims, each with six wings, crying one to another, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. The posts of the door moved at the voice, and the house was filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:1–4). Isaiah cried, Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips, for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts. A seraphim flew with a live coal from the altar and laid it upon his mouth, saying his iniquity was taken away and his sin purged (Isaiah 6:5–7). He heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And he answered, Here am I; send me (Isaiah 6:8). He was sent to a people whose hearts were made fat, whose ears were heavy, whose eyes were shut, lest they see, hear, understand, convert, and be healed. The blindness was decreed until the cities be wasted and the land utterly desolate (Isaiah 6:9–11). At the Lord’s command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign and wonder upon Egypt and Ethiopia, that the king of Assyria would lead them away captive, young and old, naked and barefoot, to the shame of Egypt (Isaiah 20:2–4). The prophet’s body became the sign, and the sign endured for three years.

cases.name: Manasseh
cases.charge: Rebuilding the high places; altars to the host of heaven in the temple; passing his sons through the fire; witchcraft; filling Jerusalem with innocent blood
cases.summary: Hezekiah's son undid everything his father had done and more: altars for Baal, a grove, worship of all the host of heaven in both courts of the Lord's house, his children through the fire, observing times, enchantments, familiar spirits, wizards. He shed innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from one end to another.
cases.offense: Manasseh rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had removed, established idolatrous altars even in the Lord's house, practised forbidden divination, and caused his children to pass through the fire (2 Chronicles 33:1-7). He reversed a reform whose work was visible before him. He also shed innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from end to end, and led Judah into greater evil than the nations expelled before Israel (2 Kings 21:9, 16). The Lord spoke to him and his people, but they would not hear (2 Chronicles 33:10). Authority amplified his departure by making it the nation's course.
cases.judgment: The Lord brought the captains of the host of Assyria, who took Manasseh among the thorns, bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. There he humbled himself greatly and prayed; the Prayer of Manasseh preserves the tradition of it. God brought him back to his kingdom and he took away the strange gods. But the sentence on Judah for his sins stood: the Lord would not pardon.
offenseFull: Manasseh rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had removed, established idolatrous altars even in the Lord's house, practised forbidden divination, and caused his children to pass through the fire (2 Chronicles 33:1-7). He reversed a reform whose work was visible before him.

He also shed innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from end to end, and led Judah into greater evil than the nations expelled before Israel (2 Kings 21:9, 16). The Lord spoke to him and his people, but they would not hear (2 Chronicles 33:10). Authority amplified his departure by making it the nation's course.

entries.commentary: Manasseh begins to reign at twelve years old and reigns fifty-five years, doing evil after the abominations of the heathen the Most High cast out before Israel. He rebuilds the high places Hezekiah destroyed, rears altars for Baal, makes a grove as Ahab did, and worships the host of heaven, even building altars in the house of the Most High where He set His name; this is a wickedness with zero fear of the Most High. The people did not serve idols for nothing but for the self-gratification in it, the same as men today keep pagan feasts for the gifts, the food, and the reveling, not for what the day claims to be. He makes his son pass through the fire, observes times, uses enchantments, and deals with familiar spirits and wizards, provoking the Most High to anger, and seduces Judah to do more evil than the nations the Most High destroyed. Repentance is always possible; our people are repenting, not repented, so no man should judge before the time who is or is not of the two-thirds. Continue in the work of the Most High and let Christ judge in the end.

The Most High speaks by His servants the prophets that because Manasseh did wickedly above all the Amorites and made Judah to sin, He is bringing such evil upon Jerusalem that both ears of whoever hears it shall tingle. He will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab, and wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish and turns it upside down; the same desolation done to Samaria will reach Judah. He will forsake the remnant of His inheritance and deliver them into the hand of their enemies to be a prey and a spoil, because they have provoked Him to anger since the day their fathers came out of Egypt. The Most High has borne with this wickedness for hundreds of years. -

Manasseh sheds innocent blood very much, filling Jerusalem from one end to the other, beside the sin with which he made Judah to sin. His remaining acts are written in the chronicles of the kings of Judah, and the prayer of Manasseh is recorded in the Apocrypha, prayed while he was held captive in Babylon. Chronicles shows the captains of the king of Assyria took Manasseh among the thorns and carried him with fetters to Babylon, then a province under Assyria; there he repented and prayed. The history shows a power struggle beginning, where Assyrian kings ruled over Babylon, and later Babylonian kings ruled over Assyria; Manasseh sleeps with his fathers and Amon his son reigns. -

Amon begins to reign at twenty-two years old and reigns two years, doing evil as his father Manasseh did, walking in all his ways and serving the idols his father served. He forsakes the Most High God of his fathers and walks not in His way. His own servants conspire against him and slay him in his house; the people of the land slay the conspirators and make Josiah his son king in his stead.

Manasseh begins to reign at twelve years old and reigns fifty five years in Jerusalem, but he does that which is evil in the sight of the Lord, after the abominations of the heathen the Most High had cast out before the children of Israel. He rebuilds the high places his father Hezekiah had broken down, rears up altars for Baal, makes groves, and worships all the host of heaven and serves them. He builds altars even in the house of the Lord, the very place of which the Most High had said, In Jerusalem shall my name be for ever.

He builds altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord, and causes his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is child sacrifice, the same spirit as abortion today. He observes times, uses enchantments, uses witchcraft, and deals with a familiar spirit and with wizards, working much evil to provoke the Most High to anger. Every one of these things is a commandment he broke. He sets a carved idol in the house of God, the very house of which the Most High said to David and Solomon, In this house and in Jerusalem will I put my name for ever, and Manasseh makes Judah do worse than the heathen the Lord destroyed before them. -

The Most High speaks to Manasseh and his people, but they will not hearken, so he brings upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria. They take Manasseh among the thorns, bind him with chains, and carry him to Babylon. The kings of Israel that were once kings are brought down into captivity, exactly as the curses warned. -

When he is in affliction, Manasseh beseeches the Lord his God and humbles himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and prays unto him. The Most High is entreated of him, hears his supplication, and brings him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom, and then Manasseh knows that the Lord he was God. This is the pattern of [2 Chronicles 7:14](/bible/2-chronicles/7#v14), that a people called by his name who humble themselves will be heard.

After this he builds a wall for the city of David, sets captains of war in the fenced cities of Judah, and takes away the strange gods and the idol out of the house of the Lord, casting them out of the city. He repairs the altar of the Lord, sacrifices peace offerings and thank offerings on it, and commands Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel, though the people still sacrifice in the high places, only unto the Lord their God. -

The rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer unto his God, are written in the book of the kings of Israel, and his prayer and how the Most High was entreated of him are written among the sayings of the seers. This is the prayer of Manasseh, a writing of the Apocrypha found before the Maccabees, which is part of the Bible. Manasseh sleeps with his fathers and Amon his son reigns in his stead. -

Amon is twenty two years old when he begins to reign and reigns two years in Jerusalem, doing evil in the sight of the Lord as Manasseh his father, sacrificing to all the carved images Manasseh had made. But Amon does not humble himself before the Lord as his father had humbled himself; instead he trespasses more and more, and his own servants conspire against him and slay him in his house. The people of the land slay the conspirators and make Josiah his son king in his stead. A sentence not executed speedily set his heart to do more evil, and his sins abounded to his own destruction. -

Josiah gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, went up to the house of the Most High with the priests, the prophets, and all the people both small and great, and read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant that was found there. Our forefathers had the Bible; the king read it openly, then stood by a pillar and made a covenant before the Lord to walk after him and keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all their heart and soul. All the people stood to the covenant to perform the words written in the book. -

The king commanded Hilkiah and the priests to bring out of the temple all the vessels made for Baal, for the grove, and for all the host of heaven, and he burned them in the fields of Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel. He put down the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places and around Jerusalem, and those that burnt incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon, the planets, and all the host of heaven. When Josiah read the law the fear of the Lord came upon him and he saw why the nation was under judgment, just as a person is cut when they first hear the truth and realize what they have been doing wrong. -

He brought the grove out of the house of the Lord to the brook Kidron, burned it, stamped it to powder, and cast the powder on the graves of the children of the people. He broke down the houses of the sodomites that were by the house of the Lord, where the women wove hangings for the grove; there should be no sodomite among the sons of Israel, yet they had grown so bold as to do this wickedness right beside the temple. He brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the high places where they had burnt incense, and though the priests of the high places did not come up to the altar, they still ate of the unleavened bread among their brethren.

Josiah defiled Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so that no man might make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech. Topheth was the place where the people sacrificed their children, and it had to be defiled because Israel would not stop the evil on its own. -

He took away the horses the kings of Judah had given to the sun and burnt the chariots of the sun with fire. He beat down the altars on the roof of Ahaz's chamber and the altars Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord, and cast their dust into the brook Kidron. He defiled the high places Solomon had built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom, the abominations of the Zidonians, Moabites, and Ammonites, and broke in pieces the images, cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men. This is repentance in action: cleaning house, getting rid of every idol and evil that causes a people to go off from the Lord and to fall under punishment. -

Josiah also destroyed the altar and high place at Bethel that Jeroboam had made when he set up the golden calves, burning it and stamping it small to powder. Turning himself, he spied the sepulchres in the mount, took out the bones, and burnt them upon the altar to pollute it, according to the word the man of God had proclaimed. When told which sepulchre belonged to the man of God who prophesied these things, he said to let him alone and let no man move his bones. -

Josiah also took away all the houses of the high places in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord to anger, and did to them as he had done at Bethel. The northern kingdom had already been carried into captivity by Assyria, so most of the people were gone, yet the idolatrous houses remained. He slew all the priests of the high places upon their altars, burnt men's bones upon them, and returned to Jerusalem.

The king commanded all the people to keep the Passover to the Lord their God as it is written in the book of this covenant. Such a Passover had not been held from the days of the judges nor in all the days of the kings of Israel and Judah, but in the eighteenth year of Josiah this Passover was held in Jerusalem. Reading the book of the law brought the nation back to keeping the appointed feasts in order, just as the feast is kept in order today. -

Josiah also put away the workers with familiar spirits, the wizards, the images, the idols, and all the abominations spied in Judah and Jerusalem, that he might perform the words of the law found by Hilkiah. There was no king before or after him that turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might according to all the law of Moses; he put things in order like a true leader. Nevertheless the Lord did not turn from the fierceness of his great wrath because of the provocations of Manasseh, and said he would remove Judah out of his sight as he had removed Israel and cast off Jerusalem.

Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates, and Josiah went against him and was slain at Megiddo. Josiah got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it, a warning not to enter into quarrels that are not one's own. His servants carried him dead in a chariot from Megiddo to Jerusalem and buried him, and the people took Jehoahaz his son and anointed him king in his father's place.

Jehoahaz was twenty three years old and reigned three months in Jerusalem, and did evil in the sight of the Lord according to all his fathers had done. Pharaohnechoh bound him at Riblah so he might not reign, put the land to a tribute of silver and gold, and made Eliakim the son of Josiah king, turning his name to Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay Pharaoh, exacting the silver and gold of every man of the land, and he also did evil in the sight of the Lord like his forefathers, not like his father Josiah.

In Jehoiakim's days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant three years, then turned and rebelled against him. The Lord sent bands of the Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites against Judah to destroy it according to the word he spake by his prophets. This came upon Judah at the commandment of the Lord to remove them out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon. -

Jehoiakim slept with his fathers and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place. The king of Egypt came no more out of his land, for the king of Babylon had taken all that pertained to Egypt from the river of Egypt to the river Euphrates. Babylon took over as had been prophesied throughout the Bible, in Daniel and in Jeremiah, that Nebuchadnezzar would ransack Jerusalem and the surrounding lands.

Jehoiachin was eighteen years old and reigned three months in Jerusalem, and did evil in the sight of the Lord according to all his fathers had done. The servants of Nebuchadnezzar came up against Jerusalem and besieged it, and the king himself came against the city while it was besieged. Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes, and officers, and the king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign.

Nebuchadnezzar carried out all the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, and cut in pieces the vessels of gold Solomon had made, as the Lord had said. He carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, all the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and smiths, leaving only the poorest of the people of the land. He carried Jehoiachin, the king's mother, wives, and officers to Babylon, along with the men of might and craftsmen and smiths, wanting them to build for him what they had built in their own land, as conquering nations always used Israel's skill and industry. -

The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's father's brother, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah. Zedekiah was twenty one years old and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, and did evil in the sight of the Lord according to all Jehoiakim had done. Through the anger of the Lord it came to pass in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out of his presence, that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. -

Though Moses and Samuel stood before Him, the mind of the Most High could not be toward this people; He says cast them out of My sight. When the people ask where they shall go, the answer is such as are for death to death, for the sword to the sword, for the famine to the famine, and for the captivity to the captivity. That is how we got removed from before the Most High.

He appoints four kinds over them: the sword to slay, the dogs to tear, and the fowls and beasts to devour, and He will remove them into all kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah did in Jerusalem. He is weary with repenting and will bereave them of children because they return not from their ways; the mother of young men gets a spoiler at noonday, and she that bore seven languishes and gives up the ghost. That hit home; there was a sister last sabbath who had seven sons and was very much depressed. The scripture speaks to a real grief among the people.

Jeremiah cries woe over being born a man of strife and contention, cursed by everyone though he lent to no one on usury. The Most High answers that it shall be well with his remnant. That remnant is those who are keeping the commandments. Their substance and treasures will be given to the spoil for all their sins, and they will pass with their enemies into a land they do not know.

Jeremiah asks the Most High to remember him, visit him, and revenge him of his persecutors, and not to take him away in His longsuffering, since for His sake he has suffered rebuke. His words were found and Jeremiah did eat them, and they were the joy and rejoicing of his heart, for he is called by the name of the Most High and sat alone, filled with indignation. He asks why his pain is perpetual and his wound refuses to be healed. This is what the prophets go through: we bring healing, order, structure and discipline to our people and get hated and treated badly, and sometimes these are the thoughts we have.

If Jeremiah returns, the Most High will bring him again to stand before Him; if he takes the precious from the vile he shall be as His mouth. Let them return to him, but he is not to return to them. He will make Jeremiah a fenced brazen wall; they shall fight against him but not prevail, for the Most High is with him to save and deliver him. That is what we live on. When we go out teaching this bible, and when brothers and sisters apply the commandments to their everyday lives, people will come against us, but the Most High is our defense. As long as we keep the commandments and the faith of Christ, no one can prevail, and if they try they will fail. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)
