cases.name: Uzziah
cases.charge: Entering the temple to burn incense, which belonged to the priests
cases.summary: A strong and prosperous king who sought God in the days of Zechariah. When he was strong his heart was lifted up, and he went into the temple with a censer. Eighty priests withstood him; while he raged at them, leprosy rose in his forehead.
cases.offense: Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah and prospered while he sought Him. His victories, fortifications, husbandry, and military preparations made his name spread abroad. When he became strong, however, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. He entered the temple to burn incense upon the altar, taking to himself a service appointed to the sons of Aaron. Azariah and eighty priests withstood him and commanded him to leave. Uzziah answered with anger while holding the censer. The offense was not his success, but the pride that made him cross a boundary God had established and resist those charged to keep it.
cases.judgment: A leper to the day of his death, cut off from the house of the Lord, dwelling in a several house while his son judged the people. He was buried in a field near the kings' sepulchres, not among them, for they said, he is a leper.
offenseFull: Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah and prospered while he sought Him. His victories, fortifications, husbandry, and military preparations made his name spread abroad. When he became strong, however, his heart was lifted up to his destruction.

He entered the temple to burn incense upon the altar, taking to himself a service appointed to the sons of Aaron. Azariah and eighty priests withstood him and commanded him to leave. Uzziah answered with anger while holding the censer. The offense was not his success, but the pride that made him cross a boundary God had established and resist those charged to keep it.

entries.commentary: All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. He reigned fifty and two years in Jerusalem and did that which was right in the sight of the Most High. He sought the Most High in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God, and as long as he sought the Most High, God made him to prosper. Prosperity comes from the Most High, and it lasts only as long as a man keeps seeking Him.

Uzziah went to war against the Philistines, broke down walls, and built cities. God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabians, and the Mehunims, and his name spread abroad, for he was marvellously helped till he was strong. He built towers in Jerusalem and in the desert, dug many wells, and loved husbandry, keeping much cattle and vine dressers. He had a trained host of fighting men, three hundred thousand and seven thousand five hundred that made war with mighty power, and he prepared for them shields, spears, helmets, and engines of war invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones. All of this came because he was helped by the Most High. The strength, the army, the wealth, and even the ingenuity of his engineers were a gift.

But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. He transgressed against the Most High and went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense, which was not his office. Azariah the priest and fourscore priests went in after him, withstood him, and told him it did not pertain to him to burn incense but to the priests, the sons of Aaron who are consecrated, and told him to go out of the sanctuary for he had trespassed. Uzziah was wroth, and while he was wroth with a censer in his hand, leprosy rose up in his forehead before the priests. The lesson to all of us is to stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in. When a man becomes lifted up he loses his humility and forgets who set him where he is. Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death and dwelt in a separate house, cut off from the house of the Most High.

The rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, Isaiah the prophet wrote. Uzziah slept with his fathers and they buried him in the field of burial that belonged to the kings, for they said, He is a leper. Jotham his son reigned in his stead. When Uzziah stayed with the Most High he prospered, and when he departed and did his own thing, going contrary to the laws of God, the Most High made an example of him. He is a warning against thinking of yourself as more than what you are, for a man who thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself.

Korah was of Levi, and Dathan, Abiram, and On were of Reuben. With them rose up two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown; that is two hundred and fifty three in all against Moses and Aaron. These were known and powerful men among the congregation, and their influence, because of who they were, is how they were able to persuade people. They charged Moses and Aaron with taking too much upon themselves and lifting themselves above the congregation. They thought Moses and Aaron carried themselves as better than the rest, but the Most High is the one who chose them as leaders and was dealing with them; the accusers were jealous of them.

When Moses heard it, he fell upon his face, and told Korah and all his company: even to morrow the Lord will shew who are his, and who is holy; the Most High himself would show whom he chose and whom he was dealing with. The test was censers: take you censers, Korah and all his company, put fire therein and incense before the Lord, and the man whom the Lord doth choose, he shall be holy. Ye take too much upon you, ye sons of Levi.

Moses exhorted Korah: seemeth it but a small thing that the God of Israel hath separated you from the congregation to bring you near to himself, to do the service of the tabernacle? Only Levi could do the service of the tabernacle, and that was a heavy job in itself. You already stand before the congregation and minister unto them; the Most High is still dealing with you. But they sought the priesthood also, and for that cause Korah and all his company were gathered together against the Lord: and what is Aaron, that ye murmur against him?

Dathan and Abiram would not come up when Moses called them. They were being rebellious against Moses because they wanted his spot, accusing him of bringing them out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness and of making himself a prince over them. Those same spirits are around today; the same thing that went on in the old time goes on now.

Moses was very wroth and said unto the Lord, respect not thou their offering: I have not taken one ass from them, neither have I hurt one of them. Every man took his censer, two hundred and fifty censers, with Aaron and Korah also, put fire and incense in them, and stood in the door of the tabernacle of the congregation; and Korah gathered all the congregation against Moses and Aaron, and the glory of the Lord appeared unto all the congregation.

The Lord told Moses and Aaron to separate themselves from among the congregation, that he might consume them in a moment: get away from them, because judgment is about to come. Moses and Aaron fell upon their faces and pleaded: O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation? They still had that love for their people and pleaded with the Lord not to deal with the whole congregation over one man's sin.

The Lord commanded the congregation to get up from about the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram; Moses warned them to depart from the tents of these wicked men and touch nothing of theirs, lest they be consumed in all their sins and put to death in all that wickedness. The congregation got up from the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram on every side; and Dathan and Abiram came out and stood in the door of their tents with their wives, their sons, and their little children.

Moses put the proof on the Most High: hereby ye shall know that the Lord hath sent me to do all these works, for I have not done them of mine own mind. If these men die the common death of all men, then the Lord hath not sent me; if the Most High does not do something out of the ordinary to put them to death, then the Lord had not sent him. But if the Lord make a new thing, and the earth open her mouth and swallow them up, and they go down quick into the pit, then ye shall understand that these men have provoked the Lord.

As he made an end of speaking, the ground clave asunder under them, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up, their houses, all the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods; anybody that had something to do with them went down, with all they owned. The earth just opened and closed upon them, and they perished from among the congregation; all Israel round about fled at the cry of them, for you could hear them crying as they were swallowed up, and they said, lest the earth swallow us up also.
The other two hundred and fifty men that followed them and offered incense did not escape either: there came out a fire from the Lord and consumed them.

The Lord told Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the burning, for they are hallowed, and scatter the fire yonder; the censers of these sinners against their own souls were made broad plates for a covering of the altar, because they were offered before the Lord. The plates were a memorial and a sign unto the children of Israel, that no stranger which is not of the seed of Aaron come near to offer incense before the Lord, that he be not as Korah and as his company.

On the morrow, the very next day, all the congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying, ye have killed the people of the Lord. After they had just seen the earth open up and swallow men, they still would not let it go and gathered against Moses again; that is just how rebellious we are. The Most High saw what was going on, and the cloud covered the tabernacle and the glory of the Lord appeared; Moses and Aaron came before the tabernacle because they knew the Most High was ready to deal with them. The Lord came down ready to put them to death again, saying get you up from among this congregation, that I may consume them as in a moment; and Moses and Aaron fell upon their faces, still pleading for their people because they loved them so much.

Moses told Aaron to take a censer with fire from off the altar and incense, and go quickly unto the congregation and make an atonement for them, for wrath had gone out from the Lord and the plague was begun; the Most High was already putting them to death. Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation, put on incense, made an atonement for the people, and stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed.

They that died in the plague were fourteen thousand and seven hundred, beside them that died about the matter of Korah; so beside the two hundred and fifty three that died with Korah, fourteen thousand seven hundred more were put to death.

The Lord told Aaron that he and his sons and his father's house would bear the iniquity of the sanctuary and of their priesthood; that was their job. This explains who should minister in the tabernacle after Israel's cry in the last chapter. The tribe of Levi was joined unto Aaron to minister unto him and keep the charge of the tabernacle, their jobs; only they were not to come nigh the vessels of the sanctuary and the altar, the ark of the covenant and the different vessels, that neither they nor the priests die. The Levites were given to Aaron as a gift for the Lord, to do the service of the tabernacle; Aaron and his sons kept the priest's office for every thing of the altar and within the vail. The stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death: an Israelite not of Levi could not come near the tabernacle.

The Lord gave Aaron the charge of the heave offerings of all the hallowed things of the children of Israel, by reason of the anointing, to him and his sons by an ordinance for ever. Of the most holy things reserved from the fire, every oblation, meat offering, sin offering, and trespass offering was most holy for Aaron and his sons; the priests kept a portion of it and ate it in the most holy place. The heave offering of their gift, with all the wave offerings of the children of Israel, was given to Aaron and his sons and his daughters by a statute for ever; every one that is clean in the house could eat of it. This is what the children of Israel gave for the Levites.

All the best of the oil, the best of the wine, and the wheat, the firstfruits which they offered unto the Lord, were given to the priests; whatsoever is first ripe in the land was theirs, and every one that was clean in the house could eat of it. Every thing devoted in Israel was theirs.

Every thing that openeth the matrix in all flesh, whether of men or beasts, was the Lord's; the firstborn was to be offered. Nevertheless the firstborn of man was surely redeemed, because you would not sacrifice the firstborn of our people, and the firstling of unclean beasts was redeemed also. Verse 16 explains how you redeem them: those to be redeemed from a month old were redeemed for the money of five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs; twenty gerahs equal one shekel. But the firstling of a cow, a sheep, or a goat was not redeemed, because those you could sacrifice: they are holy; their blood was sprinkled upon the altar and their fat burnt for an offering made by fire, for a sweet savour unto the Lord.

The flesh of them was the priest's, as the wave breast and as the right shoulder; all the heave offerings of the holy things which the children of Israel offered unto the Lord were given to Aaron and his sons and his daughters by a statute for ever, to the lineage of the Levites. [Exodus 29](/bible/exodus/29) shows how the wave offering and the heave offering were done. The wave offering was put in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved, meaning shaken, before the Lord; then it was received of their hands and burnt upon the altar. Each had a different way it was waved or lifted up to the Most High before it was actually burnt and offered to the Lord, and the breast of the ram of consecration was waved and became the priest's part. It is a covenant of salt for ever before the Lord, unto Aaron and to his seed with him, the children that come after them.

The Lord told Aaron: thou shalt have no inheritance in their land, neither any part among them; I am thy part and thine inheritance among the children of Israel. The Levites had no inheritance of land to pass down; the Most High said, I will be taking care of you. The Lord gave the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance. This is the tithe: the tenth part was given to the Levites for their service which they served, the service of the tabernacle of the congregation, their sacrificing and teaching of the laws. That tenth went to the children of Levi, and it was done away with when Christ came and died and took that priesthood; we no longer give that tenth to Levi. The children of Israel were not to come nigh the tabernacle of the congregation, lest they bear sin and die; it was a sin for the other tribes of Israel to come near the tabernacle, on pain of death. All the work to be done in the tabernacle was committed unto the Levites, and they bore their iniquity, a statute for ever.

When the Levites took of the children of Israel the tithes given them for their inheritance, they offered up of it an heave offering for the Lord, even a tenth part of the tithe: after the Levites got their tenth, the Most High wanted his tenth part of that, which they had to offer up. Their heave offering was reckoned unto them as though it were the corn of the threshingfloor and the fulness of the winepress, and the Lord's heave offering out of all their tithes was given to Aaron the priest; out of all their gifts they offered every heave offering of the Lord, of all the best thereof, even the hallowed part. When they had heaved the best thereof from it, they could eat it in every place, they and their households, for it was their reward for their service in the tabernacle of the congregation; and they bore no sin by reason of it when they heaved the best of it, neither polluted the holy things of the children of Israel, lest they die. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Azariah, also called Uzziah, begins to reign over Judah and does that which is right in the sight of the Most High as his father Amaziah had done. The high places were not removed, so the people still sacrificed and burned incense there, an incomplete obedience. The Most High smote him so that he was a leper until his death, and he dwelt in a separate house while Jotham his son judged the people. Azariah's fuller history is written elsewhere, and the teacher directs the reader to [2 Chronicles 26](/bible/2-chronicles/26) for a more detailed account of his life and acts. -

Zachariah son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel only six months and does that which is evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Shallum conspires against Zachariah, smites him before the people, slays him, and reigns in his place. The end of Zachariah fulfills the word spoken to Jehu, that his sons would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. -

Shallum reigns a full month in Samaria before Menahem son of Gadi goes up from Tirzah, smites him, and reigns in his stead. Menahem strikes Tiphsah and its coasts because they would not open to him, and he ripped up the women with child, a mark of his cruelty.

Menahem reigns ten years in Samaria and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pul the king of Assyria comes against the land, and Menahem gives him a thousand talents of silver to confirm the kingdom in his hand. Menahem raises the tribute by exacting fifty shekels of silver from each mighty man of wealth, so the king of Assyria turns back and does not stay in the land.

Pekahiah son of Menahem reigns two years over Israel and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pekah, a captain of his, conspires against him and smites him in the king's house at Samaria with fifty Gileadites, then reigns in his room. This is a military coup, where a trusted captain kills the king and seizes the throne.

Pekah son of Remaliah reigns twenty years over Israel, the same Pekah spoken of in the book of Isaiah. In his days Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria comes and takes Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, carrying them captive to Assyria. Hoshea son of Elah conspires against Pekah, smites and slays him, and reigns in his stead.

Jotham son of Uzziah reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem and does that which is right, according to all his father Uzziah had done. Again the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there. Jotham builds the higher gate of the house of the Most High. In those days the Most High begins to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.

cases.name: Jotham
cases.charge: Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; not entering the temple as his father had
cases.summary: Uzziah's son had watched his father go into the temple to burn incense and come out a leper. Jotham did what was right, and stayed out of the priests' place. The chronicler gives the cause of his strength in one line: he prepared his ways before the Lord his God.
cases.offense: Jotham did right in the sight of the Lord and did not repeat Uzziah's trespass in the temple. He built the high gate of the Lord's house, strengthened the wall of Ophel, and built cities, castles, and towers. His public work was joined to a deliberate ordering of his own conduct before God. The people still acted corruptly. Scripture does not conceal their condition in order to praise the king. Jotham's faithfulness is therefore distinguished from the conduct of those he governed; the one did not make the other disappear.
cases.judgment: Jotham prevailed against the Ammonites, who paid tribute for three years. He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God. The explanation for his strength is given in the condition of his walk, not merely in the size of his building works. He reigned sixteen years and was buried in the city of David. His account sets the preparation of one's ways before God beside the danger shown in his father's latter years: strength must remain under obedience.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, and on the wall of Ophel he built much.
Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers.

He fought also with the king of the Ammonites, and prevailed against them. And the children of Ammon gave him the same year an hundred talents of silver, and ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley. So much did the children of Ammon pay unto him, both the second year, and the third.
So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God.
In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel began Jotham the son of Uzziah king of Judah to reign.

Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, from beside the incense altar.

And Azariah the chief priest, and all the priests, looked upon him, and, behold, he was leprous in his forehead, and they thrust him out from thence; yea, himself hasted also to go out, because the Lord had smitten him.

And Uzziah the king was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house, being a leper; for he was cut off from the house of the Lord: and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land.
Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

entries.commentary: Jotham was twenty and five years old when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did that which was right in the sight of the Most High, according to all that his father Uzziah did, only he did not enter into the temple of the Most High. He would not go into the temple, and the people still did corruptly. He built the high gate of the house of the Most High and built much on the wall of Ophel, and cities in the mountains, and castles and towers. He fought against the Ammonites and prevailed, and they paid him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand measures of wheat and ten thousand of barley, both that year and the second and the third. Jotham became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Most High. It is a short chapter, but the point is plain: the Most High was with our forefathers when they followed the commandments, and Jotham ordered his ways before God.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, begins to reign over Judah and does that which is right in the sight of the Most High as his father Amaziah had done. The high places were not removed, so the people still sacrificed and burned incense there, an incomplete obedience. The Most High smote him so that he was a leper until his death, and he dwelt in a separate house while Jotham his son judged the people. Azariah's fuller history is written elsewhere, and the teacher directs the reader to [2 Chronicles 26](/bible/2-chronicles/26) for a more detailed account of his life and acts. -

Zachariah son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel only six months and does that which is evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Shallum conspires against Zachariah, smites him before the people, slays him, and reigns in his place. The end of Zachariah fulfills the word spoken to Jehu, that his sons would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. -

Shallum reigns a full month in Samaria before Menahem son of Gadi goes up from Tirzah, smites him, and reigns in his stead. Menahem strikes Tiphsah and its coasts because they would not open to him, and he ripped up the women with child, a mark of his cruelty.

Menahem reigns ten years in Samaria and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pul the king of Assyria comes against the land, and Menahem gives him a thousand talents of silver to confirm the kingdom in his hand. Menahem raises the tribute by exacting fifty shekels of silver from each mighty man of wealth, so the king of Assyria turns back and does not stay in the land.

Pekahiah son of Menahem reigns two years over Israel and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pekah, a captain of his, conspires against him and smites him in the king's house at Samaria with fifty Gileadites, then reigns in his room. This is a military coup, where a trusted captain kills the king and seizes the throne.

Pekah son of Remaliah reigns twenty years over Israel, the same Pekah spoken of in the book of Isaiah. In his days Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria comes and takes Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, carrying them captive to Assyria. Hoshea son of Elah conspires against Pekah, smites and slays him, and reigns in his stead.

Jotham son of Uzziah reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem and does that which is right, according to all his father Uzziah had done. Again the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there. Jotham builds the higher gate of the house of the Most High. In those days the Most High begins to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.

All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. He reigned fifty and two years in Jerusalem and did that which was right in the sight of the Most High. He sought the Most High in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God, and as long as he sought the Most High, God made him to prosper. Prosperity comes from the Most High, and it lasts only as long as a man keeps seeking Him.

Uzziah went to war against the Philistines, broke down walls, and built cities. God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabians, and the Mehunims, and his name spread abroad, for he was marvellously helped till he was strong. He built towers in Jerusalem and in the desert, dug many wells, and loved husbandry, keeping much cattle and vine dressers. He had a trained host of fighting men, three hundred thousand and seven thousand five hundred that made war with mighty power, and he prepared for them shields, spears, helmets, and engines of war invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones. All of this came because he was helped by the Most High. The strength, the army, the wealth, and even the ingenuity of his engineers were a gift.

But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. He transgressed against the Most High and went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense, which was not his office. Azariah the priest and fourscore priests went in after him, withstood him, and told him it did not pertain to him to burn incense but to the priests, the sons of Aaron who are consecrated, and told him to go out of the sanctuary for he had trespassed. Uzziah was wroth, and while he was wroth with a censer in his hand, leprosy rose up in his forehead before the priests. The lesson to all of us is to stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in. When a man becomes lifted up he loses his humility and forgets who set him where he is. Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death and dwelt in a separate house, cut off from the house of the Most High.

The rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, Isaiah the prophet wrote. Uzziah slept with his fathers and they buried him in the field of burial that belonged to the kings, for they said, He is a leper. Jotham his son reigned in his stead. When Uzziah stayed with the Most High he prospered, and when he departed and did his own thing, going contrary to the laws of God, the Most High made an example of him. He is a warning against thinking of yourself as more than what you are, for a man who thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself.

cases.name: Ahaz
cases.charge: Burning his children in the fire; copying the altar of Damascus; sacrificing to the gods that smote him
cases.summary: Ahaz walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, made molten images for Baalim, burnt his children in the fire after the abominations of the heathen, and hired Assyria against Syria with the temple's silver. Defeated, he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they had helped his enemies.
cases.offense: Ahaz made molten images for Baalim, burned his children in the fire, and sacrificed in the high places. In distress he became still more unfaithful. Seeing Damascus victorious, he reasoned that its gods would help him also and sacrificed to them. He mistook an enemy's success for proof that its worship was true. He stripped the Lord's house and the royal houses to purchase Assyrian help, cut up the vessels of God's house, shut its doors, and made altars throughout Jerusalem. His policy multiplied the very trespass that had brought Judah low.
cases.judgment: The Lord delivered Judah into the hands of Syria and Israel. Many were killed and many taken captive. Yet Israel's victory did not authorize its own cruelty: Oded rebuked the captors, and leaders of Ephraim required the captives to be released, clothed, fed, and brought to Jericho. The Philistines and Edomites also afflicted Judah. Assyria distressed Ahaz rather than strengthening him, despite the treasure he had paid. The gods he adopted became the ruin of him and of Israel. At death he was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel.
offenseFull: Ahaz made molten images for Baalim, burned his children in the fire, and sacrificed in the high places. In distress he became still more unfaithful. Seeing Damascus victorious, he reasoned that its gods would help him also and sacrificed to them. He mistook an enemy's success for proof that its worship was true.

He stripped the Lord's house and the royal houses to purchase Assyrian help, cut up the vessels of God's house, shut its doors, and made altars throughout Jerusalem. His policy multiplied the very trespass that had brought Judah low.

The Philistines and Edomites also afflicted Judah. Assyria distressed Ahaz rather than strengthening him, despite the treasure he had paid. The gods he adopted became the ruin of him and of Israel. At death he was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel.

verses.text: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem: but he did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father:
For he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and made also molten images for Baalim.
Moreover he burnt incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burnt his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen whom the Lord had cast out before the children of Israel.
He sacrificed also and burnt incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.

Wherefore the Lord his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria; and they smote him, and carried away a great multitude of them captives, and brought them to Damascus. And he was also delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who smote him with a great slaughter.
At that time did king Ahaz send unto the kings of Assyria to help him.
For the Lord brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the Lord.
And Tilgath–pilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not.
For Ahaz took away a portion out of the house of the Lord, and out of the house of the king, and of the princes, and gave it unto the king of Assyria: but he helped him not.
And in the time of his distress did he trespass yet more against the Lord: this is that king Ahaz.

For he sacrificed unto the gods of Damascus, which smote him: and he said, Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, therefore will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him, and of all Israel.

And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God, and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and shut up the doors of the house of the Lord, and he made him altars in every corner of Jerusalem.
And in every several city of Judah he made high places to burn incense unto other gods, and provoked to anger the Lord God of his fathers.
And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, even in Jerusalem: but they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel: and Hezekiah his son reigned in his stead.
Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord his God, like David his father.

But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yea, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out from before the children of Israel.
And he sacrificed and burnt incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.

And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath–pileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof.
And Urijah the priest built an altar according to all that king Ahaz had sent from Damascus: so Urijah the priest made it against king Ahaz came from Damascus.
And when the king was come from Damascus, the king saw the altar: and the king approached to the altar, and offered thereon.
And he burnt his burnt offering and his meat offering, and poured his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings, upon the altar.
And he brought also the brasen altar, which was before the Lord, from the forefront of the house, from between the altar and the house of the Lord, and put it on the north side of the altar.

And king Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest, saying, Upon the great altar burn the morning burnt offering, and the evening meat offering, and the king’s burnt sacrifice, and his meat offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their meat offering, and their drink offerings; and sprinkle upon it all the blood of the burnt offering, and all the blood of the sacrifice: and the brasen altar shall be for me to enquire by.
Thus did Urijah the priest, according to all that king Ahaz commanded.
For it was thy will to destroy by the hands of our fathers both those old inhabitants of thy holy land,
Whom thou hatedst for doing most odious works of witchcrafts, and wicked sacrifices;
And also those merciless murderers of children, and devourers of man’s flesh, and the feasts of blood,
With their priests out of the midst of their idolatrous crew, and the parents, that killed with their own hands souls destitute of help:

lawDetails.text: You shall not let any of your offspring pass through the fire of Molech.

entries.commentary: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years, but he did not do that which was right in the sight of the Most High like his father David. He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim. He burned incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom and burned his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen that the Most High cast out before the children of Israel. This was witchcraft and child sacrifice, the practice called Tophet, in the high places under every green tree.

Therefore the Most High delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Syria, who carried away a great multitude of captives to Damascus, and into the hand of the king of Israel, who smote him with a great slaughter. Pekah slew in Judah a hundred and twenty thousand in one day, all valiant men, because they had forsaken the Most High God of their fathers. Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew the king's son, the governor of the house, and the man next to the king. The children of Israel carried away captive of their brethren two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters, and much spoil, and brought it to Samaria. This was brother against brother, one nation of Israel captiving the other.

A prophet of the Most High named Oded went out before the host that came to Samaria and told them the Most High had delivered Judah into their hand because of His wrath, but they had slain them in a rage that reached up to heaven, and now purposed to keep the children of Judah as bondmen, which is against the law, adding to their own sins. Certain heads of the children of Ephraim also stood up against the men that came from the war, saying they had offended against the Most High already and would not add more to their sins. So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and the congregation. The men named by name took the captives, clothed all that were naked among them, shod them, gave them to eat and drink, anointed them, carried the feeble on asses, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren, then returned to Samaria. Even in the middle of the division, these men feared the Most High and would not treat their brethren as slaves.

At that time Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria to help him, for the Edomites had come and smitten Judah and carried away captives, and the Philistines had invaded the cities of the low country and the south of Judah and taken them. The Most High brought Judah low because of Ahaz, for he made Judah naked and transgressed sore against the Most High. Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to him and distressed him but strengthened him not. Ahaz took a portion out of the house of the Most High, the king's house, and the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him. Running to another nation for deliverance from the curses of God never works, then or now.

In the time of his distress Ahaz trespassed yet more against the Most High. He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that smote him, saying, Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel. Ahaz gathered up the vessels of the house of God, cut them in pieces, shut up the doors of the house of the Most High, and made altars in every corner of Jerusalem. This is the pattern of running to a nation that cannot save, the same spirit that trusts in the systems of the world instead of the Most High. Ahaz slept with his fathers and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, but not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his stead. The Most High is the only one who can bring the people out of their condition, then and now.

Ahaz son of Jotham begins to reign over Judah and does not that which is right, but walks in the way of the kings of Israel. He makes his son to pass through the fire after the abominations of the heathen whom the Most High cast out before Israel. He sacrifices and burns incense in the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree, the very idolatry the law forbade. -

Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel come up to war against Jerusalem and besiege Ahaz but cannot overcome him. Syria recovers Elath and drives the Jews out, and Ahaz is left weakened. Rather than trust the Most High, Ahaz sends to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria saying, I am thy servant and thy son, come up and save me. This is much like the nation today looking to Esau as though he were a savior instead of turning to the Most High. Ahaz strips the silver and gold from the house of the Most High and the king's treasures and sends it as a present to Assyria, who then takes Damascus and slays Rezin.

Ahaz goes to Damascus to meet the king of Assyria and sees an altar there, then sends its pattern and workmanship to Urijah the priest. Urijah builds the altar according to the pattern before Ahaz returns, and the king offers his burnt offering, meat offering, drink offering, and peace offering upon it. The true altar was made after the pattern of heavenly things given through Moses, but Ahaz copies a heathen altar he admired in Damascus. Ahaz moves the brazen altar and commands Urijah to make the new altar the place of all the offerings, keeping the brazen altar for himself to inquire by. -

Ahaz cuts off the borders of the bases, removes the laver, and takes down the brazen sea from off the oxen, dismantling the vessels of the temple. He turns the covert for the sabbath and the king's entry away from the house of the Most High for the sake of the king of Assyria. Ahaz sleeps with his fathers and Hezekiah his son reigns in his stead.

cases.name: Josiah at Megiddo
cases.charge: Going to battle against Necho without inquiring of the Lord
cases.summary: The reformer king, promised he would be gathered to his grave in peace, went out against Pharaoh Necho, who was marching to Carchemish and had no quarrel with Judah. Necho sent word that God had commanded him to make haste and that Josiah should not meddle with God, who was with him. Josiah disguised himself and fought anyway.
cases.offense: After Josiah had prepared the temple, Pharaoh Necho came to fight at Carchemish. Josiah went out against him. Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah and warned Josiah not to oppose the God who had commanded him to make haste. Josiah would not turn away. He disguised himself and entered the battle at Megiddo. Chronicles expressly says that he did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God. The king's earlier reforms and devotion to the law did not make this later decision right.
cases.judgment: Archers hit him in the valley of Megiddo; his servants carried him to Jerusalem and he died. Jeremiah lamented for him, and the lament became an ordinance in Israel. The promise of a peaceful grave was kept in the sense that he did not see the evil that followed.
offenseFull: After Josiah had prepared the temple, Pharaoh Necho came to fight at Carchemish. Josiah went out against him. Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah and warned Josiah not to oppose the God who had commanded him to make haste.

Josiah would not turn away. He disguised himself and entered the battle at Megiddo. Chronicles expressly says that he did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God. The king's earlier reforms and devotion to the law did not make this later decision right.

entries.commentary: Josiah keeps a Passover unto the Lord in Jerusalem, and they kill the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, keeping the laws pertaining to the Passover. He sets the priests in their charges, encourages them to the service of the house of the Lord, and tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built and to serve the Lord and his people Israel. He commands them to prepare themselves by their courses and stand in the holy place, then kill the Passover, sanctify themselves, and prepare their brethren to do according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses. -

Josiah gives the people thirty thousand lambs and kids and three thousand bullocks for the Passover offerings, and his princes give willingly to the people, the priests, and the Levites. The service is prepared, the priests stand in their place and the Levites in their courses, they kill the Passover, sprinkle the blood, flay the offerings, and roast the Passover with fire according to the ordinance. The singers, the sons of Asaph, are in their place according to the commandment of David, and the porters wait at every gate so they need not depart from their service.

All the service of the Lord is prepared the same day to keep the Passover and offer burnt offerings on the altar according to the commandment of king Josiah. The children of Israel present keep the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread seven days, and there was no Passover like it kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet; none of the kings of Israel kept such a Passover as Josiah kept in his eighteenth year.

After this, Necho king of Egypt comes up to fight at Carchemish by Euphrates, and Josiah goes out against him though Necho sends word that his war is not with Josiah and that God had commanded him to make haste. Josiah will not turn his face but disguises himself to fight, hearkening not to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and the archers shoot him in the valley of Megiddo. His servants take him from the chariot and bring him to Jerusalem, where he dies and is buried, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourn, and Jeremiah laments for Josiah, written in the Lamentations, a book of the Bible.
The rest of the acts of Josiah and his goodness, according to that which is written in the law of the Lord, and his deeds first and last, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.

Josiah gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, went up to the house of the Most High with the priests, the prophets, and all the people both small and great, and read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant that was found there. Our forefathers had the Bible; the king read it openly, then stood by a pillar and made a covenant before the Lord to walk after him and keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all their heart and soul. All the people stood to the covenant to perform the words written in the book. -

The king commanded Hilkiah and the priests to bring out of the temple all the vessels made for Baal, for the grove, and for all the host of heaven, and he burned them in the fields of Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel. He put down the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places and around Jerusalem, and those that burnt incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon, the planets, and all the host of heaven. When Josiah read the law the fear of the Lord came upon him and he saw why the nation was under judgment, just as a person is cut when they first hear the truth and realize what they have been doing wrong. -

He brought the grove out of the house of the Lord to the brook Kidron, burned it, stamped it to powder, and cast the powder on the graves of the children of the people. He broke down the houses of the sodomites that were by the house of the Lord, where the women wove hangings for the grove; there should be no sodomite among the sons of Israel, yet they had grown so bold as to do this wickedness right beside the temple. He brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the high places where they had burnt incense, and though the priests of the high places did not come up to the altar, they still ate of the unleavened bread among their brethren.

Josiah defiled Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so that no man might make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech. Topheth was the place where the people sacrificed their children, and it had to be defiled because Israel would not stop the evil on its own. -

He took away the horses the kings of Judah had given to the sun and burnt the chariots of the sun with fire. He beat down the altars on the roof of Ahaz's chamber and the altars Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord, and cast their dust into the brook Kidron. He defiled the high places Solomon had built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom, the abominations of the Zidonians, Moabites, and Ammonites, and broke in pieces the images, cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men. This is repentance in action: cleaning house, getting rid of every idol and evil that causes a people to go off from the Lord and to fall under punishment. -

Josiah also destroyed the altar and high place at Bethel that Jeroboam had made when he set up the golden calves, burning it and stamping it small to powder. Turning himself, he spied the sepulchres in the mount, took out the bones, and burnt them upon the altar to pollute it, according to the word the man of God had proclaimed. When told which sepulchre belonged to the man of God who prophesied these things, he said to let him alone and let no man move his bones. -

Josiah also took away all the houses of the high places in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord to anger, and did to them as he had done at Bethel. The northern kingdom had already been carried into captivity by Assyria, so most of the people were gone, yet the idolatrous houses remained. He slew all the priests of the high places upon their altars, burnt men's bones upon them, and returned to Jerusalem.

The king commanded all the people to keep the Passover to the Lord their God as it is written in the book of this covenant. Such a Passover had not been held from the days of the judges nor in all the days of the kings of Israel and Judah, but in the eighteenth year of Josiah this Passover was held in Jerusalem. Reading the book of the law brought the nation back to keeping the appointed feasts in order, just as the feast is kept in order today. -

Josiah also put away the workers with familiar spirits, the wizards, the images, the idols, and all the abominations spied in Judah and Jerusalem, that he might perform the words of the law found by Hilkiah. There was no king before or after him that turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might according to all the law of Moses; he put things in order like a true leader. Nevertheless the Lord did not turn from the fierceness of his great wrath because of the provocations of Manasseh, and said he would remove Judah out of his sight as he had removed Israel and cast off Jerusalem.

Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates, and Josiah went against him and was slain at Megiddo. Josiah got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it, a warning not to enter into quarrels that are not one's own. His servants carried him dead in a chariot from Megiddo to Jerusalem and buried him, and the people took Jehoahaz his son and anointed him king in his father's place.

Jehoahaz was twenty three years old and reigned three months in Jerusalem, and did evil in the sight of the Lord according to all his fathers had done. Pharaohnechoh bound him at Riblah so he might not reign, put the land to a tribute of silver and gold, and made Eliakim the son of Josiah king, turning his name to Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay Pharaoh, exacting the silver and gold of every man of the land, and he also did evil in the sight of the Lord like his forefathers, not like his father Josiah.

Josiah begins to reign at eight years old and reigns thirty-one years, doing that which is right in the sight of the Most High and walking in all the way of David, turning neither to the right nor the left. In his eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the scribe to Hilkiah the priest to gather the silver brought to the house of the Most High and deliver it to the workmen for repairs. The money is given to carpenters, builders, and masons and for timber and hewn stone, and no reckoning is made with them because they dealt faithfully. Josiah rebuilds and reestablishes what Manasseh and Amon destroyed, and he makes sure the workmen are paid, for by the law the workman is worthy of his hire.

Hilkiah the high priest finds the book of the law in the house of the Most High and gives it to Shaphan, who reads it. Manasseh and Amon were so wicked the very book of the law had been lost. Shaphan reports to the king about the money and the workmen, then tells him Hilkiah delivered him a book, and reads it before the king. When the king hears the words of the book of the law he rends his clothes, for the king was meant to read the law before all the people, which the wicked kings had not done. Josiah commands Hilkiah and his servants to inquire of the Most High for him and the people, for great is the wrath kindled against them because their fathers did not hearken to this book. -

Hilkiah and the king's men go to Huldah the prophetess, who dwells in Jerusalem in the college; there were women among the people who were prophetesses, known by their works. Huldah returns the word of the Most High: He will bring evil upon this place and its inhabitants, all the words of the book, because they forsook Him and burned incense to other gods, and His wrath shall not be quenched. But to Josiah, because his heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept before the Most High, the word is that he shall be gathered to his fathers and to his grave in peace, and his eyes shall not see the evil to come. Because Josiah was righteous, repaired the temple, found the book, and began to keep the commandments again, he found mercy; yet the word spoken against Israel for its sin would still come to pass. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Josiah is eight years old when he begins to reign and reigns thirty one years in Jerusalem, and he does that which is right in the sight of the Lord and walks in the ways of David his father, declining neither to the right hand nor to the left. Comparing the ages shows the point: Manasseh began at twelve, Amon at twenty two, and Josiah at eight, yet the youngest was the wisest. Better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished. In the eighth year of his reign, while yet young, he begins to seek after the God of David, and in the twelfth year he begins to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, groves, and images. -

They break down the altars of Baal in his presence, cut down the images and groves, and break the carved and molten images to powder, strowing the dust upon the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. He burns the bones of the priests upon their altars and cleanses Judah and Jerusalem, and does the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, then returns to Jerusalem. -

In the eighteenth year of his reign, when he has purged the land and the house, Josiah sends Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah to repair the house of the Lord his God. The money the Levites had gathered from Manasseh, Ephraim, and all the remnant of Israel and Judah is put into the hands of the workmen, who buy hewn stone and timber for couplings and to floor the houses the kings of Judah had destroyed. The men do the work faithfully under overseers of the Levites, with scribes, officers, and porters, that is security, set over the burdens and the service.

When they bring out the money, Hilkiah the priest finds a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses, the very Bible, and delivers it to Shaphan the scribe. Shaphan carries the book to the king and reads it before him, reporting that all committed to the servants is being done and the money delivered to the workmen. -

When the king hears the words of the law, he rends his clothes and commands Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah to go inquire of the Lord for him and for the remnant left in Israel and Judah. He knows great is the wrath of the Lord poured out because the fathers had not kept the word of the Lord to do all that is written in the book. To inquire of the Lord, one must go to a saint, a chosen prophet who has the word. -

Hilkiah and the men go to Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum, who dwells in the college in Jerusalem, and she declares the word of the Lord God of Israel. She says the Most High will bring evil and all the curses written in the book upon this place, because they forsook him and burned incense to other gods to provoke him to anger. But because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself, wept, and rent his clothes, the Most High will gather him to his fathers in peace so his eyes will not see the evil to come. -

Josiah gathers all the elders, priests, Levites, and all the people great and small, and reads in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant found in the house of the Lord. He stands in his place and makes a covenant before the Lord to walk after him and keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and soul, and causes all present to stand to it. Josiah takes away all the abominations out of all the countries belonging to the children of Israel and makes all present serve the Lord their God, and they depart not from following him all his days. All wisdom is the performance of the law.

The burden of the word of the Lord for Israel, saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him. Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling unto all the people round about, when they shall be in the siege both against Judah and against Jerusalem. In that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it. In that day I will smite every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness; and I will open mine eyes upon the house of Judah. In that day will I make the governors of Judah like an hearth of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire in a sheaf; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left.

The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah. In that day shall the Lord defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David; and the house of David shall be as God, as the angel of the Lord before them. It shall come to pass in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.

I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son. In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land shall mourn, every family apart: the house of David apart, the house of Nathan apart, the house of Levi apart, the family of Shimei apart, and all the families that remain, every family apart, and their wives apart.

verses.text: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him.

But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste: forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not.

Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.
And the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded.

His servants therefore took him out of that chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had; and they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died, and was buried in one of the sepulchres of his fathers. And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day, and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the lamentations.
In his days Pharaoh–nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him.

And his servants carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo, and brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own sepulchre. And the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father’s stead.
But to the king of Judah which sent you to enquire of the Lord, thus shall ye say to him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, As touching the words which thou hast heard;

Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the Lord, when thou heardest what I spake against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord.

Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place. And they brought the king word again.

Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, and humbledst thyself before me, and didst rend thy clothes, and weep before me; I have even heard thee also, saith the Lord.

Behold, I will gather thee to thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered to thy grave in peace, neither shall thine eyes see all the evil that I will bring upon this place, and upon the inhabitants of the same. So they brought the king word again.
In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon.

cases.name: Zedekiah
cases.charge: Breaking his oath to Nebuchadnezzar; stiffening his neck against the Lord's word by Jeremiah
cases.summary: Sworn by God to serve Babylon, Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar and would not humble himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord. Warned to the last that surrender would save the city and his life, he feared the Jews who had defected more than he feared the word.
cases.offense: Zedekiah did evil and would not humble himself before Jeremiah. He also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. Ezekiel exposed the broken covenant through the figure of the vine that turned toward another eagle, seeking Egyptian help. The oath was not made harmless by the fact that it had been sworn to a foreign king. Jeremiah told Zedekiah that surrender would preserve his life and prevent the city from being burned. Zedekiah feared that the Jews who had already fallen to the Chaldeans would abuse him. The prophet assured him that they would not and urged him to obey. The king nevertheless refused the way of escape set before him.
cases.judgment: The city was besieged until famine prevailed. Zedekiah fled by night, but the Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho and brought him to Riblah. His sons were killed before his eyes; then his eyes were put out, and he was bound and taken to Babylon. Jerusalem was burned as Jeremiah had warned. The king who feared the humiliation of surrender suffered a far greater calamity through resistance. God's warning had included mercy, but Zedekiah would not submit to receive it.

The prophet assured him that they would not and urged him to obey. The king nevertheless refused the way of escape set before him.
